audit.summary:
How the relay works (sync/src/index.ts). The Worker (566-601) serves /health and sends /room/<id> (v2) and /v3/room/<43> (v3) upgrades to separate Durable Objects: v3 uses the name "v3:<id>". It rejects any Origin header and applies a per-IP CONN_LIMITER.

SyncRoom.fetch (622-696) does the admission. For v3 it checks roomId == SHA-256(prefix||token). It pins the room's token hash and protocol in one transaction, then runs ensureV3Accounting inside blockConcurrencyWhile. Next it applies the 64-socket cap and accepts the hibernatable socket. The whole fenced snapshot (snapshot-begin, 900 KB pages, snapshot-end, then the live hello/chat-key/loc frames) is built inside blockConcurrencyWhile before the 101 goes back.

Each socket's frames go through a FIFO queue with bounded admission (732-779) and a 200-frame / 4 MiB fixed-window limiter (862-878), then processWebSocketMessage (782-810). Puts and deletes are committed in one storage transaction that covers LWW, the counter window, quota and seq (915-938, 1188-1212). The broadcast and the op-ack go out only after the commit.

A hello is checked (actorId recomputed, Ed25519 verified) before older sessions are fenced. The actor pin is stored durably before the socket is bound and acked. A failed replacement restores the old session. Presence, chat keys and chat counters live only in socket attachments. alarm() removes rooms idle for 7 days using deleteAll.

What is solid:
- v2 and v3 are fully separated.
- Token-to-room binding and the TOFU pin work.
- Parsers are strict and canonical, and frame caps count real UTF-8 bytes.
- Acks are durable.
- No mutation can slip in between a snapshot's begin and end markers.
- Every await is followed by a fresh re-read of the attachment. I found no stale read-modify-write.
- Chat is live-only, as ADR-004 says.
- Worst-case attachments are about 9.5 KB, under the 16 KiB limit. Records are about 700 KB, under the 2 MB SQLite limit. List pages are 100.
- Waking from hibernation keeps bound sessions working (proof S1-G).
- The existing 56 tests all pass.

The problems are in lifecycle and cost:
- Idle expiry wipes the seq and high-water marks that clients rely on.
- A storage write happens on every frame, including every 5-second presence update.
- The relay never checks whether a socket is still alive, so dead sockets fill the 64 slots.
- An exception inside blockConcurrencyWhile resets the whole room.
- Building a snapshot costs roughly records-per-page times more than it should, and every reconnect resends the full room.
- The rate limit closes the socket, which fights the clients' unpaced bulk sync.
- Tombstones are never cleaned up.
- The relay-only limits (CT_MAX, rate budgets) are not in the shared fixture, so neither client checks them before sending.

All proofs ran in a scratch copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cbrooker-Code-TacticalMaps/d9f42208-9d3f-40e1-9b8b-49fa6c488260/scratchpad/s1root/sync/test/audit-s1{,b,c,d}.test.ts and scratchpad/audit-sync/snapshot_chunk_bench.mjs.

findings.title: Idle-TTL deleteAll resets seq/highWater while clients keep replay state: permanent counter-window lockout and a ~1 Hz reconnect loop
findings.description:
alarm() (index.ts:834-847) calls storage.deleteAll() after 7 idle days (IDLE_TTL_MS, index.ts:33). That wipes meta:seq, meta:highWater, meta:auth and every actor pin, not just the objects.

Clients keep durable replay state across the wipe. Their counter is max(localCounter, roomHighWater())+1 (Android SyncReplayState.kt:329, iOS reserveNextCounter). When they return, the re-created relay room has highWater=0, and applyChangeV3 rejects any stamp above highWater+10,000 (index.ts:1193-1195) with op-nack counter-window, retry:false.

Both clients react to counter-window by cancelling the socket (Android SyncManager.kt:2063-2065, iOS SyncManager.swift:3091-3093). Both reset reconnect backoff on hello-ack (Android SyncManager.kt:2236, iOS SyncManager.swift:3552), and the resend reuses the same stamp (SyncReplayState.kt:435-441; iOS recoveryStamp at 2322). The result is an endless reconnect at about 1 s: connect, full snapshot, hello with an actor write, put, nack, cancel.

The snapshot seq also restarts at 0. Every reconnect therefore raises the SECURITY rollback warning (Android SyncManager.kt:1904-1910, iOS 3478). The seq will not climb back while writes are locked out.
findings.failure_scenario:
A unit uses a v3 room for a few weeks, so the room-wide Lamport counter passes 10,000 (each waypoint/drawing edit adds 1). Nobody connects for 7 days (leave, stand-down, weekend plus a week). The alarm fires and deleteAll runs.

The first member back gets an empty snapshot with seq 0 and a rollback warning. It then republishes its local objects at counter above 10,000, and every put is nacked counter-window. Both apps cancel and reconnect about once a second with no end, burning battery and relay CPU and storage writes (a hello epoch write each loop). Devices behind the same NAT also use up the 60/min per-IP CONN_LIMITER, which locks out healthy devices there.

The shared picture on the relay can never be rebuilt. New joiners see an empty map. Only a new join code recovers the room.
findings.suggested_fix:
Relay: on idle expiry, delete only obj:* and actor:* rows and keep meta:auth, meta:protocol, meta:seq and meta:highWater (plus meta:expiredAt), so seq and the counter fence stay monotonic. Alternatively, advertise an explicit expired/epoch flag in snapshot-begin so clients can tell expiry apart from a malicious rollback and deliberately republish.

Document the v3 TTL in ADR-001/README.

Clients: never treat counter-window as 'reconnect and resend the same stamp'. Surface it once and stop the loop, and don't reset backoff when the first post-ack mutation is rejected.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1.test.ts 'S1-A' (ran, passes):
1. hello, then put counters 9,000 and 18,000 (both acked). Close.
2. Set meta:lastActivity to 8 days ago and runDurableObjectAlarm(stub). Expect meta:highWater and meta:seq undefined.
3. Reconnect: snapshot-begin.seq === 0 with 0 items. hello epoch 2, then put counter 18,001. Result is {t:'op-nack', code:'counter-window', retry:false}.

Add client-side tests that a counter-window nack does not produce more than N reconnects per minute.

findings.title: Every handled frame (including 5 s presence) does a durable storage write via touchActivity: large write amplification, and a hard outage on the Workers Free row-write cap
findings.description:
processWebSocketMessage awaits touchActivity() after every put/del/loc/hello/leave/chat-key/chat frame (index.ts:805). touchActivity does storage.put('meta:lastActivity') plus getAlarm() (index.ts:1564-1568). Foreground presence is sent every 5 s on both platforms (UnitSyncPresenceCadence.kt:103, SyncManager.swift:573). That is 720 billed row writes per device per foreground hour, just for liveness, and none of them are needed:
- alarm() already re-arms while any socket exists (index.ts:836-838).
- webSocketClose touches when the last socket leaves (index.ts:825-827).

Each put also writes 5-6 rows: obj, totalRecords, bytes, seq, highWater and lastActivity (index.ts:1206-1210).

If touchActivity throws (for example the Free plan's 100,000 rows written per day, which Cloudflare fails hard once exceeded), the catch at index.ts:806-809 closes the socket with 1011. The connect path fails too, at index.ts:689-693.
findings.failure_scenario:
On the Workers Free plan, about 139 foreground device-hours per day across all rooms (for example 10 devices for 14 h) use up the daily write cap. After that, every loc, put or hello closes the sender's socket with 1011 'storage unavailable'. Every reconnect then fails at touchActivity with a 503 after the snapshot. Sync is down for everyone until 00:00 UTC.

On the Paid plan, the same traffic bills roughly 0.5M writes per always-on device per month that serve no purpose, and each write holds the output gate.
findings.suggested_fix:
Keep lastTouch in memory and write meta:lastActivity only on connect, on the last close, and at most once an hour otherwise. It never needs to be written for loc/chat/chat-key.

Rely on alarm() rescheduling while sockets exist, and have alarm() treat 'sockets present' as activity (write lastActivity there).

Collapse meta:totalRecords, meta:bytes, meta:seq and meta:highWater into one meta row, so a put is 2 writes instead of 6.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1.test.ts 'S1-F' (ran, passes): after hello, a single loc frame changes meta:lastActivity (before < after).

For a regression test, wrap state.storage.put in a counter via runInDurableObject. Send 100 loc frames and assert fewer than 2 writes. Also inject a throwing storage.put for 'meta:lastActivity' and assert the loc is still broadcast and the socket stays open.

findings.title: No relay-side liveness: sockets the server closed (CLOSING) or whose client silently vanished still count toward MAX_CONNECTIONS=64 and can be advertised as live
findings.description:
The capacity check counts every socket from getWebSockets() (index.ts:680). When a flapping device reconnects, its new hello supersedes the old socket: departure is announced and closeSocket(4015) is called (index.ts:1017-1020). If the old client is already gone (Wi-Fi to LTE handover, tunnel, dead zone), it never echoes the close. The socket then stays in getWebSockets() in CLOSING state until the edge's TCP gives up, and the relay has no way to reap it.

Sockets whose client vanished without any server close stay OPEN with hello and presence bound. collectV3Live (index.ts:1440-1455) sends them to late joiners as live members, and peers get no leave until the transport dies. Other server-initiated closes also skip the departure announcement that handleExplicitLeave makes (index.ts:1039-1045), so they have the same problem when the peer does not echo: rate-limit 4008 (index.ts:749/763), oversize 4009, invalid UTF-8 1007, and storage 1011 (index.ts:808).

webSocketError (index.ts:830-832) only aborts the queue. It neither announces nor closes.

There is no application-level heartbeat. setWebSocketAutoResponse and getWebSocketAutoResponseTimestamp are unused, and clients use transport pings only (Android SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:285, iOS SyncManager.swift:1934), which the DO cannot see.
findings.failure_scenario:
A unit moving through patchy coverage: each device flaps every few minutes, and each flap leaves a CLOSING zombie that lasts until the edge drops the dead TCP (typically many minutes). Zombies build up past 63. From then on, every connect, including from devices with perfect connectivity, gets 503 'Room full', and the room is unusable until zombies drain.

In a separate case, a device switches off without a close. Late joiners are shown its hello and last position as a live member (with signed retention up to 65 min), and no leave is ever sent.
findings.suggested_fix:
Count only live sockets toward capacity: getWebSockets().filter(ws => ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN).

Add an auto-response heartbeat: state.setWebSocketAutoResponse(new WebSocketRequestResponsePair('{"t":"ping"}','{"t":"pong"}')), which does not wake the DO. Clients send it every ~25 s. On fetch, and in a short alarm while sockets exist, reap sockets whose getWebSocketAutoResponseTimestamp is older than about 75 s: announceV3Departure('transient'), then close.

Announce the transient departure before every server-initiated close, and in webSocketError.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1c.test.ts 'S1-H' (ran): one actor opens 64 successive v3 sockets with hello epochs 1..64, never echoing the 4015 close on the superseded ones. The 65th upgrade returns 503 'Room full', and the readyState histogram is {OPEN:1, CLOSING:63}, with a single live device.

audit-s1.test.ts 'S1-C' (ran): after a 4008 close with no client echo, the peer receives no leave within 3 s, and a late joiner's post-snapshot live frames include the closed socket's hello. For comparison, S1-C2 shows that when the client does echo, the leave is sent.

findings.title: Any exception inside blockConcurrencyWhile resets the whole room (all sockets 1006); v2 snapshot 'record exceeds snapshot ceiling' is a deterministic room-wide DoS
findings.description:
Cloudflare terminates and resets the object when a blockConcurrencyWhile callback throws. The try/catch around the calls (index.ts:672-677, 686-694) runs too late, and the 503 path is never reached.

In v2, the first snapshot page embeds the live members array (index.ts:1491, 1498). Members can total up to 63 x (8,192-char presence ct + clientId). The first record can be up to CT_MAX=700,000 chars. Once members plus the first record exceed 900,000, the record fails with chunk still empty and sendSnapshot throws (index.ts:1514-1515).

In v3, any transient storage.list/get error inside sendSnapshot or ensureV3Accounting does the same thing: it drops every connected peer instead of only the joining one.
findings.failure_scenario:
A hostile or buggy v2 member opens about 26 sockets with 6 KB presence each and stores one 700 KB object. Every later connect attempt throws inside blockConcurrencyWhile. The DO is marked broken (workerd logs brokennessReason = broken.inputGateBroken) and every existing socket drops with 1006. Clients reconnect, presence rebuilds, and the next join resets the room again.

In v3, one storage hiccup while a single device reconnects disconnects the entire unit at once.
findings.suggested_fix:
Catch inside the callback and return a result: await state.blockConcurrencyWhile(async () => { try { await this.sendSnapshot(...); return true } catch { return false } }). On false, close only the new socket.

For v2, send members as separate post-fence frames, as v3 already does, or bound total members bytes, so a member list can never push a record over the page ceiling.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1.test.ts 'S1-D' (ran):
1. A bystander v2 socket.
2. 26 member sockets, each sending loc with ct=sealed(6000).
3. One put with ct=sealed(520000).
4. A new stub.fetch upgrade throws 'record exceeds snapshot ceiling' instead of returning 503, and the bystander receives close 1006.

The regression test should assert the joiner gets 503 and the bystander stays open.

findings.title: Snapshot chunking re-serializes the whole pending page for every record (O(N x records-per-page)) inside blockConcurrencyWhile, before the 101 is returned
findings.description:
For each record, sendSnapshot builds candidate=[...chunk, record], JSON.stringify's the entire page and TextEncoder-encodes it (index.ts:1512-1518). The cost is about N x F/2 full-record serializations, where F is records per 900 KB page (about 700-1400).

All of this runs under blockConcurrencyWhile (index.ts:688), so the whole room is frozen. The client sees nothing until every page is generated and buffered, because the 101 is returned only at index.ts:695. That also means a full room's snapshot, up to about 50 MB, sits in outbound buffers per concurrent joiner, with no backpressure.

Measured:
- workerd, 9,500 records with 1 KB ciphertext: 855 ms upgrade latency.
- workerd, 6,000 small records: 670 ms.
- Node reproduction of the exact algorithm, 9,900 records: 4.66 s, versus 35 ms with incremental size accounting.

After a deploy or eviction, every client reconnects within about 1 s, and the snapshots run one after another.
findings.failure_scenario:
A mature room with 5-10k objects and 20 devices. A relay deploy drops all sockets, and 20 upgrades queue behind blockConcurrencyWhile at 1-2 s each on edge CPUs. The last devices wait 20-40 s. iOS's 30 s handshake watchdog starts at task.resume() (SyncManager.swift:1666, 659), so it cancels and retries. The DO still finishes the abandoned snapshot, and that leaves another accepted socket counting toward the 64 cap (see S1-03).

The room also processes no puts or presence during those tens of seconds.
findings.suggested_fix:
Serialize each record once: len = utf8Length(JSON.stringify(record)). Keep a running page size (envelope + commas) and flush when running + len would exceed the ceiling. That is O(N) and about 30 ms for a full room.

Optionally, pre-stringify the envelope and join the record strings to avoid re-stringifying.

Consider returning the 101 first and streaming pages, which needs an in-memory per-socket 'snapshot in progress' gate so broadcasts queue behind the fence.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1b.test.ts 'S1-E2' (ran): seed 9,500 obj:* records through runInDurableObject and time openV3Socket. It logged 855 ms against 88 ms for 1,000 records.

scratchpad/audit-sync/snapshot_chunk_bench.mjs (ran) runs the exact algorithm against an incremental one: 4,658 ms vs 35 ms at 9,900 records.

Regression test: assert that the 9,500-record upgrade finishes under about 150 ms and pages remain 900,000 bytes or less.

findings.title: The rate limit closes the socket and discards already-received valid frames, while both clients burst one put per object unpaced: joins or imports with 200+ objects make ~199 objects of progress per full reconnect
findings.description:
Over-budget sockets are closed with 4008, and every queued frame is aborted (index.ts:744-751, 759-765, 862-878). The budget is 200 frames or 4 MiB per 10 s, and the hello, loc frames and client retries all count against it.

Android's syncLocalStateV3 sends every changed object in a tight loop with no pacing (SyncManager.kt:1304-1336). On first join, lastContent is empty, so that is the whole local map. Each delivery is also retried after 1/2/4/8 s (SyncManager.kt:1164-1183), and iOS behaves the same way.

The budget values are not in testdata/sync_protocol_v3.json, so clients cannot comply. README:275 calls the window 'rolling', but the code uses a fixed window that resets at windowStart+10 s. That allows about 400 frames across a window boundary.
findings.failure_scenario:
A user with 800 imported waypoints joins a unit room. The client sends 800 puts. The relay acks 199 (hello was frame 1), closes 4008 and drops the other 601 unanswered. Both apps show an error, back off about 1 s, and download a full snapshot again. This repeats for about 4 cycles, each with a new hello epoch write and a full snapshot, with made-up rate-limit errors in the UI.

Large drawings (up to 700 KB ciphertext each) hit the 4 MiB byte budget after about 5 objects.
findings.suggested_fix:
Publish RATE_MAX_MSGS, RATE_MAX_BYTES and the window semantics in the shared fixture, and have clients pace outbound deliveries with a token bucket (for example 150 frames and 3 MiB per 10 s, retries included). Alternatively, have the relay apply backpressure for well-formed mutations: nack code 'rate' with retry:true and a retry-after, instead of closing and dropping frames. Keep the close for sustained abuse.

Fix the README 'rolling' wording.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1.test.ts 'S1-B' (ran): after hello, send 260 distinct valid put frames back-to-back. The result is close code 4008 after exactly 199 op-acks.

The client regression test should feed 800 local waypoints into syncLocalStateV3 and assert no more than 150 frames go out in any 10 s window.

findings.title: Every reconnect re-streams the entire room; records carry no per-record seq, so incremental resync is impossible
findings.description:
sendSnapshot always lists and sends every obj:* record, tombstones included (index.ts:1507-1524). The stored records (SyncRecordV3, index.ts:53-62) have no commit seq; only the global meta:seq exists (index.ts:1205-1209). The relay therefore cannot answer 'changes since my lastSnapshotSeq'.

On every reconnect, clients re-download and then re-verify (Ed25519 plus AES-GCM) every record. Each reconnect of a 10k-record room also costs 10k billed row reads.
findings.failure_scenario: A device on a flaky LTE link reconnects 20 times a day in a room of 2,000 waypoints (about 2.4 MB). That is about 48 MB of mobile data and 40,000 signature verifications a day with nothing changed, costing battery. With 10k records it adds 200k relay row reads a day for one device, and more snapshot CPU (see S1-05).
findings.suggested_fix: Store each record's commit seq, either in the value plus a 'seq:<padded>' -> id index, or better, move to a SQL table indexed on seq. Clients send their durable lastSnapshotSeq (for example an X-Resume-Seq header). The relay streams only records with seq greater than resume, including tombstones, inside the same fence. It falls back to a full snapshot when resume is above the current seq or below a compaction horizon (see S1-08).
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1d.test.ts 'S1-07' (ran): after 50 puts, two consecutive reconnects with no changes in between each receive all 50 items (seq 50 both times).

Regression test: a reconnect with X-Resume-Seq: 50 receives 0 items, and one with X-Resume-Seq: 40 receives exactly the 10 newer records.

findings.title: Tombstones and actor pins are never compacted and count against MAX_RECORDS=10,000: long-lived rooms hit a permanent 'quota' wall for all new objects
findings.description:
Deletes are stored as full records permanently (index.ts:1191, 1206), and so are actor pins (index.ts:1136-1141, one per device key and per reinstall). All of them count toward MAX_RECORDS and MAX_STORED_BYTES (index.ts:19-20, 1196-1203). The only removal is the 7-day idle wipe (S1-01).

Once the total reaches 10,000, every create gets op-nack quota with retry:false. Clients show 'room is full' and the object never syncs (Android SyncManager.kt:2052).
findings.failure_scenario: A room used for months with steady create/delete churn: temporary markers, route drafts, range rings regenerated on moves, and device reinstalls. It accumulates 10,000 tombstones and actors. From then on, no new object from any member reaches peers, and the only remedy is moving the whole unit to a new join code.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add a tombstone horizon. Purge tombstones older than a retention period (or the oldest beyond a cap), record meta:tombstoneHorizonSeq, and advertise it in snapshot-begin. Clients whose lastSnapshotSeq is below the horizon do a full reconciliation.

At minimum, give tombstones and actor pins their own larger cap, and warn clients proactively (for example from 80% quota) instead of failing hard.
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1d.test.ts 'S1-08' (ran): with meta:totalRecords at 10,000 (modelling retained tombstones), a fresh put gets {t:'op-nack', code:'quota', retry:false}.

The end-to-end version: create and delete 10,000 distinct ids, then put a new id, and assert it is accepted once compaction exists.

findings.title: Relay CT_MAX (700,000 chars) is not in the shared fixture and neither client checks outbound size: oversized objects are nacked 'invalid' and re-uploaded on every local diff and reconnect
findings.description:
applyChangeV3 rejects ct over CT_MAX=700,000 (index.ts:22, 1165), which is below the 1 MiB frame cap (index.ts:25). The rejection is 'invalid' with retry:false.

The fixture constants list only snapshot limits, not CT_MAX or the rate budgets. Android sendPutV3 (SyncManager.kt:1684-1708) and iOS sendPutV3 (SyncManager.swift:~2318) seal and send without checking size, and both clients accept inbound ct up to 1,048,576 (SyncManager.kt:1760, SyncManager.swift:898).

After the nack the pending delivery is dropped but lastContent is never set. syncLocalState therefore sends the object again on every later debounced local change and on every reconnect (SyncManager.kt:1316-1322). If the ct is above about 1 MiB, the client transport refuses the send (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:293). The retry budget then runs out and the socket is cancelled (SyncManager.kt:1175-1181).
findings.failure_scenario: A user imports a GPS track or draws a freehand polygon with about 20k vertices, so the sealed ct exceeds 700 KB. It never syncs. Every later edit to any object re-uploads the roughly 700 KB object and brings back the 'rejected a change as invalid' error. Above about 1 MiB, this becomes a reconnect cycle.
findings.suggested_fix: Add CT_MAX, MAX_FRAME_BYTES, RATE_MAX_MSGS and RATE_MAX_BYTES to testdata/sync_protocol_v3.json and assert them in all three suites. Clients refuse to enqueue an object whose sealed ct exceeds CT_MAX, with a per-object 'too large to sync' state that stops re-upload until the content changes. Alternatively, raise CT_MAX to fit the frame cap (about 1,040,000).
findings.proving_test:
audit-s1d.test.ts 'S1-09' (ran): put with ct=sealed(525003), which is 700,004 chars, gets {t:'op-nack', code:'invalid', retry:false}.

Client test: a drawing whose sealed ct exceeds the fixture CT_MAX is never passed to sendFrame, and a second syncLocalState does not re-send it.

findings.title: README/ADR drift from relay behaviour
findings.description:
The docs differ from the code in five places:
1. README:275 says the rate window is 'rolling'. The code uses a fixed window (index.ts:869-873).
2. README:9-10 says v2 is available 'only for compatibility with existing 2: rooms'. The relay will still TOFU-create new v2 rooms (index.ts:649-669).
3. The op-ack/op-nack delivery protocol and its codes (stale, not-found, counter-window, quota, storage, session-replaced, session-mismatch, hello-required, invalid), and the leave frame variants (transient, explicit, replaced), are not specified in README or ADR-001.
4. The 7-day idle wipe of v3 rooms, and what it does to client replay state, is not documented for v3 (only ADR-001 Consequences mentions it for v2).
5. The README v2 table lists del as {id, v, by}, but the relay requires a sealed ct.
findings.failure_scenario: Self-hosters and client implementers build against the documented contract. Examples: expecting a rolling limiter, not handling counter-window or quota, and assuming rooms persist. The result is the interop failures in S1-01, S1-06 and S1-09.
findings.suggested_fix: Document the fixed-window budget, the ack/nack/leave frames and codes, TTL semantics and v2 creation policy in README and ADR-001. Add those constants to the shared fixture.
findings.proving_test: Doc review. Add a fixture-driven relay test that asserts each documented nack code and leave variant is actually emitted.

verdicts.reasoning:
Root cause restated: alarm() (sync/src/index.ts:834-847) runs storage.deleteAll() after IDLE_TTL_MS=7d (index.ts:33), wiping meta:seq, meta:highWater, meta:auth and actor pins along with objects. The relay counter fence reads the fresh meta:highWater (defaults to ZERO_COUNTER) and rejects stamp.counter > highWater+10,000 with 'counter-window', retry:false (index.ts:1193-1195, 1226).

Clients never adopt the relay's highWater. Android reserveLocalPut uses max(localCounter, roomHighWater())+1 (SyncReplayState.kt:329), and roomHighWater() is purely local (SyncReplayState.kt:450-455). iOS reserveNextCounter is localCounter+1 (SyncReplayState.swift:199-203). ADR-001 section 10 says highWater is a diagnostic hint only.

The loop is real on both platforms:
- A counter-window nack triggers cancel (Android SyncManager.kt:2063-2065; iOS SyncManager.swift:3091-3093).
- Backoff resets on hello-ack (Android SyncManager.kt:2236, base 1 s per SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:17; iOS SyncManager.swift:3552, PresenceQuality.swift:5).
- v3 does NOT clear lastContent on reconnect (Android SyncManager.kt:1062-1073 only clears for v2; iOS 1630-1643 likewise), so a nacked edit is re-sent with the same recovered stamp (Android SyncReplayState.kt:435-441 via SyncManager.kt:1318-1320; iOS 2293-2298, 2322). Result: roughly 1 Hz reconnect with a full snapshot, a hello, an actor-row write, then a nack.
- The rollback warning fires every cycle (Android SyncManager.kt:1904-1910; iOS 3478 wasStale).

ADR-001 documents idle expiry only for v2 (ADR-001:411, 458). I re-ran the auditor's S1-A in my own copy: after the alarm, meta:highWater and meta:seq are undefined, snapshot seq is 0, and put 18,001 gets {op-nack, counter-window, retry:false}.

Preconditions: the room Lamport counter must exceed 10k (reachable with one or two KML/GeoJSON imports) and every member must stay offline for 7 days. 'Permanent' holds when all members are mature, because a fresh device can only raise highWater by 1 per write. High is fair.

processWebSocketMessage awaits touchActivity() after every handled put/del/loc/hello/leave/chat-key/chat frame (index.ts:793-805). touchActivity does storage.put('meta:lastActivity') plus getAlarm() (index.ts:1564-1568). Presence is sent every 5 s in the foreground on both platforms (UnitSyncPresenceCadence.kt:102, SyncManager.swift:573).

The write is redundant:
- alarm() re-arms whenever getWebSockets() is non-empty (index.ts:836-838), which includes hibernated sockets.
- webSocketClose touches when the last socket leaves (index.ts:825-827).
- connect touches at index.ts:689.

Cloudflare docs confirm KV put() is billed as rows written. The Workers Free plan allows 100,000 rows written per day, and 'If you exceed any one of the free tier limits, further operations of that type will fail with an error' (developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/pricing). Incoming WS messages bill at 20:1 against a 100k/day request cap, so without touchActivity the write cap would not bind for presence at all.

When the cap is hit, a loc is broadcast (index.ts:1429) and then the socket is closed 1011 (index.ts:806-809). Every connect also fails: touchActivity at index.ts:689 throws after the full snapshot has been sent, which leads to closeSocket plus 503. So sync is down for all rooms on that account until 00:00 UTC.

The README pitches self-hosting on the user's own account and wrangler.jsonc notes Free-plan compatibility, so Free-plan deployment is plausible. 139 device-hours per day is a single mid-size unit. S1-F re-ran and passed (lastActivity changes on one loc). High for Free-plan deployments; on Paid it is a minor cost, not an outage.

Root cause is real. The capacity check counts every socket from getWebSockets() (index.ts:680), with no readyState filter, no setWebSocketAutoResponse and no timestamp-based reaping (grep finds none). Cloudflare's State API docs state that getWebSockets 'may still return WebSockets even after ws.close has been called ... the connection is in the CLOSING readyState' when no close comes back and no disconnect has been detected.

Superseding a session calls closeSocket(4015) on the old one (index.ts:1017-1020). The collectV3Live filter only skips fenced sockets (index.ts:1447). I re-ran S1-H: the 65th upgrade gets 503 'Room full' with a readyState histogram of {OPEN:1, CLOSING:63}.

I downgraded severity for two reasons:
1. The local proof relies on an in-process test client that never echoes close (compat date 2025-09-01, before web_socket_auto_reply_to_close). Real live clients do echo, and S1-C2 shows the leave is then announced via webSocketClose (index.ts:821-824).
2. In production, zombies only arise when the TCP path is dead (for example an IP change). They persist only until the edge's TCP retransmit timeout, which fires within minutes because peers' 5 s loc broadcasts keep data flowing to the dead socket.

Exhausting 64 slots therefore needs a large room (roughly 15-30+ devices) flapping repeatedly within that window. That is plausible but an edge case, not the typical 4-12 device unit.

The ghost-member half (an OPEN socket from a vanished client being advertised as live until TCP death) is also real but bounded by the same timeout. It is partly by design: transient closes are meant to retain last-known position. The fix (count only OPEN sockets, auto-response heartbeat plus reaping) is correct. What would pin down the magnitude: measuring how long a CLOSING socket survives on production workerd after its client drops its IP.

Cloudflare docs (Durable Objects State API, blockConcurrencyWhile): 'If the callback throws an exception, the object will be terminated and reset ... enclose the body of your callback in a try...catch.' Both bCW callbacks can throw without an internal catch: ensureV3Accounting (index.ts:673) and sendSnapshot (index.ts:688). The outer try/catch cannot prevent the reset.

The v2 trigger is precise. The first page embeds members (index.ts:1491, 1498). If the key-order-first record plus members exceed 900,000 bytes while the chunk is empty, sendSnapshot throws 'record exceeds snapshot ceiling' (index.ts:1513-1515).

I re-ran S1-D. stub.fetch threw 'record exceeds snapshot ceiling', workerd logged 'brokennessReason = broken.inputGateBroken', and the bystander got 1006.

The v2 trigger needs a hostile or buggy insider on legacy v2, choosing an id that sorts first. Honest presence (~1-2 KB x 63) plus CT_MAX (700k) stays under 900k. For v3 no deterministic trigger exists: a record is at most CT_MAX+~300 bytes and there are no members. It needs a storage read error. One plausible source is Free-plan row-read cap exhaustion (5M/day). Each connect reads every record (S1-07), and the reconnect loops in S1-01/S1-09 can burn that cap, after which every connect resets the room and drops every peer.

Medium stands: an edge case with room-wide blast radius.

sendSnapshot builds candidate=[...chunk, record] and JSON.stringify+TextEncoder-encodes the whole pending page for every record (index.ts:1512-1518). That is O(N x records-per-page), all inside blockConcurrencyWhile and before the 101 is returned (index.ts:684-695).

I verified this independently in workerd. I ran the same seeded-room benchmark against the current code and against a patched copy that serializes each record once and tracks a running byte total. Page counts and max frame bytes were identical (899,873 / 899,549):

| Records (ct chars) | Current | Patched |
|---|---|---|
| 500 (300) | 23-26 ms | 2 ms |
| 2,000 (300) | 182-195 ms | 4-5 ms |
| 6,000 (300) | 606-644 ms | 11-13 ms |
| 9,500 (750) | 858-904 ms | 32-35 ms |

The Node reproduction (4.6 s vs 36 ms) overstates the absolute cost relative to workerd, but the complexity claim holds.

The auditor's '20-40 s' tail is inflated: 20 joiners x ~0.9 s is about 18 s of serialized build time at near-max room size. It matters mainly for rooms of several thousand records. It interacts badly with iOS's absolute 30 s handshake budget (SyncManager.swift:659, 1666, 1854-1882), which is armed at task.resume() and never re-armed per page. I did not verify the side claim that an abandoned upgrade leaves an extra accepted socket.

Medium is fair: meaningful inefficiency with an O(N) fix.

Relay side: the per-socket budget is 200 frames / 4 MiB per window, and exceeding it closes 4008 and aborts queued frames (index.ts:744-751, 759-765, 862-878). The window is fixed, not rolling: it resets when now-windowStart exceeds 10 s (index.ts:869-873).

Client side: both clients send every changed object in a tight loop with no pacing or in-flight cap:
- Android: syncLocalStateV3 (SyncManager.kt:1304-1336) calls queueDelivery, which calls sendFrame immediately (SyncManager.kt:1157-1162).
- iOS: syncLocalStateV3 (SyncManager.swift:2270-2298) calls queueDelivery, which calls task.send immediately (SyncManager.swift:2213-2218).
- Both apply per-delivery retries of 1/2/4/8 s.

On a first join, all local waypoints and drawings are pushed; syncLocalState builds `current` from the full stores (SyncManager.kt:1258-1273). The rate budgets are absent from testdata/sync_protocol_v3.json 'constants'.

I re-ran S1-B: close 4008 after exactly 199 op-acks. It does converge: unacked items return via forcedLocalDiff/lastContent and each cycle makes at least 199 objects of progress. So the cost is repeated full snapshots, hello writes and spurious errors, not data loss. For large drawings the byte budget allows only ~5 x 700 KB per window.

The README 'rolling' wording is wrong (README:275, and the code comment at index.ts:741). Medium confirmed.

sendSnapshot lists and sends every obj:* record, tombstones included, on every connect (index.ts:1507-1524). SyncRecordV3 has no commit seq (index.ts:53-62); only the global meta:seq exists (index.ts:1205-1209). So the relay cannot serve 'changes since lastSnapshotSeq', even though both clients persist lastSnapshotSeq (SyncReplayState.kt:55, 177).

The re-run S1-07 shows two unchanged reconnects each receiving all 50 items at seq 50.

This is a design limitation rather than a bug, but the user's stated goals (flaky mobile, battery, bandwidth, relay cost) make it material. Every reconnect costs:
- about room-size bytes of mobile data;
- N Ed25519 + AES-GCM verifications on the client;
- N billed row reads on the relay.

On iOS it compounds into a hard failure. The 30 s handshake budget is absolute from task.resume() and never re-armed per page (SyncManager.swift:1666, 1854-1882), unlike Android's 20 s progress timer re-armed on every page (SyncManager.kt:1902, 1934, 1975). So an iOS device on a slow link can never finish connecting to a large room. Medium.

How the quota fills:
- A delete of an existing object keeps the record (the total is unchanged) and stores a full sealed ct (index.ts:1166, 1191-1206).
- A rid-bearing delete of an unknown id adds a new tombstone record.
- Actor pins add +1 each (index.ts:1136-1143).
- Every distinct object id ever created therefore occupies a MAX_RECORDS slot permanently (index.ts:19, 1196-1203).
- The only removal is the 7-day idle deleteAll (S1-01), which itself breaks counters.

Once the total reaches 10,000, every create gets op-nack quota with retry:false. The user cannot free space by deleting objects. Android shows 'room is full' (SyncManager.kt:2052); iOS does the same (SyncManager.swift:3073-3074).

I re-ran S1-08, which models 10,000 records via meta:totalRecords, and got {op-nack, quota, retry:false}. The README documents tombstone retention as intentional (README:28-30), but the permanent wall is still a real failure. iOS KML import allows up to 10,000 features in one import (KMLImporter.swift:18), so the churn needed is reachable faster than 'months'. Medium.

Relay side: CT_MAX=700,000 (index.ts:22) is enforced with 'invalid', retry:false (index.ts:1165). testdata/sync_protocol_v3.json 'constants' has no CT_MAX, MAX_FRAME_BYTES or rate budgets (only SNAPSHOT_FRAME_MAX_BYTES and client snapshot caps). Neither client checks outbound sealed size against 700k. The clients' only size constant is the 1 MiB inbound cap (SyncManager.kt:1760, SyncManager.swift:898).

700k to 1 MiB band: after an 'invalid' nack the delivery is dropped (no cancel, since 'invalid' is not in the cancel set at SyncManager.kt:2063 / swift:3091), and lastContent is not set. So every later local diff and every reconnect re-sends the same frame with the recovered stamp, and the error is re-raised each time.

Above 1 MiB, the auditor only traced Android:
- Android: the transport refuses the send (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:291-293), the 1/2/4/8 s retries run out, then ws.cancel (SyncManager.kt:1175-1181), giving about a 16 s reconnect cycle.
- iOS is worse. encodedFrame/queueDelivery do not bound outbound size (SyncManager.swift:2195-2199, 2213-2218). The relay closes 4009 (index.ts:704-707), and iOS treats it as a generic disconnect (no close-code handling). Backoff was reset at hello-ack (3552), and syncLocalStateV3 re-sends right after hello-ack (3565-3575). The result is about a 1 s reconnect loop with a full-room snapshot each cycle.

This is reachable: iOS KML import permits up to 100,000 coordinates (KMLImporter.swift:19), and a ~20k-vertex LineString seals to more than 1 MiB.

I re-ran S1-09 (700,004 chars gives invalid/retry:false). I raised severity from medium to high because a plausible action (importing a long track with sync on) produces a sustained reconnect loop that burns battery and data.

All five drift items verified:
1. README:275 says 'rolling 10-second window', while index.ts:869-873 implements a fixed window (the code comment at index.ts:741 also says 'rolling').
2. README:9-10 says v2 is 'only for compatibility with existing 2: rooms', yet fetch TOFU-creates any new v2 room (index.ts:649-669), with no protocol gate.
3. op-ack/op-nack, their codes and the leave variants (transient/explicit/replaced) appear nowhere in sync/README.md, ADR-001 or testdata (grep for 'op-ack' in docs/, testdata/ and README returns nothing).
4. ADR-001 mentions idle expiry only for v2 (ADR-001:411, 458); the v3 TTL is undocumented.
5. The README v2 table lists del as {id, v, by}, but applyChange requires a valid ct for deletes too (index.ts:905).

Documentation only, so low.

verify.missed:
Missed or under-described items. I verified these in code; the memory item still needs a runtime check.

1. **iOS vs Android handshake-timeout divergence (interop/stability).**
   - iOS arms one absolute 30 s v3 handshake timer at task.resume() (ios/TacticalMaps/Sync/SyncManager.swift:659, 1666, 1854-1882) and never re-arms it per snapshot page.
   - Android uses a 20 s progress timer re-armed on snapshot-begin, on every snapshot page and on snapshot-end (android/app/src/main/java/com/tacmap/sync/SyncManager.kt:1764, 1902, 1934, 1975).
   - The relay builds the entire snapshot before the 101 (sync/src/index.ts:686-695) and always streams the full room (S1-07). An iOS device on a slow or flaky link in a large room (e.g. a ~7 MB snapshot at under ~2 Mbit/s effective) can therefore never complete a connection, while Android on the same link succeeds.
   - Proving test: an iOS unit test with a fake transport delivering 10 snapshot pages 5 s apart; assert no timeout while pages keep arriving.

2. **S1-09 iOS escalation.** iOS does not bound outbound frame size (SyncManager.swift:2195-2199, 2213-2218).
   - An object sealed to more than 1 MiB gets relay close 4009 (index.ts:704-707), with no client close-code handling.
   - Backoff resets at hello-ack (3552), then an immediate re-send (3565-3575), so the loop runs at about 1 Hz with a full snapshot per cycle.
   - It is reachable via KML import (KMLImporter.swift:19 allows 100k coordinates).

3. **Unbounded snapshot buffering (needs a runtime check).**
   - sendSnapshot sends every page into the server socket before the 101 is returned (index.ts:684-695), so nothing can drain during the build.
   - A near-full room (MAX_STORED_BYTES 50 MB, clients accept up to 52 MiB) buffers the whole room in the DO for each joiner. A second joiner may arrive before a slow mobile client drains the first.
   - With 2+ concurrent joiners this could exceed the 128 MB isolate limit and reset the object, dropping all peers. Miniflare cannot show this; it needs a production-like memory test.

4. **Free-plan read-cap compounding.**
   - Each connect reads every record (S1-07), and the ensureV3Accounting/sendSnapshot reads run inside blockConcurrencyWhile.
   - The 1 Hz reconnect loops (S1-01, S1-09) can burn the Free plan's 5M rows/day read cap: about 10 minutes for a 10k-record room.
   - After that, every connect throws inside bCW and resets the room for all peers (the S1-04 mechanism, documented reset behaviour).

5. **Closes are advisory in some paths (low).**
   - For the 4009 and 1007 paths, closeSocket's abortSocketQueue is a no-op when no queue exists (index.ts:849-855). A later frame on the CLOSING socket creates a fresh accepting queue and is processed (index.ts:732-739). A 4008 queue is likewise deleted once drained (index.ts:776-778).
   - No corruption follows: commits are atomic, and the ack send on a closed socket is caught.

6. **Hypothesis tested and not reproduced.** I checked whether the room-wide ROOM_PENDING_MAX_MSGS=512 (index.ts:30, 744-746) closes well-behaved sockets when peers burst. Five hello'd sockets each blasting 150 precomputed puts were all fully acked with no closes, so there is no finding there.

audit.summary:
How it works: Android: SyncManager.connect() (SyncManager.kt:1036-1144) opens one Java-WebSocket 1.6.0 client through SyncWebSocketTransport (bounded Draft_6455, 1 MiB frame cap, fragment and wire-frame budgets, no compression, no redirects, 20 s connection-lost ping at KEEPALIVE_SECONDS). Reader-thread callbacks are sent to the main dispatcher via dispatchSocketCallback. That hop checks the socket and generation (isCurrentSocketCallback), and SyncInboundCallbackGate applies backpressure with a 10 s drain limit. v3 states are CONNECTING → SNAPSHOTTING (snapshot-begin/pages/end, then signed hello) → CONNECTED on hello-ack. A 20 s progress watchdog is armed at onOpen and on each snapshot frame. On a drop, handleSocketEnded reconnects with SyncReconnectBackoff (1 s×2^n, ±20%, 30 s cap), which resets only after hello-ack. UnitSyncRuntime owns lifecycle: on onPause it either moves the manager to egress-only background presence (location FGS feeds GPS fixes), suspends it, or disposes it. iOS: a @MainActor SyncManager uses URLSessionWebSocketTask. The receive loop re-arms after each main-actor hop. There is a 30 s absolute v3 handshake timer from connect(), and a sendPing every 20 s with an 8 s pong watchdog. Backoff is the same as Android. updateLifecycle (driven by ContentView scenePhase, app lock and DataKey state) keeps an opted-in connected socket for background presence and drops all inbound frames while not foreground. Otherwise it closes the socket, and a return to foreground always reconnects with a new snapshot.

What is solid: socket and generation fencing on every callback, timer and retry on both platforms, and stale sockets never mutate state. There is at most one live socket. A join-code change tears down the old socket (Android sends a signed leave first). Every failure goes through bounded, jittered backoff, so there is no hot loop. Wire-level inbound bounds are enforced before allocation. Protocol pings are auto-answered by Cloudflare without waking the hibernated DO. Disposal is serialized with secret zeroing (SyncLifecycleGate). All protocol state is confined to one thread (Android main, iOS MainActor).

The problems cluster in these areas:
- no pre-open timeout on Android
- slow-link and main-thread-bound handshake timeouts
- lifecycle divergence: Android drops room membership on pause, and iOS keeps retrying deliveries in background
- background sessions that are fragile and silently end, and that waste battery
- a live receive budget equal to the relay's per-sender allowance
- no use of HTTP status, close code or reachability signals

Evidence: I ran a relay probe in a scratch copy (scratchpad/s2root/sync/test/s2_budget.test.ts). In 155 ms the relay delivered 200 frames to a receiver and 199 op-acks to the sender without closing either. A reconnect-storm model (scratchpad/audit-sync/storm_sim.py) shows rooms with 56 or more foreground members never settling after a relay restart.

findings.title: Android destroys Unit Sync room membership on any Activity pause unless v3 + Share location + background opt-in are all on (iOS keeps the room)
findings.description: MainActivity.onPause (MainActivity.kt:320-336) calls UnitSyncRuntime.onActivityPausing (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:149-175). A room is kept only if optedInV3Location = backgroundUnitSyncLocation && canArmBackgroundLocationService(). canArm requires protocol 3, a '3:' room and presenceConfig.shareLocation (SyncManager.kt:377-379). Otherwise the code sets manager=null and calls dispose() (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:169-174). clearRoomStateAfterDispose nulls the room and keys (SyncManager.kt:889-924). The join code is not persisted anywhere. On resume, acquireForeground builds a fresh OFFLINE manager (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:103-106), and SyncDialog's code field starts empty (SyncDialog.kt:91). suspendUntilForegroundStores (SyncManager.kt:421-437) already provides a safe socket-less retention path, but it is gated on the location opt-in. iOS instead keeps room, keys and wantConnected across background (pauseConnectionForBackground, SyncManager.swift:1817-1831) and reconnects on return (SyncManager.swift:992-994). This is a cross-platform lifecycle divergence.
findings.failure_scenario: An Android user in a v3 room turns off 'Share my location' (SyncDialog.kt:361-363) for OPSEC, or taps 'Stop sharing' in the background notification (BackgroundUnitSyncLocationService.kt:84-87 -> UnitSyncRuntime.userStoppedBackgroundSharing persists backgroundUnitSyncLocation=false). They then open the file picker, take a call or switch to a messenger for 5 s. onPause disposes the manager. On return the map shows no Unit Sync room, peers see a transient departure, and the user must re-obtain and re-type the secret join code. v2 rooms are always lost on pause. An iOS member doing the same keeps the room and auto-reconnects.
findings.suggested_fix: In onActivityPausing, route every active room (v3 regardless of location opt-in, plus a v2 equivalent) through suspendUntilForegroundStores(). That keeps derived room keys in the app-scoped runtime with no socket or egress and reconnects in attachForegroundStores. Dispose only on explicit leave or process/key-lifetime end. If secrets must not outlive the pause for policy reasons, persist the join code sealed under the mission DEK and auto-rejoin after unlock, matching iOS behaviour.
findings.proving_test: Robolectric UnitSyncRuntime test: acquireForeground -> manager.join("3:<fixture code>") -> updatePresenceConfig(shareLocation=false) -> onActivityPausing() -> onActivityForegrounded() -> acquireForeground(...). Assert lease.manager.room.value == "3:<fixture code>" and that connect() was attempted. Today room.value is null and a new manager instance is returned. Repeat with opsec.setBackgroundUnitSyncLocation(false) and with a '2:' code.

findings.title: Android has no timeout between TCP connect and WebSocket open: a stalled TLS/upgrade leaves the client stuck in CONNECTING forever
findings.description: connect() sets Status.CONNECTING and creates the socket (SyncManager.kt:1061, 1092-1143). Neither v3HandshakeTimeout nor v2SnapshotTimeout is armed until the onOpen callback (SyncManager.kt:1094-1104). The transport's only timeouts are the 10 s TCP connect timeout (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:131, 243-248) and Java-WebSocket's connection-lost pinger (connectionLostTimeout, :283-286). In Java-WebSocket 1.6.0 the pinger starts only in WebSocketClient.onWebsocketOpen, which I checked with javap: startConnectionLostTimer is called only there. The library never calls setSoTimeout or setKeepAlive. After TCP connects, the TLS handshake and the wait for 'HTTP/1.1 101' are unbounded blocking reads. If the server response is black-holed and the client has no outstanding data (request already ACKed), no TCP retransmission timer runs and no callback ever fires, so handleSocketEnded and the reconnect never happen. iOS arms its 30 s handshake timer before resume() (SyncManager.swift:1663-1667) and also has URLSession's request timeout, so it recovers.
findings.failure_scenario: In patchy cellular coverage (vehicle on the move, or a satellite/PEP link that spoofs SYN-ACK), a reconnect attempt completes TCP. The path then drops for longer than the relay edge's retransmit budget while the 101 or ServerHello is in flight. The Android client shows 'Connecting…' indefinitely even after coverage returns. No reconnect is scheduled, and presence and edits stop until the user leaves and rejoins or backgrounds the app.
findings.suggested_fix: Arm the handshake watchdog in connect() immediately after creating the socket, not in onOpen. For example, call scheduleV3HandshakeTimeout(socket, generation) (and the v2 equivalent) right after newWebSocket, using an absolute 'open' deadline of about 15-20 s. On expiry, cancel() the socket so handleSocketEnded reconnects with backoff. Optionally also set a socket read timeout during the pre-open phase via a custom SocketFactory or setSocketFactory.
findings.proving_test: JVM test with a loopback ServerSocket that accepts connections and never writes (ws:// loopback is allowed by RelayEndpointPolicy in tests). Join a v3 room with shortened timeouts and advance 60 s. Assert that the server saw at least 2 accepted connections and status left CONNECTING. Today it accepts exactly 1 and status stays CONNECTING.

findings.title: Handshake watchdogs ignore bandwidth: iOS 30 s absolute deadline and Android 20 s per-message deadline make larger rooms un-joinable on slow links, re-downloading the full snapshot on every retry
findings.description: iOS arms SyncConnectionWatchdogPolicy.handshakeTimeout = 30 s once, at connect(), before resume (SyncManager.swift:659, 1665-1667, 1854-1883). Nothing re-arms it on snapshot progress. It covers DNS, TLS, the relay's pre-101 snapshot build, the full download, the main-actor verification and apply in finishSnapshotV3 (3455-3533), and the hello round trip. The iOS v2 10 s snapshot timeout also starts before TCP/TLS (1659-1662, 1971). Android re-arms a 20 s watchdog on onOpen and after each complete message (SyncManager.kt:1764, 1102, 1902, 1934, 1975), so any single snapshot page must fully arrive within 20 s. The relay packs pages up to SNAPSHOT_FRAME_BYTES = 900 kB (index.ts:26, 1499-1517) and rooms may hold 50 MB (index.ts:20). A timeout calls handleDisconnect/socket.cancel, and backoff is not reset (resets happen only at hello-ack, SyncManager.kt:2236 / SyncManager.swift:3552). Every retry therefore restarts the whole snapshot.
findings.failure_scenario: On a 384 kbps 3G link, iOS cannot join any room whose snapshot exceeds roughly 1.2 MB (about 3.3 MB at 1 Mbps). On EDGE (about 150 kbps), Android fails whenever the first 900 kB page takes over 20 s, and iOS fails for rooms over about 0.5 MB. Both retry forever at up to 30 s intervals, each attempt downloading the room again: tens to hundreds of MB per hour of cellular data, with the relay re-reading every record. The member never converges while on that link.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the watchdog progress-based on bytes, not messages or wall-clock totals. iOS: re-arm the timeout on every received snapshot frame, and do the same with a separate pre-open deadline. Android: pass per-chunk read progress from the reader thread, for example by bumping a volatile lastByteNanos in BoundedDraft.processFrame for continuation frames and in onWebsocketPong, and time out only when no bytes arrive for N seconds. Exclude local CPU apply time: pause the watchdog while finishSnapshotV3 or snapshot-end runs. Longer term, add incremental resume (see S2-12) so retries do not restart from zero.
findings.proving_test: Integration: local relay (wrangler dev) behind toxiproxy with a 150 kbps bandwidth toxic, room seeded with about 1.5 MB of records via the relay test helpers. Assert each client reaches CONNECTED within 3 attempts and that total bytes received are under 2x the snapshot size. Today iOS times out at 30 s every attempt and Android times out on the first 900 kB page. Unit (Android): fake SyncWebSocket that delivers snapshot-begin and then the first page after 25 s under a TestDispatcher. Assert no failSnapshot or handshake timeout while bytes are flowing.

findings.title: Client live receive budget (200 frames/10 s across all senders) equals the relay's per-sender allowance: one bulk import disconnects every member; large rooms thrash after a relay restart
findings.description: Both clients reject the 201st application frame in a 10 s LIVE window and close their own socket (iOS SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:111-113, 142-151 via SyncManager.swift:1703-1714; Android SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:94, 103-105 via SyncManager.kt:1779-1795 -> rejectInboundFrame). The relay allows each sender 200 msgs / 4 MiB per 10 s (index.ts:27-29, 862-878) and broadcasts every stored put/del (944, 1218), hello (1027), chat-key (1311) and loc (1429) to every other socket. It also returns an op-ack per put to the sender. Senders do not pace: syncLocalStateV3 emits every diff in one burst (Android SyncManager.kt:1304-1336; iOS syncLocalStateV3). Backoff resets at hello-ack (SyncManager.kt:2236, SyncManager.swift:3552), so a trip right after authentication reconnects in about 1 s. I ran a probe in a scratch copy of the relay (scratchpad/s2root/sync/test/s2_budget.test.ts). The relay delivered hello + 199 puts (200 frames) to a receiver and 199 op-acks to the sender in 155 ms without closing either, so any further frame (such as one presence update) trips the client budget. A discrete-event model of the real rules (scratchpad/audit-sync/storm_sim.py) shows rooms of 56 or 64 foreground members never stabilise after a relay restart: over 1,000 budget trips in 180 s, with 0 members stable. Rooms of 48 or fewer converge.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) A member imports a KML with about 190 or more placemarks, or 4 or more large drawings totalling 4 MiB or more. Every other member and the sender itself (from its op-acks) exceed the budget, close their sockets with 1008, reconnect, and download the full snapshot. Imports larger than 200 objects repeat this ceil(N/200) times, and the sender is also closed by the relay with 4008. (b) A Cloudflare release or DO restart drops a 56-64 member room. Each rejoin broadcasts about 3 frames to everyone, on top of 126 presence frames per 10 s. Clients trip, rejoin after about 1 s, and generate more joins, so the room never converges.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the live receive budget scale with room size and sit comfortably above what the relay can legitimately deliver. For example, allow at least RATE_MAX_MSGS × active senders, or budget only bytes with a generous frame cap, and count relay acks for your own requests separately. Add sender-side pacing: send at most about 100 frames per 10 s from syncLocalStateV3 and queue the rest. Reset reconnect backoff only after a session has stayed healthy for about 60 s, not at hello-ack. Optionally have the relay coalesce join-time hello/chat-key/loc fan-out.
findings.proving_test: Run scratchpad/s2root/sync/test/s2_budget.test.ts (passes: 200 frames delivered in about 155 ms without close). Client unit tests on both platforms: feed SyncLiveReceiveBudget/admit 199 put frames plus 2 loc frames within 1 s in LIVE phase and assert all are admitted (today the 201st returns false and closes the socket). Run python3 scratchpad/audit-sync/storm_sim.py after changing the budget rule and assert N=64 converges (0 trips after 60 s).

findings.title: iOS keeps retrying unacknowledged deliveries after leaving foreground while discarding their acks, which kills the opted-in background presence socket about 23 s later
findings.description: updateLifecycle(foregroundReady:false, …) clears chat secrets but not outbound deliveries (SyncManager.swift:965-1008). While not foreground, the receive loop discards every inbound frame, including op-ack/op-nack (1715-1727). The retry work items keep firing (2221-2248, delays 1/2/4/8/8 s, maxAttempts 5 at line 254). Each retry resends, the relay re-acks the duplicate, and the ack is discarded. After the last attempt the item reports a security-kind 'still unconfirmed' issue and calls task?.cancel. That makes the receive fail, and handleDisconnect sees !foregroundReady and does not reconnect (1784-1787). status becomes .offline, ContentView drops eligibility (ContentView.swift:623-631, 1126-1128), background location stops, and the app suspends. The same happens without the opt-in: pauseConnectionForBackground calls handleDisconnect, which returns before clearOutboundDeliveries (1787-1788), so the retries still run and raise the spurious security issue. Android explicitly clears deliveries when entering background (SyncManager.kt:448 in detachMissionStateForKeyLock).
findings.failure_scenario: A user with background Unit Sync enabled drops a waypoint and immediately locks the phone (op-ack still in flight: 250 ms debounce plus cellular RTT). About 23 s later the socket is cancelled, background sharing silently stops for the rest of the patrol, and a security warning 'A Unit Sync change is still unconfirmed…' is queued. The same happens if the user glances at the app after coverage returns and pockets it while reconciliation puts are in flight.
findings.suggested_fix: When foregroundReady becomes false, call clearOutboundDeliveries(markForReconciliation: true). This cancels retry items and forces the diff on the next foreground snapshot, matching Android. Alternatively, keep processing op-ack/op-nack frames in background, since they touch only in-memory delivery state. Also move clearOutboundDeliveries in handleDisconnect above the foregroundReady guard.
findings.proving_test: XCTest against a local relay (vitest-pool / wrangler dev): join a v3 room, reach .connected, add a waypoint, then immediately call updateLifecycle(foregroundReady:false, backgroundPresenceEnabled:true, backgroundInterval:900) before the ack is processed. Wait 30 s. Assert status == .connected, task != nil and lastErrorMessage == nil. Today status is .offline and a security issue is set.

findings.title: Android background presence socket has no wake-safe keepalive or liveness check; in a quiet room it idles through CPU suspend and the next fix goes into a dead connection
findings.description: In background, the only wake source is GPS_PROVIDER with minTime = interval (default 15 min; OpsecSettings.kt:47-57; BackgroundUnitSyncLocationService.kt:188-194). The app has no wake lock anywhere and no AlarmManager keepalive. Java-WebSocket's 20 s pinger (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:133, 285) runs on a ScheduledExecutor over System.nanoTime (CLOCK_MONOTONIC), which does not advance while the CPU is suspended. So no ping is sent and no dead-socket check runs between fixes. Cloudflare documents that idle WebSockets are closed and recommends client heartbeats, and carrier NATs expire idle TCP mappings (often within minutes). sendBackgroundPresence sends only if the status is still CONNECTED (SyncManager.kt:522-537) and never verifies liveness first. iOS differs: continuous background location keeps the app running (LocationService.swift:110-118, pausesLocationUpdatesAutomatically=false), so its 20 s ping/8 s pong watchdog keeps the path alive (SyncManager.swift:656-659, 1885-1948).
findings.failure_scenario: A squad pockets their phones with background sharing every 15 min, so the room is quiet. After a few minutes the edge or NAT drops the idle socket while the Android CPU sleeps. At t=15 min the GPS callback's signed loc is written into a dead or reset connection. Either it is lost silently (half-open, while the notification still claims sharing) or the reset surfaces and S2-07 ends background sharing. Peers see the member expire after the advertised retention.
findings.suggested_fix: On each background location callback, take a short PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK (about 10 s), send a WebSocket ping and require a pong before sending presence. If no pong arrives, treat the socket as dead (S2-07 then decides what happens). For intervals of 5 minutes or more, also schedule an inexact AlarmManager (setAndAllowWhileIdle) keepalive ping about every 4-5 minutes, or accept the idle drop and implement the presence-only reconnect described in S2-07.
findings.proving_test: Instrumented test: local relay behind a TCP proxy that closes connections idle for more than 120 s. Room contains only this device and one peer that is itself backgrounded. Background interval 5 min, screen off, device unplugged (adb shell dumpsys battery unplug; adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle). Assert the peer receives a new v3 loc at about t+5 min and at about t+10 min. Today none arrives and the FGS stops or keeps showing a stale 'on' state.

findings.title: Any transport interruption permanently and silently ends background presence on both platforms (network flap, cell handover, relay deploy)
findings.description: Background presence may only continue on the socket authenticated in foreground. Android: handleSocketEnded in background invokes backgroundTransportEnded (SyncManager.kt:1029-1031). UnitSyncRuntime.onBackgroundTransportEnded then stops the FGS (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:253-257) with no reportError and no user notification. iOS: handleDisconnect returns before any report when !foregroundReady (SyncManager.swift:1784-1787). Eligibility requires status == .connected (ContentView.swift:623-631), so background location is turned off and the app suspends. Neither platform can reconnect in background, because reserveHelloEpoch needs a durable replay-state write behind the locked mission key. Cloudflare terminates WebSockets whenever it restarts servers for releases, and every relay deploy does the same, so every screen-off device stops sharing at the first such event.
findings.failure_scenario: During a 6-hour patrol with phones pocketed, a relay deploy, a Cloudflare edge restart or a single cell handover drops every member's socket. All background sharing ends silently: the Android notification just disappears and the iOS location indicator goes away. Peers watch markers expire and assume units are down or out of range, and nobody knows until they unlock their phone.
findings.suggested_fix: First, as the minimum fix, make the end loud: post a high-priority local notification ('Background Unit Sync paused: connection lost. Open TacMap to resume'). Then support a restricted presence-only reconnect. Keep a separately sealed, device-bound hello-epoch counter that is available while the mission key is locked, and add a relay join mode (e.g. X-Presence-Only: 1) that skips the snapshot, accepts hello and loc only, and fans nothing out to the socket. Reconnect with backoff while the FGS or location session is authorised.
findings.proving_test: With a device in background presence mode (both platforms), reset the connection via toxiproxy reset_peer, or restart the local relay. Assert that (a) today no user-visible notification is posted (the test fails), and (b) after the fix a loc from that device reaches a peer within 2 × backoff cap without foregrounding the app.

findings.title: Egress-only background sessions still receive, wake for, and discard the entire room fan-out
findings.description: The relay broadcasts every loc/put/del/hello/chat-key/chat/leave to every socket (index.ts:1556-1562), and a socket has no way to declare itself send-only. In background presence mode Android receives each frame on the reader thread and dispatches it to main (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:253-259). There it is budget-checked and then dropped (SyncManager.kt:1779-1798). iOS receives and discards every frame while !foregroundReady (SyncManager.swift:1703-1727). With k foreground peers at 5 s presence cadence, a pocketed phone that is supposed to send once per 15 min receives k/5 frames per second continuously. The cellular radio never leaves the connected state, Android's CPU is woken per frame, and the frames count against the receive budget (so busy rooms also trip S2-04 in background).
findings.failure_scenario: In a 10-member room where 5 members are active in foreground, a member on the 15-minute background setting receives about 1 frame/s (about 3 MB/h) for hours and throws it all away. The cellular radio stays in connected DRX, costing on the order of a few percent battery per hour, which defeats the low-power interval. The relay also pays for fan-out to sockets that ignore it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a control frame (for example {t:"mode",m:"egress"}, bound to the authenticated socket) or reuse the presence-only join from S2-07. The relay records the mode in the socket attachment and skips broadcast() for that socket, sending only acks and pongs. Clients send it on entering background presence mode and reconnect on foreground as today.
findings.proving_test: Relay vitest: two v3 sockets, B sends the egress-mode frame, A sends 10 loc/put frames, and B must receive 0 of them. Client: with backgroundPresenceOnly=true, count frames reaching handleMessage over 60 s while 5 foreground peers publish presence. Expect 0; today about 60.

findings.title: Android applies the v3 snapshot on the main thread with O(N) full-file sealed writes per record; beyond about 10 s the 10 s inbound drain gate kills the socket (and the UI can hit an ANR)
findings.description: snapshot-end runs inside one main-thread dispatch (SyncManager.kt:1936-1976). On a first join, every record is pending (SyncReplayState.kt:192-198). resolvePendingModelApplication then calls applyValidatedV3 followed by replay.clearPendingModelApplication (SyncManager.kt:2657-2667). Each upsert commits the whole store: WaypointStore.add -> commit -> persistCandidate serialises and SafeStore-seals the entire list (WaypointStore.kt:75-79, 258-289). Each clearPendingModelApplication persists the whole replay state (SyncReplayState.kt:429-433). That is 2N full-file encrypt+write cycles of O(N)-sized files, so O(N²) bytes, on the main thread. Meanwhile the reader thread waits in SyncInboundCallbackGate for at most CALLBACK_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS = 10 s (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:132, 253-259). On timeout, failSlowConsumer terminates the socket (323-329). After apply finishes, sendHelloV3 fails on the dead socket, which leads to failConnection and a reconnect that downloads the full snapshot again.
findings.failure_scenario: First join of an established room with a few hundred to a thousand objects on a mid- or low-end phone. Each write takes 20-40 ms (serialise + AES-GCM + fsync), so apply takes 10-40 s. The main thread is frozen (any tap causes an ANR dialog), the socket is killed at 10 s ('Unit Sync inbound consumer timed out'), and a second full snapshot is downloaded before the member becomes CONNECTED.
findings.suggested_fix: Batch snapshot application: apply all APPLY_INCOMING records to each store in one commit (the addAll/update-many equivalents) and clear all pending markers in one replay persistTransaction. Move sealing and IO off the main thread while keeping the durable-before-publish order. Do not hold the reader-thread gate across local CPU/IO work: release it when the frame is queued for processing, and bound queue depth instead of latency.
findings.proving_test: Robolectric test: build a fixture v3 snapshot of 800 validly signed waypoint records and drive it through the real listener path with a counting SafeStore/persistence hook. Assert at most 3 sealed writes for the whole snapshot-end (today about 1,600) and snapshot-end wall time under 2 s. Also assert no SocketTimeoutException from SyncInboundCallbackGate.

findings.title: One authentic-but-unparseable record poisons the room: Android reconnect-loops forever re-downloading the full snapshot, iOS fail-closes permanently
findings.description: The snapshot is all-or-nothing. On Android, a record that validateRecordV3 rejects (for example GeoJsonImporter invalidSkipped != 0 at SyncManager.kt:2584-2585, or a parse or local-id mismatch) sets snapshotInvalid (1927-1929). snapshot-end then calls failSnapshot (1941-1943, 3643-3653) and failConnection (3655-3666), which cancels the socket but leaves wantConnected true. handleSocketEnded reconnects with backoff (1012-1028), and the same record fails every time. iOS returns nil for the same content (SyncManager.swift:3937-3941) and finishSnapshotV3 calls failClosedV3 (3469-3474), which sets wantConnected=false (2555-2571) and stops permanently. The relay is content-blind, so any room member with the key (or a client bug or version skew in geometry validation) can store such a record, and it will appear in every future snapshot. Live copies of the same record are merely dropped (applyLiveRecordV3), so the room seems fine until anyone reconnects.
findings.failure_scenario: A member on a different app version writes a drawing whose geometry the other platform's importer counts as invalid, or a malicious insider does so deliberately. From then on every Android member retries every 30 s, downloading the whole room each time (for a 5 MB room about 600 MB/h of cellular data), and never reconnects. Every iOS member gets a security error and stays offline until they leave and rejoin, then hits it again.
findings.suggested_fix: Separate authenticity from local applicability. If signature, AEAD and actor binding verify but content cannot be applied locally, commit the stamp to replay state and quarantine that object (surface 'N synced objects could not be displayed'), then complete the handshake. Keep fail-closed only for authentication failures. Also classify a deterministic snapshot rejection as non-retryable after 2 identical failures: stop with an actionable error instead of looping.
findings.proving_test: Add a shared fixture (testdata/malicious_frames.json) with a validly signed v3 put whose GeoJSON is a 1-point LineString. Seed it into a relay room and join from each client. Assert status reaches CONNECTED within one attempt and the object is reported as quarantined. Today Android's connect count keeps increasing with a full snapshot each time, and iOS ends with wantConnected == false.

findings.title: HTTP upgrade statuses and relay close codes are discarded: permanent conditions (room full, quota, stale epoch, forbidden) retry forever behind a generic 'disconnected' message
findings.description: The relay returns 401/403/404/426/429/503 at upgrade (index.ts:581-589, 624-680). After the snapshot it closes with 4008 rate limit, 4010 key mismatch, 4011 invalid proof, 4012, 4013 room quota, 4014 stale hello epoch, 4015 superseded, or 1011 storage unavailable (index.ts:749, 763, 961-1003, 1019, 808). On Android, Java-WebSocket turns a non-101 into onClose(-1, 'Invalid status code received: 503 …'). The transport forwards code and reason (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:271-273), but SyncManager ignores both and passes detail = null (SyncManager.kt:1130-1134). iOS handles every receive failure identically (SyncManager.swift:1676-1677) and never reads task.closeCode or (task.response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode. Both show 'Unit Sync disconnected… reconnecting' and retry forever at the 30 s cap. 4013 fires only after the full snapshot is sent, and 4014 self-heals only one epoch per attempt (reserveHelloEpoch +1, SyncReplayState.kt:236-255) because the snapshot carries no actor epochs.
findings.failure_scenario: The 65th member gets 503 'Room full' and polls every 30 s indefinitely without ever being told why. A new member of a room near MAX_STORED_BYTES gets 4013 after each full snapshot (up to 50 MB), so the device downloads about 100 MB/min forever. A device restored from an older backup is K epochs behind and needs K full-snapshot cycles to rejoin.
findings.suggested_fix: Plumb code, reason and HTTP status into handleSocketEnded/handleDisconnect. Map 503 'Room full', 4013, 4010/4011/4012, 401/403/404/426 to specific user-facing errors that stop reconnecting or use a long backoff (for example 5-15 min), and honour Retry-After or 429 with a longer delay. For 4014, have the relay return the stored epoch in the close reason (or a hello-nack) so the client can jump its counter in one step.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM test with an OkHttp MockWebServer (or a raw loopback server) answering 'HTTP/1.1 503 Room full'. Assert lastError mentions room capacity and the second retry delay is at least 5 min. iOS: the same using a local relay with MAX_CONNECTIONS reached. Relay-backed test: a quota-full room plus a new actor should produce exactly one snapshot download and then a stop.

findings.title: Every reconnect, including every foreground return (and on iOS every transient .inactive such as Control/Notification Center), rotates the session and re-downloads the full room snapshot
findings.description: The relay has no resume or since-seq parameter. sendSnapshot always streams every obj: record (index.ts:1486-1529), and clients reset snapshot state on every connect (Android SyncManager.kt:1062-1074; iOS SyncManager.swift:1611-1636) even though they persist lastSnapshotSeq. iOS treats any scenePhase other than .active as not foreground (ContentView.swift:633-639). On return, updateLifecycle always calls reconnectForForegroundReconciliation (SyncManager.swift:992-994), including with background presence enabled, where the socket stayed healthy but inbound frames were dropped. Each cycle burns a new durable hello epoch, a relay leave/hello/chat-key fan-out to every peer, and a chat key rotation that fails in-flight chats. Android does the same on every onPause/onResume (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:149-184, SyncManager.kt:468-501).
findings.failure_scenario: An iOS user glances at Notification Center 30 times during an operation: 30 full snapshots (for example 3 MB each, 90 MB), 30 join/leave churns visible to all peers, and 30 chat-session resets. Android users switching apps pay the same per switch.
findings.suggested_fix: Add incremental resume. The relay stores a per-record seq (it already maintains meta:seq) and accepts ?since=<lastSnapshotSeq> to send only newer records and tombstones plus the fence. Clients still verify signatures and replay rules. On iOS, if the socket stayed connected and no inbound frames were dropped (track a dropped-frame counter), or if the mission key never locked (device-bound mode on a transient .inactive), skip the reconnect.
findings.proving_test: Instrument bytes received per connection. On iOS, simulate scenePhase .active→.inactive→.active with a healthy socket and device-bound DataKey, and assert no new connection generation (today activeConnectionGeneration increments). Relay vitest: connect with since=seq-1 and assert the snapshot contains only the one newer record.

findings.title: No network reachability integration: after connectivity returns, clients wait up to a full 30 s backoff, and short coverage windows are missed
findings.description: Neither app registers ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback nor uses NWPathMonitor or waitsForConnectivity; a grep of android/app/src/main/java and ios/TacticalMaps finds none. During an outage every attempt fails fast (DNS or connect), so backoff climbs to the 30 s cap (SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:17-31; PresenceQuality.swift:4-18). When a usable network appears, the next attempt can be up to 30 s away. A switch from Wi-Fi to cellular on a zombie Wi-Fi is detected only by the ping watchdog: about 20-28 s on iOS (SyncManager.swift:656-659) and 30-40 s on Android (Java-WebSocket 20 s × 1.5).
findings.failure_scenario: A patrol with intermittent coverage (10-20 s windows cresting ridgelines) mostly attempts reconnects outside those windows, and when an attempt does land in one, it also needs the full snapshot plus handshake. The unit's picture stays stale for long periods despite repeated brief connectivity.
findings.suggested_fix: Android: register a default NetworkCallback. On onAvailable or onCapabilitiesChanged(VALIDATED), cancel the pending reconnectJob and connect immediately (still honouring a minimum spacing of about 2 s). On onLost of the network the socket uses, cancel it proactively. iOS: an NWPathMonitor that triggers the same, plus cancellation when the path's interface set changes and the task's path is no longer satisfied.
findings.proving_test: Android Robolectric: put the manager in backoff at attempt 6 (30 s), then fire ShadowConnectivityManager network-available. Assert connect() is called within 1 s under a TestDispatcher. iOS: inject a path-monitor protocol, fire satisfied during a 30 s backoff, and assert connect within 1 s.

findings.title: Reconnect jitter collapses at the cap: about half of retries land at exactly 30 s
findings.description: The delay is min(cap, base×2^n) × (1 ± 0.2), then clamped to the cap again (SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:26-31; PresenceQuality.swift:13-17). At the cap, every multiplier above 1 clamps to exactly 30 s, so jitter spans only [24, 30] s with about 50% of the probability mass at exactly 30 s. That weakens de-synchronisation of clients that failed together (for example after a long relay outage), which matters alongside the per-IP CONN_LIMITER of 60/min and join fan-out (S2-04).
