findings.failure_scenario: After a relay outage, clients that all hit the cap together retry in partially synchronised waves at +30 s multiples, causing burstier DO wake-ups and fan-out than intended.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply jitter below the cap, for example delay = cap_or_exp × (1 - jitter × U) ("equal jitter"), or use full jitter U(0, min(cap, base×2^n)).
findings.proving_test: Unit test on both platforms: set attemptCount ≥ 6, sample nextDelay 10,000 times with a random source, and assert the fraction equal to exactly 30 s is below 1%. Today it is about 50%.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is real, but the trigger is narrower than the title says. At UnitSyncRuntime.kt:157-174, a room is kept only when optedInV3Location is true, meaning backgroundUnitSyncLocation plus canArm (SyncManager.kt:377-379: v3, a '3:' room and shareLocation). Otherwise the manager is disposed and clearRoomStateAfterDispose nulls _room (SyncManager.kt:889-895). The socket-less retention path, suspendUntilForegroundStores (SyncManager.kt:421-437), is itself gated on the same opt-in (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:164). On resume, acquireForeground builds a fresh manager (103-106), and the SyncDialog code field starts from `room ?: ""` (SyncDialog.kt:91), so the user has to re-type the join code. Mitigating factor: the Android v3 join flow forces the opt-in first (UnitSyncJoinGate.requiresConsent, SyncDialog.kt:61-66, 263-270, 509-530), so a fresh join is safe. The trigger is a later opt-out: the Share my location switch (SyncDialog.kt:360-363) or the notification's Stop sharing (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:230-240 persists false). Any v2 room is also dropped on every pause. After such an opt-out, every onPause (app switch, SAF picker, permission dialog) silently leaves the room. iOS keeps roomId and wantConnected (pauseConnectionForBackground at SyncManager.swift:1817-1831; the guard at 1787 only skips the reconnect) and reconnects at 992-994. The cross-platform divergence is therefore real. ADR-002 and THREAT_MODEL do not require dropping the room. There is no data loss (local edits stay in the stores), but sync silently stops until the user manually re-joins. High fits: the trigger is plausible and uses a designed control.

Proven empirically. connect() sets CONNECTING (SyncManager.kt:1061). Both watchdogs are armed only inside the onOpen callback (1094-1104). The only pre-open bound is the 10 s TCP connect timeout (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:131, 243-248). javap of Java-WebSocket-1.6.0.jar shows that WebSocketClient.run never calls setSoTimeout or setKeepAlive, and that startConnectionLostTimer is called only from onWebsocketOpen. I ran a JVM harness (scratchpad/verify-S2-client-transport/jvm/StuckOpen.java) against the real 1.6.0 jar with the same config (10 s connect timeout, connectionLostTimeout=20) and a loopback server that accepts and never answers. After 45 s: accepted=1, readyState=NOT_YET_CONNECTED, no callback fired. Nothing else rescues it: the only other ws?.cancel() sites need CONNECTED deliveries (1180, 2064) or lifecycle transitions (926-933). The app stays 'Connecting…' until the user backgrounds it. iOS schedules its 30 s timer in the same main-actor turn as resume (SyncManager.swift:1663-1667). A captive portal or a black-hole-after-ACK on cellular is a plausible trigger.

iOS schedules the v3 timeout only once, in connect() (SyncManager.swift:1666). It is 30 s (659), is never re-armed on snapshot progress, and runs until hello-ack (guard status != .connected, 1854-1883). Because it is a main-queue work item, a deadline that passes during the main-actor finishSnapshotV3 validate+apply (3455-3533) fires right after the apply, before hello-ack can arrive. Android arms 20 s at onOpen and re-arms at snapshot-begin, at each page and after snapshot-end (SyncManager.kt:1102, 1902, 1934, 1975; constant at 1764). Each whole page must therefore arrive within 20 s. The relay builds and queues the whole snapshot before returning 101 (index.ts:674-684) and packs pages up to 900 kB (26, 1486-1522). On timeout neither client resets backoff (resets happen only at hello-ack/CONNECTED), so every retry re-downloads everything. The arithmetic holds: about 1.2 MB is the iOS ceiling at 384 kbps, and Android fails whenever a 900 kB page needs more than 20 s (below about 360 kbps). Snapshot progress is persisted between attempts only for applied records, so the download itself never converges on such links. High fits the tactical/slow-link domain.

I re-ran the auditor's probe in my own scratch copy (verify-S2-client-transport/sync/test/s2_budget.test.ts) and it passed: the relay delivered hello plus 199 puts to the receiver and 199 op-acks to the sender, with no closes. Both clients use a tumbling 200-frame / 4 MiB LIVE window (Android SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:83-105; iOS SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:111-150). Exceeding it closes their own socket (SyncManager.kt:1778-1795, 1822-1835; SyncManager.swift:1703-1714). The relay allows 200 msgs per sender (index.ts:27-29, 862-878), broadcasts every stored put (944, 1218) to every socket (1556-1562) and sends an op-ack per put to the sender. Senders do not pace at all: syncLocalStateV3 loops over every diff (SyncManager.kt:1304-1336), after only a 250 ms debounce (1241). This is reachable in normal use. A KML import of about 190 or more objects, or a member joining with more than about 200 local objects (the post-hello-ack diff pushes them all), trips every receiver and the sender (via its own acks). The relay also closes the sender with 4008 at message 201. Backoff resets at hello-ack, so reconnects happen at about 1 s and cause churn. Part (b), the storm model, rests on plausible rules (a 64-member room already carries about 126 presence frames per 10 s at the 5 s cadence, UnitSyncPresenceCadence.kt:103), but it is only a model. Part (a) alone justifies high. Everything converges eventually via snapshots, at heavy cost.

updateLifecycle(foregroundReady:false) clears only chat secrets (SyncManager.swift:965-1008). The receive loop drops every frame, op-ack included, when !foregroundReady (1715-1727). Retry items (2221-2248) check only the delivery's own generation and sessionDomain (nextAttempt, 295-307). The generation is unchanged on the retained background socket, so the item resends five times with delays of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 8 s (23 s in total). It then reports a .security issue and calls task?.cancel. The receive failure goes to handleDisconnect, which returns before any reconnect or clear when !foregroundReady (1784-1788). status becomes .offline, so ContentView eligibility, which requires .connected (ContentView.swift:623-631, 1126-1128), turns background location off. Android clears deliveries on entering background (detachMissionStateForKeyLock, SyncManager.kt:448). The trigger needs a delivery in flight at the transition. On LTE that window is narrow (debounce + RTT, well under 1 s), but it is wide on slow or congested links and during post-reconnect reconciliation bursts. The consequence is that background sharing silently ends for the whole session and a false security warning appears. High is fair, though borderline with medium.

There is no WakeLock, AlarmManager or setAndAllowWhileIdle anywhere in android/app/src/main (grep). In background the service only requests GPS_PROVIDER at interval.minutes (BackgroundUnitSyncLocationService.kt:188-194; default FIFTEEN_MINUTES, OpsecSettings.kt:56). Java-WebSocket's lost-connection timer is a ScheduledExecutor (AbstractWebSocket uses newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor/scheduleAtFixedRate), and it does not tick during CPU suspend. sendBackgroundPresence checks only status == CONNECTED (SyncManager.kt:522-537). Cloudflare's WebSockets docs (developers.cloudflare.com/network/websockets) state that idle connections are closed and that clients should heartbeat. The exact interval is not documented but is well under 15 minutes. So in a quiet room the socket is idle-closed long before the next fix. The close wakes the device, and handleSocketEnded then calls backgroundTransportEnded, which stops the FGS (SyncManager.kt:1029-1031, UnitSyncRuntime.kt:253-257). In practice Android background presence ends minutes after screen-off in quiet rooms, which is worse than 'the next fix goes into a dead socket'. iOS stays running under continuous CL updates (LocationService.swift:110-118, 311-317), and its 20 s ping timer keeps the path alive.

The mechanics are accurate. Android: handleSocketEnded, outside foreground, invokes backgroundTransportEnded (SyncManager.kt:1029-1031), and onBackgroundTransportEnded stops the FGS without reportError (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:253-257). iOS: handleDisconnect returns at 1787 when !foregroundReady, the status becomes .offline and eligibility is dropped (ContentView.swift:623-631). However, the no-background-reconnect behaviour is the documented, binding design: THREAT_MODEL.md:474-476 says 'If the authenticated socket drops, sharing pauses rather than creating a new background session.' 'Permanently' is overstated, because both platforms reconnect on foreground return (attachForegroundStores; SyncManager.swift:992-994). A 'single cell handover' usually preserves TCP; a network switch or coverage loss does not. What remains is a real gap: the user and peers get no loud signal. The Android notification simply disappears and the iOS indicator goes away. Because S2-06 makes these pauses frequent on Android, a user-visible alert is warranted. The suggested presence-only background reconnect conflicts with the binding threat model and would need an ADR.

broadcast() sends to every socket in getWebSockets() (index.ts:1556-1562), and there is no send-only mode. On Android, each frame is read on the reader thread, dispatched to main, budget-checked and only then dropped (SyncManager.kt:1778-1798). iOS receives and drops every frame while !foregroundReady (SyncManager.swift:1703-1727). The frames also count against the LIVE budget, because status stays CONNECTED in background, so a burst (see S2-04) can close the background socket. The waste is real: about 1 frame/s with 5 foreground peers at the 5 s cadence keeps the cellular radio connected. I rate it medium rather than high for four reasons. It needs foreground peers. iOS is already awake for continuous location. DO outbound fan-out is not billed per message. And in Android quiet rooms this fan-out is actually what prevents the S2-06 idle close, so any egress-only mode must be paired with a keepalive.

snapshot-end runs inside one main-dispatcher callback (SyncManager.kt:1936-1976). On a first join commitRemoteSnapshot marks every beating record pending (SyncReplayState.kt:192-198). Each APPLY_INCOMING runs applyValidatedV3 and then upsertWaypoint/upsertDrawing. WaypointStore.add goes to commit, then persistCandidate, which JSON-encodes and seals the whole list (WaypointStore.kt:74-78, 258-282). SafeStore.writeAtomically ends in fsync+rename (SafeStore.kt:75-80, 139-156). After that, replay.clearPendingModelApplication runs persistTransaction, and save re-encodes and re-seals the whole replay state (SyncReplayState.kt:429-433, 112-122, 478-486). The result is two O(N) sealed fsync writes per record, so O(N²) work, all on main. The reader thread waits on SyncInboundCallbackGate. consumed() fires only when the job completes (dispatchSocketCallback, 963-985), with a 10 s cap (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:132, 253-258, 323-329). failSlowConsumer marks the socket terminal, so sendHelloV3 fails and failConnection reconnects. Progress persists per record, so it converges after one or more extra snapshots, but with a long main-thread freeze and ANR risk. Timing for a few hundred to a thousand records on mid or low-end flash is plausible, not measured (no device runs allowed). iOS has the same per-record persist pattern (see missed).

Android: validateRecordV3 returns null after a successful signature and AEAD check when GeoJsonImporter fails, when invalidSkipped != 0, on a kind other than waypoint/drawing, or on a wire-id mismatch (SyncManager.kt:2574-2601). That sets snapshotInvalid (1927-1929). snapshot-end then calls failSnapshot (1941-1943, 3643-3653) and failConnection (3655-3666), which cancels the socket but leaves wantConnected true. handleSocketEnded then reconnects via backoff (1012-1027), and the same record fails every time: an infinite loop with a full snapshot on each attempt. iOS returns nil for the same content (SyncManager.swift:3937-3941), and finishSnapshotV3 calls failClosedV3 (3469-3474), which sets wantConnected=false (2555-2571). The relay accepts any kind matching /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32}$/ (index.ts:1163), so a room-key holder, a cross-platform importer mismatch or future version skew (a new object kind) can plant the record permanently. applyLiveRecordV3 silently drops the live copy (2605-2606), so the room looks healthy until someone reconnects. ADR-001 section 10 does not require failing the whole snapshot for authenticated but inapplicable content.

Android onClosed passes detail=null to handleSocketEnded, dropping code and reason (SyncManager.kt:1130-1134). A non-101 upgrade goes through Java-WebSocket's handshake rejection as a close, so the status is also lost. iOS reads no closeCode or HTTPURLResponse: grep shows closeCode used only for outbound rejects (SyncManager.swift:1740-1749), and every receive failure goes to handleDisconnect (1676-1677). The relay's permanent conditions are real: 'Room full' 503 (index.ts:670), 4013 quota emitted in handleHello after the full snapshot has been sent (index.ts:994-999), and 4010/4011/4012/4014. Both clients retry forever at the 30 s cap with a generic message. The 4013 case (a new actor in a room near 10k records or 50 MB) re-downloads the whole snapshot each cycle. These are edge conditions, so medium is right.

syncForegroundReady requires scenePhase == .active (ContentView.swift:633-639), and every scenePhase change calls updateLifecycle (1091-1097). So a .inactive state (Notification or Control Center, an incoming-call banner) either closes the socket via pauseConnectionForBackground (no opt-in, SyncManager.swift:1001-1004) or keeps it but forces reconnectForForegroundReconciliation on return (992-994). sendSnapshot always streams every obj: record (index.ts:1486-1522), because stored records carry no per-record seq. Android re-snapshots on every onPause/onResume (UnitSyncRuntime.kt:149-184; SyncManager.kt:468-501). A fresh snapshot after background is the documented design (THREAT_MODEL.md:472-473) because inbound frames are dropped. The avoidable waste is: no incremental resume, and in device-bound mode iOS treats .inactive as background even though the key is not locked. Each cycle also rotates the session and chat keys (clearChatSessionSecrets/clearChatTransport fail pending chats). It is meaningful inefficiency and churn, not breakage, so medium.

A grep for NetworkCallback, registerDefaultNetworkCallback, NWPathMonitor, waitsForConnectivity and SCNetworkReachability across android/app/src/main/java and ios/TacticalMaps returns nothing. The iOS session is a plain ephemeral config (SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:29-40). Backoff reaches the 30 s cap after about 5 fast failures (SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:24-31; PresenceQuality.swift:11-17). So after roughly 30 s of outage, the reconnect after coverage returns is 0-30 s late (about 15 s on average). This is a quality-of-service gap in intermittent coverage, not a correctness bug, so medium.

At the cap, unjittered is 30000 and the multiplier is in [0.8, 1.2], and the result is clamped to maximumDelayMs (SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:26-31; iOS PresenceQuality.swift:13-17). So every multiplier ≥ 1 yields exactly 30 s: about 50% of the mass, with the effective range [24, 30] s. Practical impact is small, because clients fail at different times and delays are relative to each client's own failure. Low.

verify.missed: 1) The iOS equivalent of S2-09 is missing. finishSnapshotV3 validates every buffered snapshot record on the main actor at snapshot-end, not while streaming (SyncManager.swift:3466-3475). It then calls resolvePendingModelApplication per record, and clearPendingModelApplication runs persist() each time (SyncReplayState.swift:298-304), plus a per-record store save in applyValidatedRecordV3. That is the same O(N²) sealed-write pattern on MainActor. It sits under the absolute 30 s v3 timer (659, 1854-1883): if the deadline passes during the apply, the timer work item runs right after it, before hello-ack arrives, and kills the session. A first join of a large room therefore freezes the iOS UI and needs extra full-snapshot attempts. 2) S2-06 understates the Android impact. Cloudflare documents closing idle WebSockets, and the Android client sends nothing between fixes while the CPU is suspended. In a quiet room the relay edge therefore closes the socket within minutes of screen-off, well before the 15-minute fix. The close then ends background presence via S2-07's path (SyncManager.kt:1029-1031, UnitSyncRuntime.kt:253-257), so Android background presence effectively works only in rooms busy enough for peer fan-out (S2-08) to keep it alive. S2-06 and S2-08 are in tension and must be fixed together: an egress-only mode needs a wake-safe keepalive. 3) Evidence: I reproduced S2-02 with /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cbrooker-Code-TacticalMaps/d9f42208-9d3f-40e1-9b8b-49fa6c488260/scratchpad/verify-S2-client-transport/jvm/StuckOpen.java against the real Java-WebSocket 1.6.0 jar. I re-ran the S2-04 relay probe in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cbrooker-Code-TacticalMaps/d9f42208-9d3f-40e1-9b8b-49fa6c488260/scratchpad/verify-S2-client-transport/sync (it passes)."

audit.summary:
How v3 works end to end. Each object gets a durable stamp, "counterHex16:actorId" (VersionStamp.kt:17-23, VersionStamp.swift:43-46, index.ts:178-191). Before a frame is sent, the client reserves the stamp and records the content hash or tombstone (SyncReplayState.kt:324-358; iOS reserveNextCounter+commit, SyncManager.swift:2321-2345). The relay keeps LWW per wire ID: a stamp wins if it is strictly newer, and an exact duplicate is acked (index.ts:1188-1227). On connect the relay sends a snapshot fenced by seq, inside blockConcurrencyWhile (index.ts:688, 1486-1529). The client checks every record for AEAD, signature and actor binding. It then commits the whole snapshot in one transaction with a pending-model marker per accepted record, applies each record, verifies the receiver-side re-export hash and clears the marker (Android SyncManager.kt:1936-1976 and 2657-2687; iOS 3455-3533 and 3824-3848). After that it sends a signed hello, waits for hello-ack, then resends recoverable deletes and diffs the local model (lastContent/forcedLocalDiff) to publish (SyncManager.kt:2227-2256; iOS 3539-3578). Hello epochs are monotonic and persisted on both relay and client. Presence counters are per session.

What is solid:
- Relay, Android and iOS pick the same winner for every pair of writes. Counter-then-actorId ordering over ASCII base64url agrees in all three and is fixture-backed. Casing of `by` has no effect in v3.
- Tombstones reject lower or equal puts across restarts. Put after delete needs a strictly higher stamp.
- Recoveries after a crash (stamp reserved, send failed, or marker persisted but model not applied) are handled identically on both platforms.
- Retries resend the identical frame and the relay dedups it.
- v3 LWW does not depend on wall clocks, so clock skew is harmless.
- The relay keeps per-socket FIFO order.
- In the normal case, two devices do converge.

The problems found are mostly liveness and stability, not LWW disagreement:
- v2 cross-platform ID casing deletes data.
- Relay idle expiry leads to reconnect loops.
- Whole-snapshot rejection lets a single bad signed record brick the room.
- Chat replay fences are never pruned.
- Watchdogs and retry timers do not account for slow links.
- Rate limits and O(n²) work hit bulk publishes and mature rooms.

I proved two findings with a relay vitest in a scratch copy (both pass): scratchpad/sync-s3/test/s3audit.test.ts.

findings.title: v2 rooms: iOS sends uppercase IDs and Android sends lowercase, so Android drops every iOS record and iOS echoes a delete that wipes Android's objects
findings.description: Android's v2 path only accepts lowercase canonical UUIDs (SyncManager.kt:50-69). isValidLegacySyncPut also requires record id == embedded feature id (:71-84). Android object IDs come from UUID.randomUUID().toString(), which is lowercase (Waypoint.kt:32, Drawing.kt:55,77). iOS v2 keys everything by `uuidString`, which is uppercase (SyncManager.swift:2084,2089,2127). Its GeoJSON feature id is lowercased (GeoJSONExporter.swift:153). So Android rejects every iOS v2 put and del. In the other direction, iOS applyRecord stores `lastContent[id] = reexport(id: id)` under the lowercase wire id (:3226). reexport compares against `uuidString`, finds nothing, and returns "" (:3321-3330). The next syncLocalState keys `current` by uppercase uuidString, so the lowercase key lands in `gone`. iOS then emits `sendDel(lowercase id, ++clock)` plus a put under the uppercase id (:2093-2111). The relay treats IDs as opaque strings (index.ts:907), stores both, and broadcasts the delete. Android verifies it and removes its own object (SyncManager.kt:2161-2219).
findings.failure_scenario: A legacy `2:` room with one Android and one iOS device. Android creates waypoint W (id 3f2a...). iOS applies it, then within about 250 ms sends del{id:"3f2a...",v:2} and put{id:"3F2A...",v:3}. Android deletes W. It ignores the uppercase put forever. iOS keeps W. The relay holds a tombstone for the lowercase id and a live record for the uppercase id. A later iOS joiner applies the put and then the tombstone (snapshot key order puts uppercase first), so it ends up with nothing. Result: permanent divergence and data loss on Android.
findings.suggested_fix: Canonicalize v2 wire IDs on iOS to lowercase on send and receive: use id.uuidString.lowercased() for the frame id, lastContent/versions keys and the comparison in reexport. Or have both sides parse the UUID and compare values. Add a cross-platform v2 vector to the shared fixtures. If v2 is kept only for legacy rooms, at minimum refuse mixed-platform v2 with a clear error.
findings.proving_test: iOS XCTest: join a `2:` room with a fake socket. Deliver an Android-sealed v2 put with a lowercase id (signed with the fixture device key), advance the 250 ms debounce, and assert that no outbound frame has t=="del" for that id. Android JVM test: feed an iOS-produced v2 put (uppercase frame id, lowercase embedded id) to handleMessageV2 and assert the waypoint is applied. Both fail today.

findings.title: Relay idle expiry (7 days) wipes seq and high-water; mature clients then get counter-window nacks forever in a tight reconnect loop
findings.description: alarm() calls deleteAll() once there have been no sockets for 7 days (index.ts:834-847). That resets meta:seq and meta:highWater to 0. Clients keep their replay state, including localCounter. The next reservation is max(localCounter, roomHighWater)+1 (SyncReplayState.kt:329, SyncReplayState.swift:199-203), and recoverable resends reuse old stamps. The relay rejects any counter above highWater+10000 with op-nack counter-window, retry:false (index.ts:1193-1195). Both clients treat that as fatal and cancel the socket (SyncManager.kt:2063-2065, SyncManager.swift:3091-3093). Backoff was already reset at hello-ack (SyncManager.kt:2236, SyncManager.swift:3552), so the reconnect comes about 1 s later. Each cycle downloads a full snapshot, reserves a new hello epoch and republishes, and nothing is ever stored. On top of that, snapshot seq 0 < lastSnapshotSeq raises a SECURITY rollback warning on every connect until the relay's seq catches up (SyncManager.kt:1904-1910, SyncManager.swift:3478,3522-3528). Clients also resend every historic own tombstone that is missing from the snapshot, which feeds S3-07.
findings.failure_scenario: A unit uses a room until the counter passes 10,000, which takes only about 10k object edits across the unit. The unit then pauses for more than 7 days. On return, every device cycles connect → snapshot(0 items) → hello → put(counter 10,001+) → nack counter-window → cancel → reconnect about 1 s later, forever. Objects are never republished for new joiners, and users see rollback-warning banners. Proven: the vitest 'S3 expiry' builds a high-water of 20,000, runs alarm(), reconnects, and gets {t:"op-nack",code:"counter-window",retry:false} for put(20,001) (scratchpad/sync-s3/test/s3audit.test.ts, passes).
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one. (a) Do not expire rooms that have durable data, or persist a tiny tombstone of meta (seq, highWater) across expiry. (b) Have the relay accept the first authenticated write into an empty room without the window, or set highWater from the first hello's advertised counter. (c) On the client, treat counter-window/stale on a fresh or rolled-back snapshot as non-fatal: do not cancel, and surface a 'relay reset' state instead of looping. Also do not report a rollback when the snapshot is empty and seq==0 (the relay-reset case). Tell the user instead.
findings.proving_test: Relay: the vitest in scratchpad/sync-s3/test/s3audit.test.ts ('S3 expiry...'). Client: an Android JVM SyncManager test whose fake relay answers every put with counter-window. Assert that at most one reconnect happens and that the backoff is not reset. Today the socket cancels and reconnects without bound.

findings.title: One signed record that the receiver cannot parse or verify rejects the whole snapshot for everyone, permanently (Android reconnects forever; iOS stops syncing)
findings.description: The relay stores any put/del whose outer fields are well formed (index.ts:1158-1166). It cannot check the inner signature or the content. Android marks the snapshot invalid for any record that validateRecordV3 rejects: an unknown kind (:2536), a GeoJSON parse failure or invalidSkipped!=0 (:2576-2585), a wire-id mismatch, or an invalid signature. At snapshot-end it calls failSnapshot → failConnection → ws.cancel → reconnect (:1927-1929, :1941-1942, :3643-3666, :1012-1028). iOS calls failClosedV3 (wantConnected=false) when any record fails (SyncManager.swift:3469-3474, 2555-2571). The same record arriving live is just dropped (SyncManager.kt:2605-2606, SyncManager.swift:3790-3792). Once one such record is stored, every client that connects afterwards loops or stops.
findings.failure_scenario: (1) A newer app version adds an object kind (e.g., "route") or a drawing geometry that older parsers skip. After the newer device publishes one, every older Android device reconnects every 30 s, downloading the full snapshot each time, and never syncs again. Older iOS devices drop out of the room. (2) Any join-code holder, such as a lost or captured phone or a hostile member, sends one put that is properly sealed but has a bad inner signature or content "{}". The relay accepts it and the room is bricked for all members until the room is recreated.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep whole-snapshot rejection only for structural or relay-tamper conditions: fence mismatch, duplicate IDs, ceilings, and AEAD failure under the room key. Handle AEAD-valid records that fail signature, kind or parse checks one at a time, as the live path does: skip them, count them, and warn. Optionally record the stamp so older equal copies are not re-applied. Also consider a relay-side kind allow-list per protocol version.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM test: deliver a snapshot with one valid put and one put with kind "route" (validly sealed and signed with the fixture key B). Assert that status reaches CONNECTED and the valid object is applied. Today failSnapshot fires and a reconnect is scheduled. Mirror this in iOS XCTest (today wantConnected becomes false).

findings.title: The chat replay-fence table is capped at 256 and never pruned, and every peer reconnect adds a fence, so all incoming chat is eventually dropped silently for good
findings.description: Fences are keyed by (actorId, sessionDomain, chatKeyId) (TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:191-193; TacMapChatStore.swift:339-343). Both the session domain and the chat key are new on every WebSocket (SyncManager.kt:1063-1065,1434; SyncManager.swift:1612-1617,1509-1515). A sender session gets a new fence the first time one of its messages is accepted. Once 256 fences exist, any new identity is rejected: 'Never evict a durable high-water mark' (TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:212-216,449; TacMapChatStore.swift:356-362,58). The fences are persisted and nothing ever prunes them. The receiver drops the message silently (SyncManager.kt:2492; SyncManager.swift:3721-3722), while the relay has already sent chat-ack, so the sender shows the message as routed.
findings.failure_scenario: A 10-person unit chats daily. Phones reconnect several times a day (foreground/background, network changes, relay deploys). After about 256 sender-sessions have delivered at least one message to a given device (a few weeks), that device silently stops showing any new chat in that room. Senders keep seeing 'routed'. Nothing short of wiping chat history fixes it.
findings.suggested_fix: Prune fences for sessions that are superseded. A fence whose actor has a higher accepted hello epoch in SyncReplayState (or a different persisted sessionDomain) can never validate again, because applyChatV3 requires the active session. Delete it when a newer hello is accepted. Keep the cap only as a defensive limit on concurrently active identities, evicting superseded fences first.
findings.proving_test: TacMapChatHistoryStoreTest and TacMapChatStoreTests: call acceptInbound for 257 distinct (actor, sd, kid) identities (for example one actor with 257 successive session domains), one message each. Assert that the 257th is ACCEPTED once earlier sessions are marked superseded. Today it returns REPLAY_REJECTED / .rejected.

findings.title: iOS v3 handshake watchdog is a fixed 30 s from connect to hello-ack and is never re-armed, so large snapshots on slow links never finish and re-download forever
findings.description: handshakeTimeout = 30 (SyncManager.swift:656-659). It is armed once in connect() (:1666). Nothing re-arms it: there is no call at snapshot-begin, on snapshot pages, or at snapshot-end (:1854-1883, :3362-3400). Those 30 s must cover TLS, the upgrade, downloading the whole snapshot (relay pages up to 900 KB, total up to about 50 MB; index.ts:20,26), main-actor validation of every record (AEAD, Ed25519, GeoJSON parse and export per record, plus the O(n²) lookups in S3-10), the hello, and the hello-ack. On timeout it disconnects and reconnects with backoff, then starts from zero. Android instead re-arms a 20 s progress timer per phase and per page (SyncManager.kt:1902,1934,1975,3599-3623). That is more robust, but it is still tied to 900 KB pages, which need at least about 360 kbps.
findings.failure_scenario: A room with 2,000 objects and tombstones (about 3-4 MB snapshot) on a degraded cellular link (about 500 kbps) or a satellite link takes over 60 s. iOS times out at 30 s, reconnects, and downloads the snapshot again, every ≤30 s plus backoff, forever. It never converges and burns data. Android on the same link succeeds.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the iOS watchdog progress-based, as Android is: re-arm it on each received frame or byte and at each phase. Move snapshot validation off the main actor. Reduce the relay's page size (e.g., 128-256 KB) so per-frame progress checks work on slow links for both clients.
findings.proving_test: iOS XCTest with an injected clock and fake socket: deliver snapshot-begin and then one page every 10 s for 60 s, then snapshot-end and hello-ack. Assert status becomes .connected. Today the timeout fires at 30 s. Android analogue: pages every 25 s at 900 KB should not time out if progress is byte-based.

findings.title: Delivery-retry timers start when a frame is queued, not when it is sent, so slow uplinks get duplicate frames and a 23 s cancel that stops large objects from ever syncing
findings.description: queueDelivery enqueues the frame and immediately schedules a retry at 1 s. The retries resend the whole frame at 1, 3, 7 and 15 s. At 23 s, with no ack, it reports an error and cancels the socket (SyncManager.kt:1157-1187; OutboundDeliveryTracker.kt:133,176-181; SyncManager.swift:2213-2248, maxAttempts 5 at :252-254,300). Nothing waits for the transport to finish writing the first copy. A v3 ciphertext can be up to 700 KB (index.ts:22). The retry copies queue behind the first one, which multiplies upload volume up to 5x. The relay then dedups them one by one (index.ts:1190) and applies its 4 MiB / 200-message window (index.ts:27-29).
findings.failure_scenario: A long freedraw (about 500 KB) on a 150 kbps uplink needs about 27 s to upload. At 23 s the client cancels mid-frame and reconnects, forced-diffs, resends, and cancels again. The object never syncs and the loop never ends. A bulk queue of 200 × 5 KB on the same link is similar: tail frames pass 23 s before they are even written, the retry copies starve the queue, and every cycle ends in cancel or 4008.
findings.suggested_fix: Start the ack watchdog from the transport's write completion. iOS already has one in URLSessionWebSocketTask.send; on Android, track OkHttp queueSize() draining. Do not re-send a frame while an identical copy is still queued. Scale the timeout with frame size and measured throughput. Treat 'no ack' as a transport problem only after the bytes have actually left.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM test with a fake SyncWebSocket that 'transmits' at 150 kbps and acks only after the bytes drain. Send one 500 KB put and assert it is acknowledged with ≤1 copy sent and no socket cancel. Today it cancels at 23 s after queuing 5 copies. iOS equivalent with a stub task that delays its send completion.

findings.title: A bulk publish of about 200 or more objects (e.g., a KML import) trips the relay's 200 msg/10 s limit and every client's 200-frame live receive budget, so all devices flap
findings.description: syncLocalStateV3 sends one frame per changed object back-to-back with no pacing. So does the hello-ack path, which also resends all recoverable deletes (SyncManager.kt:1304-1336, 2249-2255; SyncManager.swift:2271-2313, 3563-3575). The relay closes a socket with 4008 once it exceeds 200 messages or 4 MiB per 10 s, or 200 queued frames (index.ts:27-31, 744-751, 862-878). Each stored put is broadcast to every peer. Clients close their own socket (1008) past 200 frames per 10 s in LIVE phase (SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:98-106; .swift:109-113). On the sender, the 200 op-acks alone fill its budget. Convergence then happens only through repeated disconnect → full snapshot → publish-the-rest cycles.
findings.failure_scenario: A user imports a 500-placemark KML while in a room. After about 200 frames the relay closes the sender with 4008. Every receiver trips its own 200-frame budget and disconnects too. All devices re-snapshot, the sender publishes about 200 more, and the flap repeats about 3 times with 'disconnected' banners on every device. The same happens on first join with a large existing mission, or after S3-02. Proven: vitest 'S3 rate' sends 250 puts after hello-ack and observes close code 4008 (scratchpad/sync-s3/test/s3audit.test.ts, passes).
findings.suggested_fix: Pace outbound mutations on the client with a token bucket (e.g., ≤15 frames/s and ≤300 KB/s, with a bounded in-flight window waiting on acks). Exclude op-ack and op-nack from the client's live receive budget, or give them a separate budget. Consider a relay batch-put frame or a higher per-socket budget for authenticated durable writes.
findings.proving_test: Relay: vitest 'S3 rate' above. Clients: a JVM/XCTest harness that inserts 500 waypoints while CONNECTED. Assert the emitted frames never exceed 200 per rolling 10 s and that no socket cancel occurs.

findings.title: Snapshot records are all validated before any is applied, so records carrying different metadata for the same unknown layer fail the post-apply hash and stop sync with a security error
findings.description: Android computes expectedModelHash when each page arrives, using the layers present at that moment plus the record's own newLayers (SyncManager.kt:2574-2601, 2635-2647). iOS does the same for all records at snapshot-end, before applying any (SyncManager.swift:3467-3476, 3972-3985). Application then runs in order. Only the first record's copy of an unknown layer id is added (SyncManager.kt:2738-2743; DrawingStore.swift addLayersVerbatimDurably). Each exported object carries its layer's name and colour (GeoJsonExporter.kt:71-74,163-166; GeoJSONExporter.swift:80-83,166-171). A later record whose layer name or colour differs therefore re-exports to a different hash. That hits `modelContentHash != expected` → persistenceFailure (SyncManager.kt:2662-2666, 3668-3684) or failClosedV3 (SyncManager.swift:3831-3834, 3498-3500). Both set wantConnected=false. Layer metadata is never synced separately, so rooms carry mixed names and colours whenever one device renames or recolours a layer, or when devices store default-layer names in different languages.
findings.failure_scenario: Device B renames custom layer L from 'Recon' to 'Scouts', which republishes B's objects in L as 'Scouts'. Device A still has 'Recon' and later edits one object in L. A new device C joins. The first snapshot record in L adds L='Recon', the 'Scouts' record fails its hash check, and C shows 'Sync stopped because rollback state could not be secured'. C has to rejoin manually; the second join heals because L now exists locally.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the expected model hash after preceding snapshot records have been applied: validate for authenticity up front, but compute the receiver-local hash immediately before each apply. Alternatively compute it against a staged layer set that accumulates newLayers in apply order. Treat a mismatch that only comes from layer adoption as success, and baseline to the actual re-export.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM and iOS XCTest: a snapshot with two drawing records signed by fixture key B. Both reference layer_id L, which is absent locally; one has tacticalmaps:layer='Recon', the other 'Scouts'. Assert that hello is sent and the status is CONNECTED. Today Android calls persistenceFailure and iOS calls failClosedV3.

findings.title: Offline edits are silently overwritten whenever a peer changed the same object while this device was offline: whoever reconnects first wins, whatever the edit order
findings.description: At snapshot-end each pending marker captures priorModelHash from the current model, which already includes the offline edit. It also captures acceptedGeneration from the current journal, which already counts that edit (SyncManager.kt:1945-1949; SyncManager.swift:3480-3487). pendingModelDecision therefore sees an unchanged generation and current==prior, and returns APPLY_INCOMING (SyncReplayState.kt:414-426; SyncReplayState.swift:287-296). The remote version replaces the offline edit, and only a transient toast is shown. The generation journal only protects the window between marker and apply. There is no per-object 'generation or hash at last sync' baseline, even though the ADR says the journal is updated 'even while disconnected'.
findings.failure_scenario: A and B both edit waypoint W while offline. B reconnects first and publishes W at a new stamp. A reconnects later and its (possibly newer) edit is replaced by B's without any conflict prompt. The same applies to an offline delete, which resurrects the object. Both devices converge, but user data is lost, always against the device that reconnects later.
findings.suggested_fix: Persist a per-object sync baseline, for example the journal generation at the last accept or ack, inside the replay state. At snapshot time, if the local generation is above that baseline, treat the object as LOCAL_DIVERGED: keep the local edit and republish at a new stamp, or surface a conflict. Document the chosen semantics in ADR-001.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM test: sync W at S0, disconnect, edit W locally (generation bumps), then deliver a snapshot with W at S1 from actor B. Assert the local edit is kept and republished at a stamp above S1, or that a conflict is surfaced. Today W is overwritten. Mirror this in XCTest.

findings.title: Snapshot processing and bulk acks do O(n²) main-thread work (a full HMAC scan per tombstone and a full-model re-export per ack), risking ANRs and feeding the iOS timeout
findings.description: Every snapshot or live delete calls findLocalIdForWireId. That computes an HMAC for every lastContent key, then every waypoint, then every drawing (SyncManager.kt:2559-2564, 2961-2977; SyncManager.swift:3930, 4173-4196). Android also creates a new Mac instance for each HMAC (SyncIdentity.kt:55-61). Tombstones are never garbage-collected (see S3-13), and a missing object scans everything, so a snapshot costs about 2·N_tomb·M HMACs. This runs on Dispatchers.Main.immediate (SyncManager.kt:180-182) and on the iOS main actor. Separately, every op-ack triggers a full syncLocalState that re-exports and hashes every object (SyncManager.kt:2041-2043; SyncManager.swift:3041-3050), so K acks cost K·M GeoJSON exports.
findings.failure_scenario: A room with 1,500 tombstones and 700 local objects costs about 2M HMACs, roughly 10-30 s on Android's main thread, on every reconnect. That means an ANR, or a handshake timeout on iOS (S3-05). A 500-object import costs 500 acks × 500 exports on the UI thread.
findings.suggested_fix: Build a wireId→localId map once per connection and keep it updated incrementally. Reuse one Mac/HMAC key per room. Coalesce post-ack syncLocalState calls into the existing debounce. Run snapshot validation off the main thread and apply results on it.
findings.proving_test: A JVM test with a counting metadataKey HMAC wrapper: a snapshot of 1,000 tombstones with 1,000 local objects should need ≤ 3,000 HMAC calls (today about 2,000,000). A second test counts GeoJsonExporter.export calls across 200 acks: it should need ≤ 400 (today about 40,000).

findings.title: If the replay state is lost or quarantined while the device seed survives, the hello epoch restarts at 1 and the relay returns 4014 on every attempt, locking the device out for N reconnects
findings.description: SafeStore moves an undecodable replay file aside (SafeStore.kt:127-134; SafeStore.swift:243-246). The next join starts from empty state, but the device seed is stored separately, so the actorId is unchanged. reserveHelloEpoch goes from 0 to 1 (SyncReplayState.kt:240-248; SyncReplayState.swift:173-175). The relay requires the epoch to exceed its stored value and closes with 4014 otherwise (index.ts:1126-1129, 999-1004). Neither client handles 4014 specially: each attempt is a generic disconnect and reconnect with backoff, and each one downloads the full snapshot and raises the epoch by 1.
findings.failure_scenario: The replay decoder rejects a state, as happened with the historical orphan-epoch bug that needed repair code. The file is quarantined. On rejoin, a device whose relay epoch is 800 needs 800 connect attempts (hours at the 30 s backoff cap), each re-downloading the snapshot, before it can sync again.
findings.suggested_fix: When no epoch is persisted, seed the hello epoch from wall-clock milliseconds (epoch = max(persisted+1, nowMs)). Epochs are u64, and the ones previously used were small counters, so this is always higher. Alternatively have the relay report its stored epoch on 4014 (it is not secret) so the client can jump past it.
findings.proving_test: Relay vitest: register actor A at epoch 800, then connect with epoch 1 and expect 4014. Client unit test: start with an empty replay state, reserveHelloEpoch, and assert the result is above 0x0000017000000000 (a time-seeded value). Today it returns 0000000000000001.

findings.title: Every accepted presence frame rewrites and reseals the whole replay state, so write I/O grows with room size × peers
findings.description: commitPresence calls persistTransaction, which calls save() → SafeStore.writeAtomically(encode()) (SyncReplayState.kt:305-315, 112-122, 478-487). acceptPresence calls persist() (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195, 488-492). Each call serializes every stamp, tombstone and content hash (about 230 B per object), AEAD-seals the result, fsyncs and renames. Presence arrives every 5 s from each peer (SyncManager.kt:2894; SyncManager.swift:4127).
findings.failure_scenario: A room with 2,000 objects and tombstones (state about 460 KB) and 10 peers produces about 2 presence frames per second. That is about 1 MB/s of sealed, fsynced writes for as long as the device is connected, which costs battery and flash wear. The cost grows without bound as tombstones accumulate.
findings.suggested_fix: Store the presence high-water separately in a small sealed file, or batch it. For example, persist it only when the counter advances by at least 1,000 or every 60 s, and on load reject counters no higher than persisted+window. This is still replay-safe, because the relay also enforces per-session counters and a new session resets. Alternatively keep the object state in an append-only journal.
findings.proving_test: A JVM/XCTest with a counting persistOverride or persistenceWriter: 100 accepted presence frames with 2,000 stamps loaded. Assert ≤ 2 full-state writes (today 100) and bytes written < 1 MB (today about 46 MB).

findings.title: Tombstones and actor pins are never garbage-collected, so long-lived rooms reach MAX_RECORDS; new objects are then rejected and new devices reconnect-loop on 4013
findings.description: Deletes are stored as records permanently (index.ts:1206). Actor pins count toward MAX_RECORDS=10,000 (index.ts:19, 1136-1140, 1196-1204). Only 7-day idle expiry removes data. Once the room is full: a new put gets nack 'quota', and the object remains local-only (SyncManager.kt:2052, 2059-2066). A new device's hello gets close 4013 (index.ts:1001-1004), which both clients treat as a normal disconnect: reconnect with backoff and a full snapshot, forever.
findings.failure_scenario: A busy unit room accumulates 10k create/delete events over some months, plus pins from reinstalls. After that, newly created objects never reach peers (divergence with a 'room full' banner), and a replacement phone can never join; it loops every 30 s.
findings.suggested_fix: Add tombstone compaction: drop tombstones older than a horizon and track a durable per-room 'compacted below counter C' floor that clients use to reject older resurrecting puts. Garbage-collect actor pins with no live objects that have not been seen within the horizon. Handle 4013 and quota specifically on the client: stop reconnecting and show a room-full state.
findings.proving_test: Relay vitest: fill 9,999 records with put+del pairs, then send hello from a new actor and assert a graceful non-loop signal. Client test: assert that close code 4013 does not schedule a reconnect.

findings.title: v2 equal-version tie: the relay picks the higher `by`, but both clients reject an equal `v`, so the first writer keeps its version until it reconnects
findings.description: On the relay, isNewer is `a.v > b.v || (a.v===b.v && a.by > b.by)` (index.ts:174-176, 922). Android accepts only `versions[id] < v` (SyncManager.kt:62-69, 2086). iOS returns if `known >= v` (SyncManager.swift:3179). Each sender sets versions[id]=clock before sending (SyncManager.kt:1289-1291; SyncManager.swift:2099-2101). When two devices that have seen the same history edit the same object, both send the same v. The first to arrive is acked. The second overwrites it only if its `by` is higher, and it is then broadcast to the first writer, who drops it as not newer. Nothing triggers a reconnect.
findings.failure_scenario: In a v2 room, A and B (both at clock 41) move the same waypoint; both send v=42. The relay stores A's, then replaces it with B's because B.by > A.by, and broadcasts B's to A. A rejects it and keeps showing its own position, while the relay and all other peers show B's. This lasts until A reconnects.
findings.suggested_fix: In v2 clients, accept an equal v when `by` is greater, mirroring the relay: compare (v, by) tuples and store the last-applied `by` per id. Alternatively make the relay nack equal-v writes so the sender reconciles.
findings.proving_test: Android JVM and iOS XCTest (v2): set versions[X]=42 from a local send, then deliver a verified put {id:X, v:42, by:<greater clientId>}. Assert it is applied. Today it is dropped.

findings.title: A same-stamp recovery resend that the relay already stored is nacked 'stale', which both clients treat as fatal (cancel and reconnect)
findings.description: recoverableLocalPut resends an already-reserved stamp under the new session's sd, with a new signature and IV (SyncReplayState.kt:435-441; SyncManager.kt:1319; SyncManager.swift:2295-2298, 2322). If the relay already holds that exact (id, vs, by) from an earlier session, sameV3Record fails because sd and ct differ, and isNewerStamp is false, so the relay replies stale/retry:false (index.ts:1190-1192, 1235-1238). The clients cancel the socket (SyncManager.kt:2063-2065; SyncManager.swift:3091-3093). A stamp is reserved only once per actor mutation, and recoverable resends require an identical content hash, so equal (vs, by, kind, deleted) means the same logical write. If a platform's own import→export is not an exact fixed point for some object, the snapshot's NONE branch forces this resend on every connect and the reconnect never ends.
findings.failure_scenario: A sends put X@S1 and loses the network. The frame reaches the relay after A has already reconnected and snapshotted without X@S1. A resends X@S1 with sd2 and gets 'stale', which costs an extra reconnect. Where re-export differs from the sent bytes, this repeats forever.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the relay ack as 'duplicate' whenever the existing record has the same id, vs, by, pub, kind and deleted, even if sd or ct differ. Have clients treat a stale nack whose stamp equals their persisted stamp as confirmed.
findings.proving_test: Relay vitest: hello(sd1) then put(5) acked; reconnect with hello2(sd2), then put(5, {sd: SD_2, ct: other}). Expect op-ack. Today it returns op-nack 'stale'.

findings.title: The relay writes meta:lastActivity to storage (and reads the alarm) on every presence, chat and mutation frame
findings.description: processWebSocketMessage calls touchActivity() after every non-ping frame (index.ts:793-805). touchActivity performs storage.put('meta:lastActivity') and getAlarm() (index.ts:1564-1568). The idle TTL is 7 days (index.ts:33), so activity at a granularity of minutes or hours is enough. Presence at a 5 s cadence dominates the traffic.
findings.failure_scenario: A room with 10 connected devices does about 170k billable Durable Object writes per day purely for liveness bookkeeping. That scales linearly with the number of active rooms and adds latency to every frame.
findings.suggested_fix: Cache the last-written activity time in memory and only persist it when more than one hour has passed. alarm() already re-checks the live socket count.
findings.proving_test: Relay vitest wrapping state.storage.put: send 50 loc frames and assert ≤ 1 'meta:lastActivity' write. Today there are 50.

verdicts.reasoning: Traced both directions and the finding holds. Android accepts a v2 id only if it matches a lowercase-only regex and then round-trips unchanged through UUID.toString() (SyncManager.kt:50-59). The version check happens after that canonicalization (:62-69), and isValidLegacySyncPut also requires objectId==recordId (:71-84). iOS sends v2 frames keyed by uppercase uuidString (SyncManager.swift:2084,2089,2099-2101) and does no lowercasing anywhere in SyncManager.swift (checked with grep), so Android drops every iOS v2 put and del. In the other direction, iOS applyRecord stores lastContent under the lowercase wire id (:3226). reexport compares against $0.id.uuidString and returns "" (:3321-3330). The next syncLocalState keys `current` by uppercase, so the lowercase key lands in `gone`. iOS then sends sendDel(lowercase) (:2104-2111, 2139-2161), which is validly sealed and signed over the lowercase id, plus a put under the uppercase id. Android verifies the del (v > versions[id]) and removes its own object via removeSyncedObject (:2161-2219). The relay treats ids as opaque. v2 is still reachable, but only with an explicit "2:" prefix and a legacy-warning confirmation (SyncDialog.kt:258-260; SyncManager.swift:1166,1229-1236). That is why I keep this at high rather than critical: silent data loss on Android, but only in a deprecated, explicitly warned mode.

alarm() calls deleteAll after 7 days with no sockets (index.ts:834-847), which resets meta:seq and meta:highWater. Client replay state keeps localCounter, and reservations use max(localCounter, roomHighWater())+1 (SyncReplayState.kt:328-329,350; SyncReplayState.swift:199-203). The relay's counter-window check is stamp.counter > highWater+10000 → nack retry:false (index.ts:1193-1195). Both clients cancel the socket on counter-window (SyncManager.kt:2059-2066; SyncManager.swift:3088-3093). Backoff is reset at hello-ack (SyncManager.kt:2236; SyncReconnectBackoff.kt base 1 s), so the loop runs at about 1 s. The rollback SECURITY warning fires on every connect (SyncManager.kt:1904-1910; iOS wasStale at :3478,3522-3528) because lastSnapshotSeq only ratchets up. I re-ran the auditor's 'S3 expiry' vitest in my own copy and it passes. One nuance the auditor missed: after an app restart (lastContent empty), own objects are resent at their OLD stamps via recoverableLocalPut, and old own tombstones via recoverableLocalDeletes. Those at or below highWater+10000 are accepted and raise highWater, so a device can climb out only if its own stamp set chains up from 10,000 or less with gaps of 10,000 or less. Objects authored by others always get fresh stamps above localCounter. So for a device that joined after the counter passed 10k, or that holds peers' objects, the loop is effectively permanent. If lastContent survives and nothing is edited, nothing is republished at all, and new joiners silently see an empty room.

The relay stores any put/del with a well-formed outer (kind regex only, index.ts:1156-1166). On Android, parseOuterV3 rejects any kind other than waypoint/drawing (SyncManager.kt:2536). validateRecordV3 returns null on a signature failure, a parse failure, invalidSkipped!=0 or a wire-id mismatch (:2544-2601). The snapshot page handler then sets snapshotInvalid (:1921-1929), and snapshot-end calls failSnapshot → failConnection → ws.cancel (:1941-1942, 3643-3666). onClosed/onFailure ignore close codes (:1130-1140), so the client reconnects with backoff forever, and the backoff is never reset because hello-ack is never reached. iOS finishSnapshotV3 calls failClosedV3 on the first invalid record (SyncManager.swift:3467-3474), which sets wantConnected=false (:2555-2571). The live path just drops the same record (Android :2605-2606; iOS 3790-3792). The threat model says room members are only 'partly trusted' (THREAT_MODEL.md:56), so a single join-code holder, for example a lost or captured phone, can brick the room for everyone. Caveat on the suggested fix: the relay cannot check AEAD, so an insider can also store garbage ct. Keeping AEAD failure fatal for the whole snapshot would still leave the insider DoS open. AEAD failures also need per-record skipping.

Fences are keyed by (actorId, sessionDomain, chatKeyId) (TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:191-193; TacMapChatStore.swift:339-343). sessionDomain is regenerated on every connect (SyncManager.kt:1063-1064; iOS similar). Once 256 fences exist, any new identity returns REPLAY_REJECTED / .rejected (kt:212-216, MAX 256 at :449; swift:356-362, max 256 at :58). Nothing removes entries from `replay`: close(), lock() and the fail* helpers only clear memory, and the persisted file keeps them. The receiver silently ignores the rejection (SyncManager.kt:2492; SyncManager.swift:3721-3722), while the relay has already acked routing to the sender. Pruning superseded sessions is safe: commitActorHello rejects older epochs and only re-activates an equal epoch with the same sd (SyncReplayState.kt:268-277; ADR-001), so fences for superseded sessions can never validate again. With realistic daily chat and reconnects, a device hits 256 in weeks and then stops showing new chat in that room for good.

SyncConnectionWatchdogPolicy.handshakeTimeout = 30 (SyncManager.swift:659). scheduleV3HandshakeTimeout is called only from connect() (:1666). All other references cancel it (:1272,1596,1760,1821,1837,2558,3550), and snapshot-begin, pages and snapshot-end never re-arm it (:3364-3399). On expiry it calls handleDisconnect and cancel (:1854-1883). So TLS, the upgrade, the whole snapshot download, main-actor validation of every record, and the hello round trip all share one fixed 30 s budget, and every retry starts again from zero. Android re-arms a 20 s progress timer at snapshot-begin, on every page and after snapshot-end (SyncManager.kt:1902,1934,1975,3599-3623), so the two platforms genuinely diverge. On a degraded link of about 500 kbps, 30 s covers only about 1.9 MB of snapshot, which a mature room with freedraws exceeds. The relay's serialized, quadratic snapshot generation (see missed item 1) makes this worse during reconnect storms.

Android queueDelivery sends the frame and immediately schedules a retry at 1000<<(attempts-1), capped at 8 s (SyncManager.kt:1157-1187). Attempts start at 1 and maxAttempts is 5 (OutboundDeliveryTracker.kt:37,133,176-190). That gives identical resends at 1, 3, 7 and 15 s, then an 'unconfirmed' error and ws.cancel at 23 s. iOS matches: min(8, 2^(n-1)), send completion ignored `{ _ in }`, then task.cancel (SyncManager.swift:2213-2248). Neither timer is tied to write completion, so copies queue behind the unsent original in OkHttp or URLSession. Each duplicate also counts against the relay's 200 msg / 4 MiB per 10 s window (index.ts:744-751, 862-878), which feeds S3-07. On links where the ack takes more than 1 s (satellite, EDGE, bufferbloat), every frame is sent at least twice. A single frame that needs more than 23 s to upload (e.g., about 430 KB at 150 kbps) never converges. Bulk backlogs do converge, but only through repeated cancel and reconnect churn.

syncLocalStateV3 sends one frame per changed object back-to-back with no pacing (SyncManager.kt:1304-1336; iOS 2271-2313). The hello-ack path also resends recoverable deletes (kt:2249-2255). The relay closes with 4008 when a socket passes 200 pending or 200 messages per 10 s (index.ts:27-31, 744-751, 862-878). Both clients close themselves once they receive more than 200 frames per 10 s while CONNECTED (SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:59-106 with the phase chosen at SyncManager.kt:1779-1794; SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:103-113 with the phase at SyncManager.swift:1703-1707). op-acks count against the sender's budget, and each stored put is broadcast to every receiver. I re-ran the auditor's 'S3 rate' vitest in my own copy: 250 puts after hello-ack → close 4008, and it passes. Importing a KML of more than 200 placemarks while connected, or joining with a large local mission, is ordinary use. The result is several flap cycles across all devices, with the backoff reset to about 1 s at each hello-ack.

Android computes expectedModelHash at page arrival from the current doc.layers plus that record's own newLayers (SyncManager.kt:2574-2601, 2635-2647). Nothing is applied until snapshot-end. The importer mints a new layer from the record's layer_name and colour when neither the id nor the name is known (GeoJsonImporter.kt:247-282). applyValidatedV3 adds a new layer only if its id is absent, so the first record wins (:2738-2743). The exporter embeds the layer name and colour (GeoJsonExporter.kt:71-74,163-166). A second record carrying the same unknown layer_id with a different name or colour therefore re-exports to a hash that differs from its expected value. APPLY_INCOMING returns false (:2662-2666) → persistenceFailure → wantConnected=false (:3668-3684). iOS behaves the same: receiverModelHash is computed from all records up front (SyncManager.swift:3972-3985), addLayersVerbatimDurably is first-wins (DrawingStore.swift:175-185), the exporter embeds the name and colour (GeoJSONExporter.swift:80-83,166-171), and a mismatch → false → failClosedV3 (:3831-3834, 3498-3500). Mixed metadata is realistic: a rename on B republishes B's copies of every object in L (the export changes), while A keeps its old name and publishes it on the next edit. The problem heals on the second join because the pending marker then resolves as ALREADY_APPLIED. Medium is right.

The mechanism is exactly as described. Offline edits reserve no stamp (syncLocalState is gated on CONNECTED). At snapshot-end, priorModelHash and acceptedGeneration are captured from the current, already edited model and journal (SyncManager.kt:1945-1949; SyncManager.swift:3480-3487). pendingModelDecision therefore returns APPLY_INCOMING (SyncReplayState.kt:414-426; SyncReplayState.swift:287-296), and a concurrent remote stamp overwrites the unpublished offline edit. I downgrade severity because this is the documented v3 LWW design, where stamps are assigned at publish time and there are no wall clocks (ADR-001 invariants at 290-313 only protect the marker-to-apply crash window). The edits are genuinely concurrent, so any LWW must discard one. Devices converge. An offline edit that has no concurrent remote change is preserved via the NONE → forcedLocalDiff path (kt:2677-2684). The real gap is conflict surfacing and UX. The suggested 'keep local and republish' fix only changes which device loses.

findLocalIdForWireId computes an HMAC for every lastContent key, then every waypoint, then every drawing (SyncManager.kt:2961-2977; SyncManager.swift:4173-4196). It is called for every delete record in validateRecordV3 (kt:2559-2564; swift:3930), and an absent object triggers a full scan, so a snapshot costs about 2·T·M HMACs. Android creates a new Mac instance for every call (SyncIdentity.kt:55-61), and scope is Dispatchers.Main.immediate (SyncManager.kt:180-182). Every op-ack runs a full syncLocalState synchronously (kt:2041-2043; swift:3041-3050), and that exports and hashes every object and computes its wire-id HMAC (kt:1265-1316). K acks therefore cost K·M exports on the UI thread. Mature rooms or bulk imports reach seconds of main-thread work, which means ANR or jank and more pressure on the iOS 30 s watchdog.

A corrupt replay file is quarantined and load fails closed (SafeStore.kt:127-134; SyncReplayState.kt:503-521), so the next join starts from empty state. The device seed is stored separately (iOS: sealed in UserDefaults, SyncManager.swift:1135-1153), so the actorId is unchanged. reserveHelloEpoch goes 0→1 (SyncReplayState.kt:240-248; .swift:166-179). registerActor returns 'replay' when incoming <= stored → close 4014 (index.ts:1126-1129, 999-1004). Neither client looks at close codes (Android onClosed → handleSocketEnded at SyncManager.kt:1130-1140; grep shows no 4013/4014 handling), so the device needs N backoff-paced attempts, each downloading a full snapshot. My vitest (verify.test.ts 'S3-11') registers epoch 800, connects with epoch 1 and observes close 4014. The trigger is rare: there is no Forget Room feature, and a reinstall wipes both the seed and the state. That makes this an edge case with a severe hours-long lockout, so medium.

Android commitPresence → persistTransaction → save() → SafeStore.writeAtomically(encode()) of the whole state: all stamps, tombstones, hashes, actors, epochs and pending markers (SyncReplayState.kt:112-122, 305-315, 478-487). It runs on the main-dispatcher message path for every accepted loc frame (SyncManager.kt:2894). iOS acceptPresence → persist() on every frame (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195). The foreground presence cadence is 5 s per peer (UnitSyncPresenceCadence.kt:103). Tombstones are never compacted, so each write grows with the room's history, multiplied by the peer count. For large rooms that is a real battery and flash cost.

Tombstones are stored as records permanently (index.ts:1196-1212). Actor pins count toward MAX_RECORDS=10,000 (index.ts:19, 1136-1140), and only the 7-day idle expiry clears anything. When the room is full, new objects get nack 'quota' with retry:false. That does not cancel the socket (SyncManager.kt:2052,2059-2066), so the object stays local-only. A new actor's hello gets 4013. My vitest (verify.test.ts 'S3-13') sets meta:totalRecords=10000 and observes 4013. Clients ignore close codes and reconnect forever with full snapshots. Reaching 10k records takes months of create/delete churn in an active room, so medium.

The relay's isNewer breaks ties on `by` (index.ts:174-176, 922). Android accepts only versions[id] < v (SyncManager.kt:62-69), and iOS returns when known >= v (SyncManager.swift:3179). Senders set versions[id]=clock before sending (kt:1289-1291; swift:2099-2101), and v2 clocks are Lamport-like, so concurrent editors that have seen the same history emit equal v. When the later writer has the higher `by`, the relay stores it, but the first writer and any third party that already applied the first write reject it, so they diverge. I downgrade to low because this is legacy v2 only and it heals on the next reconnect: v2 clears versions and lastContent in connect() (kt:1075-1081; swift:1640-1643) and applies the relay's winner from the snapshot. Mobile clients reconnect often.

recoverableLocalPut reuses the reserved stamp (SyncReplayState.kt:435-441). It is re-signed under the new sd and freshly sealed, so the ct differs. sameV3Record requires sd and ct to be equal, and isNewerStamp is false on equality, so the relay returns stale with retry:false (index.ts:1190-1192, 1235-1238). Both clients cancel on stale (SyncManager.kt:2063-2065; SyncManager.swift:3091-3093), and the ~1 s loop comes from the hello-ack backoff reset. My vitest (verify.test.ts 'S3-15') shows put(5) acked in session 1, then put(5) with SD_2 and a different ct → {op-nack, stale, retry:false}. The trigger needs a narrow race (the old socket's frame is stored between the new snapshot and the new hello), or a hypothetical non-fixed-point import/export (NONE branch → forcedLocalDiff, kt:2677-2684), so low.

processWebSocketMessage calls touchActivity after every handled non-ping frame (index.ts:793-805). touchActivity does storage.put('meta:lastActivity') plus getAlarm on every call (index.ts:1564-1568), while IDLE_TTL is 7 days. My vitest (verify.test.ts 'S3-16') sends 10 loc frames and observes a distinct persisted lastActivity after each one. That is one billable write per presence frame. The cost is minor but real and scales with rooms × peers.
