A Node replica (scratchpad/audit-sync/snapbench.mjs) measured 0.9 s of CPU for 2k records and 5.0 s for 10k records on an M-series Mac; workerd will be slower. Every connect blocks the whole room for that long. During a reconnect storm (relay deploy, or the S3-02/S3-03/S3-13 loops) the snapshots run one after another, so later iOS clients pass their fixed 30 s watchdog (S3-05) and reconnect, which feeds the storm. Fix: keep a running byte total (sum of per-record JSON lengths plus separators) instead of re-serializing the chunk.

(2) Generalizing S3-02 and S3-15. Both clients reset the reconnect backoff at hello-ack (SyncManager.kt:2236; SyncManager.swift:3552), so any fatal nack after the handshake (stale, counter-window, session-*) loops at about 1 s instead of backing off. The backoff should only reset once the session has actually been stable, for example after the first op-ack or after N seconds.

(3) The S3-03 suggested fix is incomplete. The relay cannot verify AEAD, so an insider can store undecryptable ct. Keeping AEAD failure fatal for the whole snapshot still leaves the room-brick DoS open, so AEAD-invalid records also need per-record skip-and-warn. Only structural and fence violations should stay fatal.

(4) Snapshot validation and apply run on the main thread on both platforms, beyond the HMAC cost in S3-10: per-record AES-GCM, Ed25519 verify, GeoJSON parse and export. Android does this per page on Dispatchers.Main.immediate (SyncManager.kt:1921-1929, 2544-2601). iOS does it for all records at snapshot-end on the main actor (SyncManager.swift:3467-3476). Large rooms get ANRs or jank on every reconnect.

audit.summary:
How it works: the Worker (sync/src/index.ts:566-601) routes /room (v2) and /v3/room to a per-room SyncRoom Durable Object that uses hibernatable sockets. On connect, fetch() checks the token or room binding, runs ensureV3Accounting, and then, inside blockConcurrencyWhile, sends a seq-fenced snapshot (snapshot-begin, 900 KB snapshot pages, snapshot-end), followed by each live peer's hello, chat-key and loc (1486-1529).

webSocketMessage checks the frame size in UTF-8 bytes before parsing (698-729). It keeps a per-socket FIFO queue with pending caps per socket (200 frames / 4 MiB) and per room (512 / 8 MiB), plus a rolling limit of 200 frames / 4 MiB per 10 s per socket (744-878). Parsers are strict: exactKeys, canonical base64url checked by re-encoding, and Ed25519 verification before any fence, pin or route. put/del are written in a transaction with room-wide record and byte quotas and a counter window (1148-1228). Presence and chat counters are per session.

Clients check UTF-8 bytes before JSON parsing and enforce an aggregate live budget of 200 frames / 4 MiB per 10 s. Android also has a bounded Draft_6455 (frame and fragment caps, wire budget, reader-thread backpressure with a 10 s timeout); iOS sets maximumMessageSize and suppresses compression. Integer parsing is strict (no float/bool confusion), base64 must be canonical, chat signatures are verified before decryption, and hello/presence are verified before any commit. Replay counters are stored durably. v3 snapshots are validated record by record, then committed to SyncReplayState and applied to the model stores.

What is solid: size limits before parse on all three components, crash safety (no force-unwrap or `!!` on untrusted paths, catch-all around parsing, stamps capped at 63 bits), ordering of signature checks, the replacement-fence logic, and atomic quota accounting. I found no crash bugs.

The weaknesses are availability under an authenticated insider and at scale:
- The snapshot fails closed on a single bad stored record (both platforms, permanent).
- The client's aggregate inbound budget equals the relay's per-sender budget, and neither side paces its sends.
- Several non-evicting caps and O(N²) or O(T×L) paths run on the main thread.
- A throw inside blockConcurrencyWhile resets the whole room (proven in workerd).

Relay proofs and benchmarks are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-cbrooker-Code-TacticalMaps/d9f42208-9d3f-40e1-9b8b-49fa6c488260/scratchpad/sync-s4/test/{s4,s4v2,s4touch}.test.ts and in audit-sync/{snapshot_bench.mjs,WireScan.java}.

findings.title: One stored record that a client cannot validate blocks every v3 client from ever reconnecting to the room
findings.description:
Relay: for v3 put/del the relay checks only the outer shape. `kind` can be any `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32}` (index.ts:1163) and `ct` any canonical base64 of at least 28 bytes (1165). A delete that carries a rid is stored even if the id never existed (1191). Accepted records are returned in every later snapshot (1486-1529).

Android: any record that fails validation makes the whole snapshot fail. SyncManager.kt:1920-1931 sets snapshotInvalid. Snapshot-end then calls failSnapshot (1941-1943, 3643-3653), which calls failConnection. handleSocketEnded then reconnects forever with backoff up to 30 s (1011-1028), downloading the full snapshot each time.

iOS: finishSnapshotV3 calls failClosedV3 on the first invalid record (SyncManager.swift:3467-3474). That sets wantConnected=false (2563), so sync stays off and every manual rejoin fails the same way.

The same record arriving live is silently dropped (Android 2606, iOS 3790-3792), so the damage only shows at the next reconnect.

Reasons a relay-accepted record fails client validation:
- AEAD open fails (Android 2549, iOS 3915-3917).
- kind is not waypoint/drawing (2536 / 3906).
- The importer reports invalidSkipped != 0 or the wrong object count (2585-2590 / 3935-3941).
- The wire id does not match the embedded UUID (2594 / 3945).
- The signature is bad.
- Platform divergence: iOS rejects a tombstone whose inner JSON contains "c" (3925), but Android accepts it (2553-2565).
- iOS only: a valid waypoint that reuses a local drawing's UUID throws identityCollision (SyncManager.swift:486-493). That calls failClosedV3 on both the snapshot path (3496-3499) and the live path (3806-3809).

Nothing can remove such a record:
- Honest clients never reach CONNECTED, so they cannot overwrite it.
- The relay has no admin delete.
- The 7-day idle expiry (834-847) never fires, because every reconnect calls touchActivity (689).
findings.failure_scenario:
1) A hostile or compromised member sends one frame after hello: {t:'put', id:<random 43-char b64url>, kind:'x', ct:<base64 of 64 random bytes>, rid}. The relay acks it. From the next reconnect on, every Android member loops every ~30 s downloading up to 54 MB and failing, and every iOS member's sync switches off permanently.
2) Benign version skew: TacMap vNext syncs a new kind (e.g. 'route') or emits a GeoJSON property or geometry that the older importer counts as invalidSkipped. All members still on the older version lose sync permanently.
3) An update that tightens importer validation makes records already stored invalid, so updated clients can never rejoin.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Treat per-record auth/parse failures in a snapshot as skip-and-quarantine: do not apply the record, do not advance replay state for that id, and show a non-fatal warning with a count. This is what the live path already does. Keep fail-closed only for fence, seq and structural violations.
- Skipping is security-equivalent to the relay omitting the record, which it can already do.
- On iOS, map identityCollision and invalidPayload to LOCAL_DIVERGED/skip instead of failClosedV3.
- Relay: accept only kind ∈ {waypoint, drawing} for v3 put and 'del' for del.
- Longer term: add a signed supersede or compaction path so members can tombstone a poison id.
findings.proving_test:
Relay (passes today): scratchpad/sync-s4/test/s4.test.ts 'S4-01'. The relay op-acks a garbage-ct record with kind 'future_kind' and a tombstone for a random id, and returns both in a later snapshot.

Android: SyncManager test feeding snapshot-begin{seq:1}, then a snapshot page {items:[validSignedWaypoint, sameShapeWith ct=base64(64 random bytes)], more:false}, then snapshot-end{seq:1}.
- Expected: hello is sent and the valid waypoint is applied.
- Today: failSnapshot runs and a reconnect is scheduled.

iOS: the same sequence through handleParsedMessageV3.
- Expected: wantConnected stays true.
- Today: failClosedV3.

findings.title: Client inbound budget (200 frames per 10 s) equals the relay's per-sender limit; no fan-out cap or send pacing, so one burst disconnects the room
findings.description:
Relay: each sender is limited to 200 msgs / 4 MiB per 10 s (index.ts:27-28, 862-878). There is no per-room fan-out cap; broadcast() sends to up to 63 peers (1556-1562).

Clients: both cap total inbound live traffic at the same 200 frames / 4 MiB per 10 s (Android SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:101-106, enforced at SyncManager.kt:1779-1794; iOS SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:111-114, enforced at SyncManager.swift:1703-1714). On overflow they close the socket with 1008/policyViolation (Android 1822-1835, iOS 1733-1750) and reconnect with a full snapshot.

Neither client paces what it sends: syncLocalStateV3 sends every pending diff in one loop (Android 1304-1336, iOS 2271-2312).

Baseline load: foreground presence every 5 s (UnitSyncPresenceCadence.kt:103, SyncManager.swift:573) is 2 frames per 10 s per peer. The client's own op-acks also count against its budget. Every reconnecting peer sends leave+hello+chat-key+loc to all others, so a storm feeds itself.
findings.failure_scenario:
Benign: 20-member room. One member imports a 250-waypoint KML, or joins the room already holding 250 local objects.
- The sender emits 250 puts; the relay closes it with 4008 around #200.
- Each receiver gets ~199 puts plus ~38 presence frames plus acks in under 10 s, which is over 200.
- All 19 receivers close with 1008, reconnect ~1 s later (backoff was reset at the last hello-ack), and each join broadcasts hello/chat-key/loc to the others, which can trip them again.

Hostile: one insider sends 199 valid loc frames per 10 s with increasing counters. The relay forwards all of them (proven: 199 delivered in under 3 s). Every honest client overflows at its first other frame and loops. More actors multiply the effect.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Make the limits consistent. Either the relay enforces a per-room aggregate fan-out bucket no higher than the client budget, or the client budget scales with authenticated sessions (e.g. 200 + 50×activeSessions frames, bytes similarly). For well-formed authenticated frames, throttle or drop rather than close.
- Add a client outbound token bucket (e.g. ≤100 mutations per 10 s) with the backlog carried across windows.
- Count op-ack/chat-ack separately from the budget.
- Do not reset reconnect backoff to 1 s immediately after a budget-triggered close.
findings.proving_test:
Relay (passes today): scratchpad/sync-s4/test/s4.test.ts 'S4-02' logs 199 loc frames delivered to the receiver within 3 s.

Client unit test: in one window, feed SyncLiveReceiveBudget 40 presence + 150 put + 11 ack frames (201 total). Today admit() returns false at frame 201 and SyncManager closes with 1008. Expected: no close.

Integration: two emulators on a local relay; import 250 waypoints on A. Today B goes OFFLINE with close code 1008.

findings.title: Each tombstone in a snapshot triggers a full HMAC scan of local objects on the main thread, on every reconnect
findings.description:
For every delete record, validateRecordV3 calls findLocalIdForWireId (Android SyncManager.kt:2563 → 2961-2980; iOS 3930 → 4173-4196). That function recomputes the HMAC-SHA256 wire id for every lastContent key, every waypoint and every drawing until one matches.

For a tombstone of an object the device does not hold, which is the normal case for deleted objects, this is a full scan of about 2L HMACs (L = local objects). Tombstones are kept for the room's lifetime (sync/README.md), and every record is re-validated on every snapshot, not only new ones.

Android also calls Mac.getInstance and init on every HMAC (SyncIdentity.kt:55-61), and all of this runs on the main thread (SyncManager.kt:180-181, Dispatchers.Main.immediate). Android validates one snapshot page at a time (~1,900 tombstones per 900 KB page). If a page takes over 10 s, SyncInboundCallbackGate (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:43-58, 132, 253-259) calls failSlowConsumer. The client reconnects, gets the same page, and never finishes.

iOS validates all records in one @MainActor loop at snapshot-end (3467-3475).

The relay accepts rid-bearing tombstones for ids that never existed (index.ts:1191), so an insider can create about 10k of them cheaply.

Desktop JVM benchmark reproducing the Android pattern (audit-sync/WireScan.java, M-series):

| local objects | tombstones | HMACs | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1,000 | 2M | 2.1 s |
| 2,000 | 2,000 | 8M | 8.2 s |
| 2,000 | 5,000 | 20M | 20 s |

Phones are typically 3-10× slower (Conscrypt JNI plus a Mac.getInstance on every HMAC).
findings.failure_scenario:
Long-lived room: 1,000 local objects and 2,000 retained tombstones, from benign create/delete churn or ~100 s of insider tombstone spam.
- Android: each snapshot page is about 1,900 × 2,000 HMACs, ~4 s on desktop and well over 10 s on a mid-range phone. The callback gate kills the socket, the reconnect loop never ends, and the user also sees ANRs.
- iOS: every reconnect freezes the UI for tens of seconds.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Keep a wireId→localId map, computed once per room key and updated on local add/remove/import.
- Reuse one initialised Mac, or cache per-UUID wire ids.
- Skip the reverse lookup for records that exactly match the persisted replay state.
- Move snapshot validation off the main thread.
findings.proving_test:
Benchmark: audit-sync/WireScan.java (included).

Android: SyncManager test with 1,000 local waypoints and one snapshot page of 1,800 valid signed tombstones for random ids. Assert handling takes under 1 s; today it performs ~3.6M HMACs.

iOS: XCTest measure{} on finishSnapshotV3 with the same fixture.

findings.title: Each remote record and presence frame rewrites and re-encrypts entire stores on the main thread (snapshot apply is O(N²) I/O)
findings.description:
Every accepted presence frame and every applied remote record synchronously rewrites the entire sealed replay-state file on the main thread (AES-GCM plus atomic rename; Android also fsyncs, SafeStore.kt:139-156). For records, the entire waypoint or drawing store file is rewritten as well.

Android:
- Presence: applyPresenceV3 → replay.commitPresence (SyncManager.kt:2894; SyncReplayState.kt:305-315) → persistTransaction (112-122). That copies all 9 maps via memorySnapshot (94-98) and calls save (775-788).
- Live record: commitRemoteAuthenticated (148-159), then a model write (WaypointStore.kt:75-79 → persistCandidate 258-270, which encodes the whole list), then clearPendingModelApplication (429-433). That is 3 full-file writes per record.
- Snapshot-end: calls resolvePendingModelApplication once per record.
- Every new peer actor's hello is also persisted (SyncReplayState.kt:280-284).

iOS mirrors this: acceptPresence persists (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195), clearPendingModelApplication persists (298-304), and addDurably rewrites the full file (WaypointStore.swift:129-137).

Size estimate: replay state holds ~220 B per object (+~450 B while pending), and the store ~600 B per waypoint. Applying N new objects on first join writes about 745·N² bytes with 2N fsyncs: N=1,000 ≈ 0.75 GB; N=2,000 ≈ 3 GB; N=5,000 ≈ 19 GB.
findings.failure_scenario:
(a) Joining a room with 2,000 objects means minutes of main-thread encrypt+fsync. Android ANRs, and the 10 s callback gate drops the socket partway through the apply. iOS freezes.
(b) Steady state with 20 peers and 3,000 objects: 4 presence frames/s × ~700 KB is ~2.8 MB/s of sealed rewrites plus fsyncs on the UI thread, which costs battery, flash wear and causes jank.
(c) Hostile: an insider sends 199 loc frames per 10 s, or 10k tombstones. Every member then does 20 full rewrites per second, or 20k rewrites of a growing file.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Use per-entry or append-only persistence (SQLite, or a WAL with compaction).
- Apply a whole snapshot with one model write plus one replay write.
- Keep presence counters in memory with debounced persistence, or in a tiny separate file.
- Do all persistence off the main thread.
findings.proving_test:
Android: inject persistOverride on SyncReplayState and a counting persistence on WaypointStore.
- Apply a 1,000-record snapshot and assert O(1) writes. Today: ~2,001 replay writes and 1,000 store writes.
- Feed 10 accepted loc frames and assert ≤1 replay write. Today: 10.

iOS: inject the persistenceWriter closures and count writes the same way.

findings.title: One member can exhaust the room-wide quota permanently; tombstones and actor pins are never freed and the room never expires
findings.description:
Quotas exist only per room: MAX_RECORDS 10k and 50 MB (index.ts:19-20), enforced atomically at 1196-1204 and 1136-1140. There is no per-actor or per-session quota.

Nothing is ever freed:
- Tombstones (deletedAt is written but never read) and actor pins are never garbage-collected.
- Idle expiry (834-847) never fires while any client keeps reconnecting (touchActivity 689).
- An insider can mint any number of actors, since each new keypair's hello creates a durable actor record.

Once the room is full:
- Every new put gets a non-retryable nack 'quota' (1200-1203).
- A new device's hello closes with 4013 (1000-1004). The existing test at relay.test.ts:1128 shows this, so a new device never reaches CONNECTED.
- Android keeps resending unsynced objects on every local change, because applyDeliveryNack leaves lastContent stale. With more than 200 unsynced objects, each resend trips the relay's 4008 limit.

Fill rate from one socket: 4 MiB per 10 s fills 50 MB in about 2.5 min; 200 msgs per 10 s reaches 10k records in about 8 min. Parallel actors are faster.
findings.failure_scenario:
An insider sends 72 puts of ~700 KB, or 10k tiny tombstones or new actors. From then on nobody can create or grow objects, new team members cannot join (endless 4013/reconnect loop), and the room cannot be recovered short of a new join code.

Benign version: heavy create/delete churn reaches 10k tombstones over months, with the same result.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Add per-actor record and byte quotas.
- Limit actor-pin creation per connection/IP, and GC pins with no records and no live session after N days.
- Compact tombstones behind a relay-published horizon that clients honour.
- Add an authenticated room reset.
- Do not count failed joins as activity.
findings.proving_test:
Relay vitest:
1. Preload 72 × 699,996-char records for actor A with runInDurableObject.
2. Actor B sends a put: expect op-nack 'quota'.
3. A new actor C sends hello: expect close 4013.
4. Assert nothing in storage ever decreases meta:totalRecords after deletes.

The existing relay.test.ts:1128 already demonstrates step 3.

findings.title: Chat replay fence table (max 256) is never pruned; once full, messages from any new session are silently dropped for good
findings.description:
Both chat stores keep one durable replay fence per (actor, session domain, chat key). They refuse the 257th rather than evicting any: Android TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:212-215 (cap at 449), iOS TacMapChatStore.swift:58 and 359-362.

Session domain and chat key are new on every connection (Android SyncManager.kt:1065; iOS 1617). So every peer reconnect that sends at least one message uses up a fence.

Once the table is full, every message from a new session returns REPLAY_REJECTED and is dropped without notice (Android SyncManager.kt:2492; iOS 3721-3722). The sender's UI meanwhile shows ROUTED, from the relay's chat-ack.

Pruning superseded sessions would be safe, because an old session can never become active again:
- hello epochs are durably monotonic (Android SyncReplayState.kt:275-276; iOS acceptHello);
- chat is accepted only for the current activeSessions entry (Android 2412-2417; iOS 3677-3682).
findings.failure_scenario:
12-person unit whose phones flap or background, giving ~2 chatting sessions per person per day. After roughly 11 days, all inbound chat from reconnected peers vanishes on every device, with no error shown on either side.

Hostile version: an insider runs 256 reconnect-plus-one-message cycles (~5 min under CONN_LIMITER 60/min) and disables chat reception for every member.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Keep fences only for each actor's current authenticated session; drop a fence once a newer hello epoch is committed for that actor.
- Alternatively, evict fences of inactive sessions whose epoch is below the actor's durable epoch.
- Show a visible issue if a message is ever rejected for capacity.
findings.proving_test:
Android TacMapChatHistoryStore unit test: call acceptInbound for 256 distinct (actor, session, kid) triples. Then send from actor #1 under a new session, after committing a newer hello epoch for it.
- Today: returns REPLAY_REJECTED.
- Expected: ACCEPTED, with the stale fence pruned.

iOS TacMapChatStore XCTest equivalent.

findings.title: Chat history is capped at 2 MiB but pruned only by message count; once over the cap every chat write fails for good
findings.description:
History has two limits: 500 messages and 2 MiB encoded (Android TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:441-442 and 381-384; iOS TacMapChatStore.swift:120-121 and 445-447). Retention only prunes by count (Android 231 takeLast(500); iOS 467-473).

Why the byte limit is reachable:
- Bodies may be 4,096 UTF-8 bytes, limited only by the 8 KB plaintext cap.
- Control characters, quotes and backslashes JSON-escape to 2-6 bytes; iOS JSONEncoder also escapes '/' as '\/'.
- Android keeps 64 fingerprints per fence (~3 KB) for up to 256 fences, about 0.8 MB in the same file.

Once the encoded document is over 2 MiB, every persist fails:
- Android: acceptInbound returns STORE_UNAVAILABLE, which calls clearChatTransport (SyncManager.kt:2493-2496). append, markRead and updateDelivery all fail too.
- iOS: historyTooLarge is thrown, which calls clearChatSessionSecrets (3724-3727).

Neither store has a clear-history path, so it never recovers.
findings.failure_scenario:
An insider sends ~260 room messages, each with ~4,000 '"' or '/' characters (~8 KB encoded; ~15 s at 200 per 10 s). Every member's chat file then exceeds 2 MiB and chat is permanently broken for the room on all devices.

Benign version: ~470 maximum-length ASCII messages, or fewer on Android with many fences.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Prune the oldest messages by encoded bytes (e.g. down to 1.5 MiB) before persisting.
- Give fences their own budget and reduce the fingerprints kept per fence.
- Add a user-facing 'clear chat history' recovery action.
findings.proving_test:
Android unit test: acceptInbound 300 messages whose body is '"'.repeat(4000).
- Today: around message 260 it returns STORE_UNAVAILABLE and all later appends fail.
- Expected: the oldest messages are pruned and all are accepted.

iOS XCTest with '/'-heavy bodies: today acceptInbound throws historyTooLarge.

findings.title: An exception during the join snapshot resets the whole Durable Object and disconnects every member
findings.description:
ensureV3Accounting and sendSnapshot run inside blockConcurrencyWhile (index.ts:673 and 688). Cloudflare's documentation says a throw inside that callback terminates and resets the object. The surrounding try/catch intended to return 503 (690-694) therefore never works as a graceful path.

sendSnapshot throws in two cases:
- Deterministically, when the first v2 page, which also carries `members` (1498), plus the first record exceeds 900 KB (1514-1516).
- On any storage get/list error.

Proven in workerd: after 25 v2 members with ~8 KB presence and one 700 KB record with id '!' (which sorts first), the 26th join rejects with {durableObjectReset:true} (brokennessReason broken.inputGateBroken), and all 26 existing sockets close with 1006.
findings.failure_scenario: In a legacy v2 room, one member with 25 sockets and a large first record can disconnect everyone on every later join. In v3, a single transient storage error while one phone joins drops all connected members at once and causes a reconnect storm.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Never let the callback throw: return a result object instead.
- Build the snapshot inside blockConcurrencyWhile, but send it and handle errors outside it.
- For v2, send `members` in its own frame or include it in the ceiling calculation.
findings.proving_test: scratchpad/sync-s4/test/s4v2.test.ts (passes today). It demonstrates the durableObjectReset and 1006 closes on every existing socket.

findings.title: Snapshot chunking re-serializes the whole pending page for every record while blocking the room
findings.description:
For each record, sendSnapshot builds `candidate=[...chunk, record]` and then JSON.stringifies and UTF-8-encodes the entire payload (index.ts:1512-1519). Each 900 KB page therefore costs O(k²) work, about 450 KB of stringify per record. This runs inside blockConcurrencyWhile on every connect and reconnect, so the whole room is blocked meanwhile.

Measured in workerd (s4.test.ts S4-03):

| records | current | with a running byte counter |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 93 ms | 4 ms |
| 10,000 | 1,172 ms | 21 ms |

That is a 56× difference. The Node replica (audit-sync/snapshot_bench.mjs) stringifies 4.4 GB for 10k records.

All snapshot frames are also buffered before the 101 response is returned; I did not measure the memory impact at the 50 MB cap.
findings.failure_scenario: After a relay deploy or eviction, 30 members of a 10k-record room reconnect together. That is 30 serialized ~1.2-3 s blocks, during which no put, presence or chat is processed and iOS upgrade requests queue toward their 60 s timeout. The stall adds to the reconnect storms from S4-02.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Keep a running byte total per page (utf8Length(JSON.stringify(record))+1 per item plus the envelope), as in the tested patch.
- Consider seq-based delta snapshots so reconnects don't resend everything.
findings.proving_test: scratchpad/sync-s4/test/s4.test.ts 'S4-03' prints the timings. Re-run it with the patched loop (audit-sync/index.orig.ts is the original) to see 1,172 ms drop to 21 ms at 10k records.

findings.title: Sockets that never send hello hold room slots indefinitely, so the 64-socket room fills up
findings.description:
MAX_CONNECTIONS=64 counts every accepted socket (index.ts:18 and 680), including v3 sockets that never send hello.

There is no handshake deadline; the alarm only handles idle expiry (834-847). Hibernation makes idle sockets free to hold. compatibility_date 2025-09-01 predates web_socket_auto_reply_to_close, so sockets closed by the server can also linger in getWebSockets() in the CLOSING state.

Clients treat the resulting 503 as transient and retry indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario:
A holder of the join code opens 64 idle sockets (~1 min at CONN_LIMITER 60/min), and no honest member can join while they stay open.

Benign version: phones that drop partway through a large snapshot on poor networks leave half-open pre-hello sockets that use up slots.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Record acceptedAt in the socket attachment and close pre-hello sockets older than ~30 s, both when near capacity and from the alarm.
- Reserve slots for authenticated sessions.
- Cap sockets per IP per room.
- Consider a compatibility date of 2026-04-07 or later so server-closed sockets leave the CLOSING state quickly.
findings.proving_test: scratchpad/sync-s4/test/s4.test.ts 'S4-05' (passes today): 64 idle v3 sockets, and the 65th join gets 503 'Room full'.

findings.title: Every handled frame, including rejected ones, triggers a durable storage write
findings.description:
processWebSocketMessage calls touchActivity after every put/del/loc/hello/leave/chat-key/chat frame, whatever the outcome (index.ts:805). touchActivity does storage.put('meta:lastActivity') plus getAlarm (1564-1568).

This includes frames rejected for missing hello, bad shape or counter replay. Anyone can create a room (v2: any token of 20+ characters; v3: a self-generated token), so the write cost can be driven by an outsider. Legitimate presence also costs one write per frame.

Proven: 190 rejected frames from an unauthenticated socket caused 190 storage.put calls.
findings.failure_scenario:
An attacker opens ~60 sockets per minute per IP into their own room and sends 20 junk loc frames per second on each. That is ~1,200 SQLite writes per second per Durable Object (~100M per day), which the relay operator pays for.

Even legitimately, 30 members × 1 presence per 5 s is 6 writes per second per active room, indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix:
- Touch activity only on accepted durable mutations and hello.
- Throttle the write in memory to once every few minutes; the TTL is 7 days, so precision does not matter.

findings.title: malicious_frames.json is v2-only and neither platform's test runs frames through the real message handler

verdicts.reasoning:
Root cause: the relay accepts any v3 put whose kind matches [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,32} and whose ct is canonical base64 of at least 28 bytes (sync/src/index.ts:1163-1165, isValidCiphertext 243-249). It also stores a rid-bearing delete for an id that never existed (1191). Every later snapshot then serves that record (1506-1522).

Android: parseOuterV3 rejects any kind other than waypoint/drawing (SyncManager.kt:2536). validateRecordV3 returns null on AEAD, signature, invalidSkipped or wire-id mismatch (2549-2596). The snapshot handler sets snapshotInvalid (1921-1928). snapshot-end then calls failSnapshot, which calls failConnection (1941-1943, 3643-3665). handleSocketEnded still reconnects with backoff (1011-1028), and backoff only resets at hello-ack (2236), so the loop never ends.

iOS: finishSnapshotV3 calls failClosedV3 on the first invalid record (SyncManager.swift:3467-3474), and failClosedV3 sets wantConnected=false (2563). The identityCollision path is real too: SyncRemoteModelApplier throws at 486-493, and both the snapshot (3496-3499) and live (3806-3809) catch blocks call failClosedV3. The tombstone divergence is also real: iOS rejects a delete whose inner JSON has "c" (3925), and Android never checks for it (2553-2565).

The relay half passes in my copy (s4.test.ts S4-01).

Downgraded from critical because there is no benign trigger in the current code. Both clients emit only waypoint/drawing, and honest tombstones carry only pub+sig (Android 1362/1721, iOS 2146/2382). Triggering it today needs a join-code holder, and the threat model (THREAT_MODEL.md section 7) treats room membership as the trust boundary. Version skew, such as a future kind or stricter importer, is a design time bomb, not a present defect. The effect is still a permanent room brick: Android loops re-downloading the snapshot, and iOS sync stays off. The only recovery is a new join code. High.

The client aggregate live budget is 200 frames / 4 MiB per fixed 10 s window (Android SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:88-106, iOS SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:111-114). It counts every inbound frame, including op-acks and presence. On overflow the client closes with 1008 (Android SyncManager.kt:1779-1794 and 1822-1835; iOS 1703-1750).

The relay limits each sender to the same 200 per 10 s (index.ts:27-28, allow() 862-878) but has no aggregate fan-out limit (broadcast 1556-1562). The re-run S4-02 test delivered 199 junk-ct loc frames from one socket to a receiver within 3 s, so one insider sending about 20 frames/s keeps every other member cycling through 1008 and reconnect.

Benign trigger: syncLocalStateV3 sends every diff in one loop, and nothing caps in-flight sends (Android 1304-1336, iOS 2271-2312). Joining a room while holding more than about 200 local objects, or importing a large KML, therefore gets the sender 4008'd, and in rooms of 3 or more members pushes receivers over 200.

The benign case converges after one full-room reconnect and snapshot re-download. The 'storm feeds itself' claim is overstated: after a reconnect the LIVE window resets per generation, and roughly 4 frames per reconnecting peer stays under 200. The insider variant is sustained. High.

For every delete, validateRecordV3 calls findLocalIdForWireId (Android SyncManager.kt:2563; iOS 3930). That function recomputes the HMAC wire id over lastContent, then all waypoints, then all drawings (Android 2961-2977, iOS 4173-4196). It stops only on a match, so a tombstone for an object the device no longer holds (the normal case) costs about 2L HMACs.

Every snapshot record is re-validated on every connect, and a new snapshot is required on every foreground return. Android's wireObjectId calls Mac.getInstance and init per call (SyncIdentity.kt:55-61). The handler runs on Dispatchers.Main.immediate (SyncManager.kt:180-181). SyncInboundCallbackGate waits 10 s, then failSlowConsumer closes the socket (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:43-58, 132, 253-259, 323-329).

I re-ran WireScan: 2M HMACs took 2,059 ms and 1.9M took 1,941 ms on desktop JVM (about 1 us each). A phone page of about 1,900 tombstones with L of 500-1,000 is therefore plausibly over 10 s, which gives an ANR plus a reconnect loop.

The iOS 'tens of seconds' figure is probably exaggerated because CryptoKit HMAC is faster, but a multi-second freeze at snapshot-end is real. High, driven mainly by Android.

On Android, every persistTransaction copies all 9 maps (SyncReplayState.kt:94-122). It then calls save(), which rewrites the whole sealed file with fsync and an atomic rename (478-482; SafeStore.kt:139-156).

This runs on each of these paths:
- commitPresence, once per accepted loc frame (305-315, called from SyncManager.kt:2894).
- commitRemoteAuthenticated (148-159).
- clearPendingModelApplication (429-433), once per record during snapshot-end resolution (SyncManager.kt:1953-1957 → 2662-2675).

applyValidatedV3 → upsertWaypoint → WaypointStore.commit → persistCandidate encodes and writes the whole list for each record (WaypointStore.kt:258-270).

iOS mirrors this. acceptPresence (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195) and clearPendingModelApplication (298-304) each persist the full document.

First-join apply of N new objects is therefore about N² bytes of sealed, fsynced writes on the main thread. At N=1,000 that is roughly 0.7 GB plus 2,000 fsyncs, which is tens of seconds of main-thread work (ANR). Steady-state presence rewrites the whole replay file for every peer frame.

One nuance: the loop is synchronous, so a socket killed by the 10 s gate does not interrupt the apply. It completes, and the next reconnect sees NONE decisions, so data still converges. The harm is freeze, battery use and flash wear, not loss. High (major waste plus ANR on joining a mature room).

Quotas exist only per room: MAX_RECORDS=10,000 and 50 MB (index.ts:19-20). They are enforced in the put/del transaction (1196-1204) and in registerActor (1136-1140). A new actor pin adds a record, and when the room is full it closes with 4013 (1000-1004). The existing relay.test.ts:1128 demonstrates this.

Tombstones are kept for the room's lifetime (README:28-30), and no code path deletes obj: or actor: keys or decrements totalRecords.

The idle-expiry alarm returns early while any socket is connected and is re-armed by every touchActivity (index.ts:834-847, 689, 805).

Byte usage can be reclaimed if honest members delete large valid objects. The record count cannot: tombstones and actor pins stay forever.

Insider fill time: 200 msgs/10 s gives 10k records in about 8 min. Benign fill: long-lived rooms with create/delete churn reach 10k lifetime ids eventually. After that, new objects get a non-retryable 'quota' nack (Android SyncManager.kt:2052) and new devices can never join. Recovery requires a new join code. High.

Both stores cap replay fences at 256 per room and refuse a new identity instead of evicting one (Android TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:212-215, constant at 449; iOS TacMapChatStore.swift:58, 359-362). The fence key is (actor, sessionDomain, chatKeyId) (Android 191-193; iOS replayKey). Nothing prunes the replay list: it is only assigned from load or persist (Android 355/374/389).

The session domain is regenerated on every connect (Android SyncManager.kt:1065-1066; iOS 1617), and so is the chat key. A new snapshot and connect happens on every foreground return. So each reconnect of a peer that sends even one message uses up one fence on every receiver.

Once the table is full, the 257th session's messages return REPLAY_REJECTED. Android drops them silently (SyncManager.kt:2492) and iOS does the same (3721-3722), while the sender got a chat-ack/ROUTED from the relay (index.ts:1400-1406).

Pruning is safe. Chat is accepted only from the current activeSessions sd and chat key (Android 2411-2416), and hello epochs are durably monotonic, so a superseded session can never be accepted again.

A normal unit using one room for a couple of weeks reaches 256 sessions. High.

The mechanism is real. Android persistAndPublish refuses to write when the encoded envelope exceeds 2 MiB (TacMapChatHistoryStore.kt:381-384, 442), and iOS throws historyTooLarge (TacMapChatStore.swift:445-447). Retention prunes only by count (Android 231 takeLast(500); iOS 467-473). Neither store has a clear or delete API (function list: open, close, lock, append, updateDelivery, acceptInbound, markRead).

Once the history is near the cap with fewer than 500 messages, every append fails. Android gets STORE_UNAVAILABLE and calls clearChatTransport (SyncManager.kt:2493-2496). iOS clears the session secrets (3724-3727). Nothing ever frees space, so chat stays permanently broken for that room on that device.

Downgraded from high. The only realistic trigger is a hostile insider sending about 250 escape-heavy messages near the 4,096-byte body limit (TacMapChatModels.kt:72-79). The payload escaping is bounded by the 8,192-byte plaintext cap. The benign trigger needs an average encoded message size of about 4.2 KB across 500 messages, which normal chat never approaches. Android's 64 fingerprints × 256 fences (~0.75 MB) narrows the margin but still needs large messages. Map sync is unaffected. Medium.

ensureV3Accounting and sendSnapshot run inside blockConcurrencyWhile (index.ts:673, 688). Cloudflare's documentation (DO State API) says a throw inside that callback terminates and resets the object, so the surrounding try/catch returning 503 never runs as a graceful path.

sendSnapshot throws deterministically when the first v2 page's `members` plus the first record exceeds 900 KB (1498, 1514-1516). Re-running s4v2.test.ts in my copy shows the effect: after 25 joins the 26th gets {durableObjectReset:true} with inputGateBroken, and all 25 existing sockets close with 1006.

It is limited:
- The v2 path cannot be hit benignly. Honest presence is a few hundred bytes, and the maximum record is 700 KB.
- The v3 path only fires on storage read errors inside the callback. Those are rare, and the object is then likely reset anyway.
- The reset also closes the attacker's 25 presence sockets, so each attempt must be rebuilt (it can be repeated about every 30 s under CONN_LIMITER).

Medium is fair.

For every record, sendSnapshot builds candidate=[...chunk, record] and JSON.stringifies and UTF-8-encodes the whole page (index.ts:1512-1519). That is O(k²) per 900 KB page, and it runs inside blockConcurrencyWhile, which blocks the room.

Re-run in my copy: 1,000 records took 93 ms and 10,000 took 1,166 ms. I then patched the loop to use a running byte counter (utf8Length(JSON.stringify(record))+1 plus the envelope). The same test dropped to 4 ms and 26 ms. That confirms the root cause is the repeated stringify, not storage.list.

The cost is paid on every connect or reconnect, so reconnect storms serialize multi-second stalls in large rooms. It is a meaningful inefficiency and room stall but not a correctness bug. Medium.

The capacity check counts every accepted socket (index.ts:18, 680), and nothing closes pre-hello sockets. The alarm only handles idle expiry (834-847), and there is no acceptedAt field in the attachment.

Re-running S4-05 in my copy: 64 idle v3 sockets made the 65th join get 503 'Room full'. The compat-date sub-claim checks out against Cloudflare's docs: web_socket_auto_reply_to_close became the default at 2026-04-07, while sync/wrangler.jsonc pins 2025-09-01, so server-closed sockets can linger in CLOSING inside getWebSockets().

The attack needs the join-code token (an insider). The benign half-open accumulation is plausible but unproven. Medium.

processWebSocketMessage awaits touchActivity after every recognized frame type, whatever the handler did (index.ts:795-805). The handlers return normally on rejection, for example handlePresenceV3 when there is no hello (1417-1420) or applyChangeV3 with 'hello-required'. touchActivity does storage.put('meta:lastActivity') plus getAlarm (1564-1568).

Re-run in my copy: 190 rejected frames caused 190 storage.put calls. On SQLite-backed Durable Objects every put is a billed row write, which costs roughly 100 times more than the WebSocket message itself. Legitimate presence also pays one write per frame.

The 'outsider' framing is a little loose. An outsider can only reach this in a room it created itself (ROOM_LIMITER 10/min/IP). The amplification is still real and throttling the write is trivial. Medium.

testdata/malicious_frames.json has 25 cases, all v2-shaped (numeric v, clientId loc, v2 snapshot with members). None are v3 (hello, stamped put/del, the snapshot fence, chat, chat-key, leave).

SyncMaliciousFrameTest.kt:57-81 re-implements strictVersion with kotlinx and never drives SyncManager. The iOS SyncMaliciousFrameTests.swift likewise only exercises JSON parsing and strict integer helpers.

It is a real coverage gap, and the shared corpus would not catch S4-01, S4-03, S4-06 or S4-07. It is not a runtime defect. Low.

verify.missed:
1) The relay's room-wide pending limit disconnects an innocent member (sync/src/index.ts:744-751). When roomPendingMessages reaches 512 or roomPendingBytes would exceed 8 MiB, the relay closes whichever socket's frame arrives next with 4008. That socket is usually not the one filling the queue. I confirmed this with a deterministic test in the scratch copy (verify-S4-adversarial-robustness/test/skeptic.test.ts): with roomPendingMessages=512 injected, an honest socket's ping closed it with 4008. I could not reproduce the saturation itself locally: 4 insiders sending 199 puts each, and 3 insiders sending 4 × 700 KB puts, both kept up. So an insider may be able to force honest members off during crypto-heavy bursts, but that is not proven. Suggested fix: when the room is saturated, close the socket with the largest pending count, or drop the frame, instead of closing the arriving sender. Severity: medium at most.

2) Android does an HMAC per object on every local edit (SyncManager.kt:1310-1314). syncLocalStateV3 computes the HMAC wire id for every current object, with Mac.getInstance per call, before it checks lastContent. So every local model change costs O(L) HMACs on the main thread even when only one object changed. This adds to S4-03. Low.

3) The S4-03 iOS impact is probably overstated. CryptoKit HMAC is several times faster than Android's per-call Mac.getInstance, so expect a multi-second freeze at snapshot-end, not tens of seconds.

4) S4-04 converges despite the socket drop. When the 10 s gate kills the socket during snapshot-end, the synchronous apply loop still finishes. The next connect sees NONE decisions, so the damage is freezes and ANRs, flash wear and battery use, not data loss.

audit.summary:
How it works, end to end. Each client (Android SyncManager on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, iOS @MainActor SyncManager) derives the room keys once at join with 210k-iteration PBKDF2 and caches them for reconnects. It then opens a hibernatable WebSocket to the SyncRoom Durable Object and receives a full, byte-chunked snapshot. sendSnapshot runs inside blockConcurrencyWhile, and the client verifies every record (AES-GCM, Ed25519, GeoJSON parse/export, wire-id HMAC) before sending a signed hello. In the foreground, presence goes out every 5 s. With the screen off, an opted-in session sends at the chosen 1-60 min interval on the same socket. Outbound edits are diffed from store emissions (250 ms debounce), their stamps are reserved durably, and they are sent with a request id (rid). The relay commits a storage transaction, serialises the broadcast JSON once for all sockets, acks, and the client retransmits at 1/2/4/8 s. For inbound presence the client decrypts, verifies 3 signatures, persists the counter in the sealed replay-state file, then publishes to the UI.

Solid:
- Relay broadcast and chat routing serialise each frame only once (index.ts:1556-1562, 1314-1339).
- Both clients use RFC 6455 control-frame pings (Java-WebSocket connectionLostTimeout=20; URLSessionWebSocketTask.sendPing). Cloudflare answers these without waking or billing the DO, and no client sends the app-level {t:"ping"}.
- The alarm runs only every 7 days, and per-socket state lives in attachments, not storage.
- PBKDF2 is not re-run on reconnect.
- Android background GPS uses GPS_PROVIDER with minTime equal to the chosen interval and takes no wake locks. iOS screen-off location uses 100 m accuracy with a 50 m filter.
- Chat history is bounded.

Main problems:
- Write amplification: every inbound presence frame, and every record applied, rewrites and fsyncs the full replay file.
- Quadratic algorithms: the relay snapshot chunker, the client wire-id reverse lookup, and iOS's undebounced full re-hash.
- The relay writes one storage row per frame, which exhausts the Workers Free write quota.
- No delta snapshots.
- Background sockets remain full subscribers.
- No outbound pacing against the 200-frame budgets.
- Retransmission is timer-based and ignores the send queue.
- Stationary devices send every 5 s, and each presence frame is ~1.5 KB.
- iOS redraws the whole map on every presence frame.

Measured, in a scratch copy of the relay under vitest-pool-workers (scratchpad/sync-s5/test/s5.test.ts):
- 50 presence frames → 50 storage.put calls.
- 250-put burst → closed with 4008 after 199 acks; the peer received 199 puts in 116 ms.
- 10k-record snapshot → 936 ms to the 101 response, vs 35 ms with a linear chunker.

Measured with desktop-JVM/node scripts (scratchpad/audit-sync):
- Reverse lookup at 2k objects × 2k tombstones → 8.2 s.
- Presence frame → 1,465 B.

No findings require changing the wire format except S5-06b, S5-07(1) and S5-11. Those are version-gated so the store clients already shipped keep working.

findings.title: Every inbound presence frame reseals and fsyncs the ENTIRE replay-state file on the main thread
findings.description:
Android: applyPresenceV3 calls replay.commitPresence (SyncManager.kt:2894). That goes through persistTransaction (SyncReplayState.kt:112-122), which first copies all 7 maps via memorySnapshot (94-98). save() (478-487) then encodes the WHOLE state (every stamp, tombstone, content hash, actor, epoch, presenceSeq and pending record; 576-596). stateFile() re-derives the HMAC file name and runs about 15 path/symlink syscalls (459-475; SyncIdentity.kt:285-305). Finally SafeStore.writeAtomically decrypts the sentinel, seals the whole file with AES-GCM, writes a tmp file, calls fd.sync() and does an ATOMIC_MOVE (SafeStore.kt:75-80, 139-156). All of this runs on the main dispatcher (SyncManager.kt:180-182, 963-985).

iOS is identical. applyPresenceV3 calls rs.acceptPresence (SyncManager.swift:4127), which calls persist() (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195, 488-492). That serialises the full state with sortedKeys (578-594), then SafeStore.write runs. SealedMigrationPolicy.markSealed does a Keychain SecItemCopyMatching plus a decrypt on EVERY write (SafeStore.swift:32-44, 60-73). Everything is @MainActor.

ADR-001 §8 (lines 328-333) only requires the counter to be durable before the peer is shown. Only presenceSeq changes (1.3-8 KiB), yet the whole room history is rewritten each time. The same amplification applies to every other replay transaction: each outbound put (reserveLocalPut) and each inbound put (commitRemoteAuthenticated plus clearPendingModelApplication, i.e. 2 full writes).

Quantified with scratchpad/audit-sync/replay_size.mjs (~220 B of state per object or tombstone):
- 1,000 objects + 500 tombstones, 10 peers at 5 s: 326 KiB × 1.8 frames/s = 587 KiB/s = 2.2 GB/h of sealed, fsync'd writes.
- 3,000 + 2,000, 30 peers: 6.3 MB/s (23 GB/h).
- 64 peers, 10k records: 27 MB/s.
findings.failure_scenario:
A 30-member company room has 5,000 records and everyone shares location in the foreground. Each Android device must seal and fsync about 1 MB roughly 6 times per second on the main thread. The main thread saturates: the map freezes, an ANR is likely, and the reader thread applies backpressure. iOS hangs the same way.

Even a 10-person room with 1k objects writes about 17 GB to flash over an 8-hour operation, with the matching CPU and battery drain.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Split presenceSeq/sessionDomains (and hello epochs) into a separate, tiny sealed per-room file written by commitPresence/acceptPresence. This keeps ADR 'persist before expose' semantics exactly and cuts bytes per frame by more than 99% (326 KiB → ~1.3 KiB).
2. Do the replay I/O on a serial background executor. Await it before publishing peers, so the ordering does not change.
3. Cache the resolved file URL per room. On iOS, cache the already-marked SealedMigrationPolicy identifiers in memory so the Keychain is not hit on every write.
4. Optional, and only with an ADR amendment: coalesce counter persistence to at most one write per ~5 s. Trade-off: after a crash, a hostile relay could replay a signed position up to 5 s old within the same session.

Local-only; no wire change.
findings.proving_test:
Android JVM:
1. Create `SyncReplayState(roomId, filesDir = null, persistOverride = { saves++; true })`, call load(), commitActorHello(actor, pub, sd, "0000000000000001"), then reserveLocalPut ×1000 to grow the state.
2. Reset the counter and call commitPresence for counters 1..100.
3. Assert saves == 100. With a temp filesDir and a test keyProvider, also assert each write is ≥ ~220 KB.

iOS XCTest:
1. Create `SyncReplayState(roomId:…, persistenceWriter: { d, _, _ in sizes.append(d.count) })`, acceptHello, then 1,000 commits.
2. Call acceptPresence ×100.
3. Assert sizes.count == 100 and that every entry is roughly the full state size.

Reproduce the numbers with `node scratchpad/audit-sync/replay_size.mjs`.

findings.title: Snapshot validation does an O(tombstones × objects) HMAC reverse lookup on every reconnect; Android exceeds its 10 s consumer gate and never converges
findings.description:
For every tombstone in a snapshot, validateRecordV3 calls findLocalIdForWireId (Android SyncManager.kt:2552-2564 → 2961-2977; iOS SyncManager.swift:3924-3931 → 4173-4196). That recomputes the HMAC wireObjectId for every lastContent key, then every waypoint, then every drawing. On Android each call also does Mac.getInstance plus init (SyncIdentity.kt:55-61).

A tombstone for an object already deleted locally never matches, so it always costs 2N HMACs. lastContent is not cleared on a v3 reconnect (Android connect 1062-1074; iOS 1611-1637).

Tombstones are kept for the room's lifetime (MAX_RECORDS 10,000) and are re-sent in EVERY snapshot (see S5-06), so this cost repeats on every network flap and every foreground return. The relay packs about 1,700 tombstones (~530 B each) into one 900 KB page (index.ts:1512-1519).

Android validates each page inside one main-thread callback (SyncManager.kt:1911-1932). The reader thread fails the socket if a frame is not consumed within 10 s (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:132, 46-58, 253-259, 323-329). iOS validates the whole snapshot in one @MainActor pass (3469-3478), with no gate.

Measured with scratchpad/audit-sync/WireIdBench.java on a desktop JVM (1.02 µs per HMAC):
- 500 objects × 500 tombstones: 0.55 s
- 2,000 × 500: 2.1 s
- 2,000 × 2,000: 8.2 s

ART on mid-range ARM is expected to be several times slower (not measured on a device).
findings.failure_scenario:
An Android device in a room with ~2,000 live objects and ~1,700 historic deletions reconnects after a network flap.
1. Validating the first tombstone-heavy page takes more than 10 s, so failSlowConsumer closes the socket.
2. After backoff it reconnects and receives the same page.
3. Validation is not cached, so it fails the same way.

The device never reaches CONNECTED again (non-convergence), with continuous jank or ANRs. Every iOS foreground return hangs the UI for seconds.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Build a HashMap<wireId, localId> once per snapshot, and maintain it incrementally on local create/delete. That is N HMACs instead of T×2N: about 4k instead of 8M at 2k/2k.
2. On Android, reuse a single Mac instance per metadata key.
3. Before any lookup or crypto, short-circuit a tombstone that is already an exact persisted tombstone (same wireId and stamp in replay state).

Local-only and wire-compatible.
findings.proving_test:
Android JVM, using the SyncManagerLiveSessionTest harness:
1. Seed 2,000 waypoints.
2. Deliver snapshot-begin, then one snapshot page containing 1,700 validly signed v3 tombstones for absent wire ids.
3. Time handleMessage and count wireObjectId calls. Today: ~6.8M calls and more than 10 s on device. Assert under 1 s after the fix.

Quick reproduction: `cd scratchpad/audit-sync && java WireIdBench 2000 2000` → 8,000,000 HMACs, 8.2 s.

iOS: run the same fixture through handleParsedMessageV3 and wrap finishSnapshotV3 in XCTest measure().

findings.title: First-join and bulk apply/publish are O(N²): per-record full-file rewrites, and on iOS an undebounced full-model re-hash on every store mutation
findings.description:
When a snapshot is applied, every new record takes the APPLY_INCOMING path.

Android, per record, in ONE main-thread callback (SyncManager.kt:1936-1972, 2657-2667):
- applyValidatedV3 → waypointStore.add or drawingStore.addFeature. For waypoints, add rewrites the whole list through persistCandidate (WaypointStore.kt:75-78, 258-266).
- replay.clearPendingModelApplication does a full replay save (SyncReplayState.kt:429-433).
- reexport (3005-3020) and upsertWaypoint's any{} (2992-3002) each scan the full store linearly.

iOS, per record:
- SyncRemoteModelApplier.apply → addDurably writes the full list (SyncManager.swift:477-517; WaypointStore.swift:338-341).
- rs.clearPendingModelApplication persists (SyncReplayState.swift:298-303).
- Every @Published store mutation also fires observeModelRevisions (SyncManager.swift:2013-2056), which is NOT debounced. It calls modelHashes, i.e. GeoJSON export plus SHA-256 of EVERY object (2058-2071), before checking resolvingPendingModel.

Outbound bulk work has the same problem. On first join with an existing local map, on an import, or when replaying an offline backlog, each put reserves its stamp with a full replay save (Android SyncReplayState.kt:324-340; iOS SyncReplayState.swift:199-225). Android syncLocalStateV3 also hashes and HMACs every object before checking lastContent, on every store emission (SyncManager.kt:1310-1316).

Estimated scale:
- Replay writes ≈ 110·N² bytes; N=2,000 → ~440 MB, plus a similar amount for the model stores and ~4,000 fsyncs.
- iOS, N=1,000 → about 10⁶ single-object GeoJSON exports.
findings.failure_scenario:
A user joins a room that already holds 2,000 objects.
- Android blocks the main thread for tens of seconds and shows an ANR. The 10 s gate kills the socket, so a second full snapshot follows.
- iOS hangs.

This repeats whenever a peer bulk-imports a KML/GPX file, and whenever a user joins with a large existing local map.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Apply snapshot and bulk records in batches: one addAll/commit per store (WaypointStore.addAll already exists, WaypointStore.kt:81-95) and one replay commit that clears all verified pending markers. The ADR order still holds per batch: persist pending → apply → verify hash → clear.
2. Batch the reservation of outbound stamps the same way.
3. iOS: debounce observeModelRevisions, skip it while resolvingPendingModel, and only hash objects whose value actually changed.
4. Android: check lastContent before computing SHA-256/HMAC.

This turns O(N²) into O(N): at N=2,000, roughly 1 GB of writes becomes ~1 MB. No wire change.
findings.proving_test:
Android JVM:
1. Give SyncReplayState a counting persistOverride.
2. Call commitRemoteSnapshot with 500 remotes, then clearPendingModelApplication once per record, as snapshot-end does.
3. Assert saves == 501.
4. Separately, give WaypointStore a counting persistence writer and apply 500 remote adds: 500 full-list writes.

iOS XCTest: count calls to modelHashes (or to GeoJSONExporter.export) while applying a 300-record snapshot through finishSnapshotV3. Expect about 300 × 300 exports today.

findings.title: Relay snapshot chunking is O(n²) and runs inside blockConcurrencyWhile on every connect
findings.description:
sendSnapshot builds `candidate = [...chunk, record]` for every record, then JSON.stringify()s and TextEncoder-encodes the whole growing page (index.ts:1512-1519). That is quadratic within each 900 KB page. It runs inside blockConcurrencyWhile (index.ts:688), so while it runs, frames from every other peer in the room are held back.

Measured with vitest-pool-workers in scratchpad/sync-s5/test/s5.test.ts, time until the 101 response:

| Records (1 KB ct) | Current | Linear chunker patch |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 77 ms | 5 ms |
| 6,000 | 529 ms | 21 ms |
| 10,000 | 936 ms | 35 ms |

The patch produces the same 17 frames and 13,170,660 bytes. A node replica (scratchpad/audit-sync/snapshot_bench.mjs) stringifies 4.4 GB for one 10k-record snapshot, versus 13 MB when linear.

This runs on every connect, and connects happen on every flap and every foreground return (S5-06). Backoff is 1 s ±20% jitter (SyncReconnectBackoff.kt:16-32), so after a relay deploy or DO eviction all members reconnect together and the DO serialises 64 × ~0.94 s ≈ 60 s of blocked CPU. Meanwhile the clients' handshake timers (Android V3_HANDSHAKE_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT_MS 20 s; iOS handshakeTimeout 30 s) expire, and their retries queue even more snapshot work.
findings.failure_scenario: A relay deploy hits a 64-member room with 10k records. The room stalls for about a minute or more: presence and puts from connected peers are held, clients time out and retry, and duration is billed for all of it. On a slower host this approaches the 30 s blockConcurrencyWhile limit, whose reset drops every socket.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Serialise each record once, keep a running byte count plus a fixed envelope margin, and build each page by joining the pre-serialised record strings. This is 27× faster at 10k records and wire-identical apart from page boundaries. See the patch applied in scratchpad/sync-s5.
2. Clients: use full-jitter backoff (a random delay between 0 and the cap) so reconnect herds spread out.
3. Optional: keep only the seq/highWater fence reads inside blockConcurrencyWhile and stream the pages outside it, relying on seq fencing.
findings.proving_test: scratchpad/sync-s5/test/s5.test.ts, test "S5 snapshot: connect latency with N stored records": it seeds N records via runInDurableObject and times stub.fetch until the 101. Result: 936 ms at 10k on the current code, 35 ms with the linear patch. Add the assertion `< 100 ms` to the repo test.

findings.title: The relay writes a storage row for every presence/chat frame; Workers Free's 100k rows/day then runs out and every socket is closed
findings.description:
processWebSocketMessage awaits touchActivity() after every handled frame type, including loc, chat and chat-key (index.ts:792-805). fetch also calls it after every snapshot (689). touchActivity is storage.put("meta:lastActivity") plus getAlarm (1564-1568).

For SQLite-backed DOs each KV put is billed as one row written. Presence and chat are otherwise storage-free, yet each frame now costs a row. Proved: 50 presence frames → 50 storage.put + 50 getAlarm (s5.test.ts "S5 presence"). A v3 put costs 5-6 rows: obj, totalRecords, bytes, seq, highWater (1206-1210) plus lastActivity.

lastActivity is only read by alarm() when no socket is connected (834-847), and webSocketClose already refreshes it when the last socket leaves (825-827). Per-frame writes buy nothing.

wrangler.jsonc advertises Workers Free for self-hosters. That plan allows 100,000 rows written per day, account-wide, and "further operations fail with an error". When the storage write fails:
- processWebSocketMessage catches it and closes the socket with 1011 (806-809), even though the presence had already been broadcast.
- New connections fail with 503 "Snapshot unavailable" (690-693).

10 members sharing location at 5 s = 7,200 rows/h: the quota is gone in 13.9 h. 20 members: 6.9 h. 64 members: 2.2 h. On Paid it is pure waste: ~1.7M rows per room-month (10 users, 8 h/day) on top of 5-6 rows per put.
findings.failure_scenario:
A 12-person unit self-hosts on Workers Free and starts sharing location at 06:00 UTC. Around 17:30 UTC:
- Every frame from every member closes that member's socket (1011).
- Every reconnect gets a 503.
- Every room on the account stays down until 00:00 UTC.

If the official relay is on the Free plan, the same limit is shared by all users worldwide.
findings.suggested_fix:
All relay-only and wire-compatible:
1. Throttle touchActivity with an in-memory timestamp: persist at most once per hour and whenever the last socket closes.
2. Cache in memory whether an alarm is already set, and never call touchActivity for loc/chat/chat-key.
3. Make it best-effort with its own try/catch; a failed activity marker must never close a socket or fail a connect.
4. Optional: fold totalRecords/bytes/seq/highWater into one meta key (5 → 2 rows per put; needs a one-time read of the old keys).

Result: ~0 rows for presence and chat, and ~1 row per hour per room.
findings.proving_test:
scratchpad/sync-s5/test/s5.test.ts, test "S5 presence: every relayed presence frame performs a durable storage write": it wraps state.storage.put and asserts puts === 50 for 50 loc frames. After the fix, expect ≤ 1.

Add a second test: make storage.put throw, then assert that presence is still broadcast to a second socket and the sender is not closed with 1011.

findings.title: Every connect downloads and re-verifies the whole room (no since-seq delta); triggered by every flap and every foreground return
findings.description:
sendSnapshot always lists every obj: row (index.ts:1507-1523). Clients persist lastSnapshotSeq (Android SyncReplayState.kt:55, 177) but never send it.

Connects happen on:
- every flap (Android handleSocketEnded 987-1031; iOS handleDisconnect);
- every foreground return (iOS updateLifecycle 992-993 → reconnectForForegroundReconciliation 1833-1853; Android prepareForForegroundUnlock/attachForegroundStores 468-501 → connect);
- every rate-limit close (S5-08).

Each connect costs:
- At the relay: N rows read (the Free plan allows 5M/day).
- On the wire: ~1.3 KB per record (13.17 MB for 10k records, measured).
- On the client: AES-GCM, an Ed25519 verify (BouncyCastle 45 µs on a desktop JVM), GeoJSON parse/export/SHA and an HMAC for EVERY record, even when nothing changed. S5-02 and S5-03 come on top.
findings.failure_scenario: A room with 10k records. A user on cellular opens the app about 30 times a day and downloads ~400 MB/day, doing about 30 full re-verifications. A link that flaps every few minutes multiplies this.
findings.suggested_fix:
(a) Local-only, can ship now: after authenticating a record, persist SHA-256(ct) together with vs/pub/sd/kind per wireId. When a snapshot record is byte-identical, treat it as an exact persisted mutation and skip the AES, Ed25519 and GeoJSON work. This saves nearly all client CPU per reconnect, with no wire change.

(b) Version-gated delta:
- The relay stores seq in each record. Shipped parsers ignore extra fields (Android parseOuterV3 2513-2541; iOS validateRecordV3 3895-3915).
- The relay honours an optional `X-Since-Seq` header and answers `snapshot-begin{seq, since}` with only the records where seq > since.
- It falls back to a full snapshot if since > meta:seq (room expired) or if records lack seq.
- Old relays ignore the header, so clients must keep accepting full snapshots. Old clients never send it.
- Clients must treat a delta as non-exhaustive: skip the 'omitted by snapshot' reconciliation (SyncManager.kt:2707-2721).
- This needs an ADR-001 amendment: omission in a delta is equivalent to a dropped live broadcast.

Savings: a reconnect after <1 min offline goes from 13 MB to a few KB, and relay rows read go from N to Δ.
findings.proving_test:
Relay vitest:
1. Seed 10k records and connect; drain the snapshot.
2. Reconnect with nothing changed.
3. Assert the second snapshot's bytes equal the first (13,170,660), which is the current behaviour.

Android: count SyncSigning.verify calls across two consecutive snapshots of an unchanged room. Expect 2N today; after fix (a), expect N.

findings.title: Screen-off 'presence-only' sessions remain full broadcast subscribers with a 20 s keepalive, so the radio never idles
findings.description:
Android enterBackgroundPresenceOnly keeps the v3 socket open (SyncManager.kt:387-417). handleMessage still receives each frame, UTF-8 encodes it and charges it to the budget, and only then drops it (1770-1798). iOS likewise keeps reading and discarding (SyncManager.swift:1715-1728). Both keep a 20 s keepalive (SyncWebSocketTransport.kt:133, 285; SyncManager.swift:657, 1885-1896).

The relay has no per-socket opt-out and broadcasts every loc/put/del/chat/hello/leave to every socket (index.ts:1556-1562).

A 10-member room pushes ~2 discarded frames/s, about 9.7 MB/h (scratchpad/audit-sync/presence_size.mjs); a 64-member room pushes ~68 MB/h. Using a typical LTE model (~10 s RRC tail; estimate, not measured on a device), the pings alone keep the modem in connected state ~50% of the time, and peer traffic keeps it there ~100%, although the user chose 'every 15 minutes'.

Those discarded frames also count toward the 200-frames/10 s budget. A peer burst (S5-08) closes the background socket, and it is never reopened while the phone is locked (backgroundTransportEnded, SyncManager.kt:1029-1031), so background sharing stops silently.
findings.failure_scenario: A 10-person patrol spends 4 hours screen-off at the 15-minute interval. Each phone receives ~39 MB and ~29k frames it throws away, and battery drain approaches foreground levels. If any peer imports a map, background sharing silently stops until the phone is unlocked.
findings.suggested_fix:
(1) Version-gated relay 'quiet' frame, e.g. `{"t":"quiet","q":1}`, v3 only:
- A new relay flags the attachment and skips that socket in broadcast()/routeChat for loc/put/del/chat/chat-key/hello/leave, while still sending acks/nacks to it.
- Old relays drop unknown `t` values (index.ts:804), so a new client simply gets today's behaviour.
- Foreground return already forces a fresh snapshot, so no state is missed.

(2) In presence-only mode, raise the keepalive to ~55-90 s: Java-WebSocket setConnectionLostTimeout at runtime, and heartbeatInterval on iOS. The Cloudflare idle timeout is about 100 s. Keep 20 s in the foreground.

(3) Do not charge frames to the live budget while in background mode.

Savings: ~100% of background downlink, and pings drop from 180/h to 40-65/h.
findings.proving_test:
Relay vitest:
1. Open socket A (standing in for the background client) and socket B.
2. B sends 20 loc frames; A receives 20 today.
3. After the fix, A sends quiet first and receives 0, while B still gets its own acks.

Android: an instrumented test puts SyncManager into backgroundPresenceOnly and counts frames admitted by liveReceiveBudget while a peer publishes presence.

findings.title: No outbound pacing: publishing more than 199 objects trips the relay limit (4008) and every receiver's live budget (1008), causing room-wide reconnect storms
findings.description:
syncLocalStateV3 sends every changed object back to back (Android SyncManager.kt:1304-1336 via queueDelivery 1157-1163; iOS 2271-2314 via 2213-2219). This happens on first join with an existing map, on KML/GPX import, on an offline backlog, and on forcedLocalDiff after a reconnect.

The relay closes a socket at 200 frames or 4 MiB per 10 s, and drops everything still queued (index.ts:744-751, 862-878).

Proved in s5.test.ts "S5 burst": 250 puts → close 4008 after 199 acks and 199 stored objects. A second peer received 199 put broadcasts in 116 ms.

Every client's LIVE receive budget is also 200 frames / 4 MiB per 10 s (Android SyncInboundFramePolicy.kt:59-106; iOS SyncInboundFramePolicy.swift:106-150). Those 199 broadcasts plus any other frame in the same window make every other member close with 1008 (Android rejectInboundFrame 1822-1835; iOS 1734-1751). The whole room then reconnects and downloads full snapshots (S5-04/S5-06). Then the sender reconnects and pushes the next ~199.

In a 64-member room, presence alone is 126 frames/10 s, so two members editing at once can trip it.
findings.failure_scenario: A member imports 800 waypoints. That produces 4 cycles of the sender being closed with 4008 and every other member being closed with 1008. Each cycle costs every member a full snapshot download and re-verification plus a 'disconnected' error, and background members lose their session until unlock.
findings.suggested_fix:
Client-only and wire-compatible:
1. Add one outbound token bucket per socket, e.g. ≤12 frames/s and ≤2.5 MiB per 10 s, covering presence, chat and retries.
2. Queue puts/dels behind it with a window of about 32 unacked operations, released as op-acks arrive; let presence and chat jump the queue.
3. Scale the live receive budget with room fan-in (for example per sender actor, or 200 × min(peers, 8)), keeping the byte ceiling.

Later, optionally, a version-gated batched `puts` frame on the relay.
findings.proving_test:
1. Run scratchpad/sync-s5/test/s5.test.ts "S5 burst": it logs close=4008 acks=199 storedObjects=199 peerBReceivedPuts=199 within 116ms.
2. Android JVM: SyncLiveReceiveBudget().admit(gen, 100, LIVE, t) returns true 200 times and false on the 201st.
3. After the fix: a harness test that imports 500 waypoints against the relay should finish with no socket closes on either peer.

findings.title: Fixed 1/2/4/8 s retransmission ignores send-queue drain: large objects on slow links are uploaded up to 5× and the watchdog then kills the socket, indefinitely
findings.description:
queueDelivery enqueues the frame and starts the retry clock at the same moment (Android 1157-1187; iOS 2213-2248). Both Java-WebSocket and URLSession sends are asynchronous.

Retries resend the identical full frame at t = 1, 3, 7 and 15 s (maxAttempts 5: OutboundDeliveryTracker.kt:133, 175-188). At t = 23 s the watchdog cancels the socket (Android 1175-1181; iOS 2228-2238).

On a 64 kbit/s link, a 200 KB drawing (for example a 1,000-vertex freehand route) needs ~25 s just for the first copy. Four more copies (800 KB) queue behind it, and the relay runs a 'duplicate' storage transaction for each. The first ack arrives after the 23 s cancel. After reconnecting, forcedLocalDiff resends the object (1189-1205) and the same thing happens again.
findings.failure_scenario: On a satellite, EDGE or congested tactical link, any object whose frame is larger than ~150-180 KB can never be confirmed. The device reconnects every ~25 s and downloads a full snapshot each time (S5-06), burning bandwidth and battery indefinitely.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Start the ack timer only once the frame has drained from the socket: Android can use Java-WebSocket's outQueue/onWebsocketWrite; iOS can use the send completion handler.
2. Make the ack timeout proportional to size, e.g. 10 s + bytes / measured uplink.
3. Never re-enqueue a rid that is still queued.
4. Treat 'still draining' as progress, not as a watchdog failure.

Wire-compatible; the relay already de-duplicates exact records.
findings.proving_test:
Android JVM: give SyncManager a fake SyncWebSocket whose send() accepts frames but delivers acks 25 s later. Assert that 5 sends share the same rid and cancel() fires at ~23 s (today), and that after the fix there is 1 send and no cancel.

iOS: the same using a stub URLSessionWebSocketTask.

Relay: send one put 5 times and count storage.transaction calls (5).

findings.title: Stationary devices re-send identical presence every 5 s
findings.failure_scenario: A TOC, observation post or parked vehicle with 10 members, mostly stationary, generates 7,200 frames/h and fans them out to everyone, although the positions do not change.
findings.proving_test:
UnitSyncPresenceCadenceTest: feed 60 fixes at 1 s intervals with identical lat/lon and count isSendDue == true. Today: 12. Expect 3 with a 20 s heartbeat.

iOS: the same using UnitSyncPresenceCadence and stubbed CLLocations.

findings.title: A v3 presence frame is ~1,465 B for ~50 B of position: payload sent twice, three signatures, static identity repeated every time
findings.description:
sendPresenceV3 (Android SyncManager.kt:3209-3287; iOS 2468-2553, makePresenceEnvelope 2628-2645) builds the envelope wastefully:
- The 9 fields appear twice: flat, and again as base64 'p'.
- pub appears both inside and outside the ciphertext.
- It carries 3 separate Ed25519 signatures (payload, accuracy, retention), each with its own base64 payload.
- The whole envelope is AES-GCM sealed and then base64'd (+33%).
- callsign, affiliation, echelon, function and isHQ are resent every 5 s.

Measured with scratchpad/audit-sync/presence_size.mjs: signed payload 202 B, inner envelope 889 B, ct 1,224 chars, frame 1,465 B. Dropping only the flat duplicates and the inner pub gives ~1,127 B (−23%).

Per frame, the sender does 3 signs (BouncyCastle 33 µs each on a desktop JVM) and every receiver does 3 verifies (45 µs each).

Per device at 5 s this is 1.08 MB/h up; in a 64-member room, 68 MB/h down.
findings.failure_scenario: A 30-member room on cellular downloads ~31 MB/h per device of presence alone, most of it redundant encoding.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Once the fleet's minimum supported version reads 'p' (pv:1, which the README already describes as the authoritative field), stop sending the flat duplicate fields. Gate this on a minimum-version policy: legacy v3 receivers that ignore pv need the flat fields.
2. Define pv:2: one signature over a compact binary payload (lat/lon as int32 × 1e-7°, heading/speed/accuracy as int16, plus ttl), with static identity sent only when it changes or every ~60 s. Estimated ~400-500 B per frame (−65%), and 1 sign/verify instead of 3.

Because presence is broadcast and a sender cannot tailor frames per receiver, pv:2 can only be sent once every store client in the room can parse it. Receivers must ship first, followed by a sender gate or forced upgrade.
findings.proving_test: Fixture test: build a frame with PresencePayloadV3.encode plus PresenceAccuracyV3/PresenceRetentionV3 exactly as sendPresenceV3 does. Assert the frame is ~1,465 B and that SyncSigning.sign is called 3 times per sendPresenceV3. To reproduce: `node scratchpad/audit-sync/presence_size.mjs`.

findings.title: On iOS every inbound presence frame re-renders the root view and fully redraws every map drawing
findings.description:
ContentView owns SyncManager as a @StateObject (ContentView.swift:514) and passes syncManager.peers into TileMapContainer (755).

applyPresenceV3 assigns 3 @Published properties per frame:
- peers (SyncManager.swift:4134);
- onlineMembers (4155), even when unchanged;
- chatRecipients, via refreshChatRecipients (4165, 1566-1581).

Each assignment re-evaluates ContentView.body and runs TileMapContainer.updateUIView (TileMapContainer.swift:102-139). That rebuilds the vector shapes, decorations and edit handles for every drawing and calls DrawingsOverlayView.update(shapes:). update unconditionally calls setNeedsDisplay, so every drawing is redrawn full-screen with Core Graphics (DrawingsOverlayView.swift:67-97).

With 63 peers this is ~12.6 full redraws per second while the map is idle.

Android reads presence at MapScreen scope (MapScreen.kt:350, 902). StateFlow equality and Compose skipping limit the fan-out there; not verified in detail.
findings.failure_scenario: An iPhone showing a map with a few hundred drawings in a 20-member room redraws the whole overlay ~4 times per second even while nobody touches it. That is continuous CPU/GPU load and battery drain.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Move presence into a separate ObservableObject observed only by PresenceOverlayView, or push peers straight into the coordinator.
2. Publish onlineMembers and chatRecipients only when their values change.
3. In updateOverlays, fingerprint the drawing inputs and call setNeedsDisplay only when the shapes actually changed.
findings.proving_test: Add a DEBUG counter in DrawingsOverlayView.draw(_:). In a UI test, open an idle map with 200 drawings while a stub peer injects presence every 1 s for 60 s. Today: ~60 draws. Expect 0 after the fix.

findings.title: PBKDF2 (210k iterations) runs synchronously on the UI thread at join
findings.description:
Android: join() calls SyncCrypto.deriveRoomV3 (SyncManager.kt:668; SyncCrypto.kt:119-126) from the SyncDialog onClick (SyncDialog.kt:274, 530), i.e. on the main thread.

iOS: join calls deriveRoomV3 (SyncManager.swift:1197; SyncCrypto.swift:97-115) on the @MainActor, from SyncSheet (286, 314).

Reconnects reuse the cached authToken/room keys and do not re-derive, which is good. 210k HMAC-SHA256 iterations take ~0.1-0.3 s on current phones and up to ~1 s on low-end Android, so there is a single UI freeze per join.
findings.failure_scenario: On a low-end Android device, tapping Join freezes the UI for about 1 s.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive on Dispatchers.Default or in a detached Task, then hop back to the main thread to commit the result; show progress while it runs. No wire impact.
findings.proving_test: Enable StrictMode, or time join() on the main thread on a low-end device. Expect ≥ 300 ms spent inside SyncCrypto.masterV3.

verdicts.reasoning:
Root cause confirmed. Every accepted v3 presence frame rewrites the whole replay document before the peer is published. Android: applyPresenceV3 calls replay.commitPresence (SyncManager.kt:2894) → persistTransaction (SyncReplayState.kt:112-122), which first copies 7 maps via memorySnapshot (94-98). save() (478-487) then encodes every stamp, tombstone, hash, actor, epoch, session and pending record (576-596). SafeStore.writeAtomically seals the result and writes tmp + fd.sync() + ATOMIC_MOVE (SafeStore.kt:75-80, 139-156). It runs on Dispatchers.Main.immediate (SyncManager.kt:181), dispatched through dispatchSocketCallback (963-985). iOS: acceptPresence (SyncReplayState.swift:188-195) → persist (488-492) → a full sortedKeys JSONSerialization (578-594) → SafeStore.write, with a Keychain SecItemCopyMatching in markSealed on every write (SafeStore.swift:32-44, 60-73). The ~220 B per record figure checks out: stamps entry ~109 B plus hash or tombstone entry ~110 B. The same full rewrite happens for reserveLocalPut/Delete, commitRemoteAuthenticated and each clearPendingModelApplication.

Corrections:
- iOS writes with Data.write(.atomic) and has no fsync (SafeStore.swift:254-255), so the fsync cost applies to Android only.
- 'Main thread saturates / ANR likely' is overstated at the headline sizes.
